documents/agriculture-policy-2025-2026.m.text:
# Agriculture Policy (Green Party policy document)

<!-- page 1 -->

Agriculture Policy
The Green Party will support all parts of the agricultural sector to look after our environment so
that it sustains our communities and builds our resilience to multiple impacts, including climate
and market instability. This policy shows that everyone in Aotearoa New Zealand can eat good
food that is more affordable for our local consumers and gets a fair price for our food and fibre
producers. Our sustainable agricultural practices will create products that are in high demand
globally. Farmers will be supported to keep innovating and improving, and good data collection
will ensure that agencies provide real-time feedback to inform that progress.

Vision
The agricultural sector upholds the mana of the land, people, and animals.

Values and Principles
Agriculture policy must be guided by the following values and principles:
- Kawanatanga: Governance of the agricultural sector recognises the unique expertise and
rights of Māori. Māori participation in shaping the future of agriculture is equitable.

- Tiakina te taiao, tiakina te iwi e: The agricultural sector protects our diverse ecosystems
to sustain our communities using a precautionary approach for future generations.
Mātauranga Māori guides our agricultural practices and environmental standards.

- Ka mua, ka muri: The agricultural sector recognises its impact on climate change and
commits to reduced emissions.

- Te Rāngai aumangea: The agricultural sector is supported to adapt to a changing
environment, including the land and weather patterns.

- Te Rāngai tōnui: The agricultural sector is supported to be financially viable. This viability
includes ecological health and egalitarian human systems.

- Tauutuutu: Agriculture depends on relationships. Where these relationships have been
undermined or damaged, they must be repaired.

- Tiaki kararehe: Farm animals are sentient beings deserving of our care and protection.

Strategic Priorities
The Green Party’s strategic goals include:
Our nation will lead the world in sequestering carbon through ecologically sound means.

“...regenerative practices in all areas of economic activity, including land use and food
production, will predominate.”

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Agriculture Policy --- Reviewed: 2025 --- Version: 09 March 2026

1

<!-- page 2 -->

“Aotearoa will be in transition, creating green work and broad prosperity while moving
Aotearoa away from carbon-dependent, extractive and resource-intensive industries.”
Actions in this policy that will help achieve this include:
- Implement the recommendations of the Waitangi Tribunal to ensure that governance of
the agricultural sector upholds Te Tiriti o Waitangi. (1.2)

- Establish an Agricultural Standards Framework that includes… sustainability standards
for all food and fibre sectors. (2.1.3)

- Incentivise low greenhouse gas agricultural initiatives. (3.3)

- Strengthen the collective resilience of grassroots community collaborations such as local
catchment groups. (4.4)

- Provide startup funding for innovative systems and/or new food and fibre trials. (5.1)

- Resource a Māori-led authority that oversees the distribution of start-up funding to Māori
agricultural initiatives that are locally led and sustainable. (6.3)

Connected Policies
Agriculture is an important Business and Food-producing activity that is shaped by the
Government in the Economy. It is important for Rural Communities, Animal Welfare, and Trade
and Foreign Investment. It is interconnected with and key to safeguarding the natural world,
including Climate Change, Land Use and Soils, and Freshwater. A range of risks, including exotic
organisms and emerging technologies, are addressed in our Biodiversity and Environmental
Regeneration Policy, and Research, Science and Technology Policy. Also related are our policies
on Forestry and Marine aquaculture.

Policy Positions
1.

Kawanatanga | Governance

Our Vision
Māori have full access to their own land, which they have resettled and regenerated. They enjoy
economic prosperity and have rangatiratanga over mahinga kai. The agriculture sector and
regional councils work in partnership with local iwi and hapū in decisions that affect the land,
and their expertise is respected.

Actions
1.1.

Fund mana whenua to provide culturally appropriate support and guidance to local
groups relevant to agriculture, such as catchment groups.

1.2.

Implement the recommendations of the Waitangi Tribunal to ensure that governance
of the agricultural sector upholds Te Tiriti o Waitangi.

1.3.

Support Māori to address barriers found in banking, tax, company and co-operative
laws that prevent te ao Māori principles from being applied to the production of food
and fibre and/or Māori land use and development.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Agriculture Policy --- Reviewed: 2025 --- Version: 09 March 2026

2

<!-- page 3 -->

2.

Tiakina te taiao, tiakina te iwi e | Look after our environment so that it sustains our
communities

Our Vision
Aotearoa New Zealand is known for its premium-quality and environmentally sustainable
products. Our native flora and fauna are thriving, and land, soil, and water ecosystems are healthy
and valued. Our food and fibre supports the health of both people and the environment.

Actions
2.1.

3.

Establish an Agricultural Standards Framework that includes:
2.1.1.

Requirements to measure all agricultural inputs and outputs;

2.1.2.

Robust and consistent measures of environmental impacts caused by
agriculture;

2.1.3.

Sustainability standards for all food and fibre sectors; and

2.1.4.

Incentives and other support to farmers to continuously improve ecosystems on
productive land.

2.2.

Prohibit palm kernel expeller (PKE) imports.

2.3.

Impose nitrogen caps on all agricultural practices and prohibit the production of
nitrogenous fertilisers from fossil fuels

2.4.

Phase out most grazing concessions on public conservation land and require
sustainable farm plans for active concessions.

2.5.

Support farmers in sensitive ecosystems to work collaboratively to protect indigenous
biodiversity.

Ka mua, ka muri | Look to our past practices, to inform the future

Our Vision
The agricultural sector has achieved a significant cut in gross emissions. The sector works
together as a whole to maintain this. All agricultural businesses are proud of their positive
contribution to clean air and a safe climate.

Actions
3.1.

Require the agriculture sector to provide data that enables greenhouse gas emissions
to be measured.

3.2.

Reduce agricultural emissions in Aotearoa New Zealand by:

3.3.

3.2.1.

Adjusting stocking rates according to the holding capacity of the land;

3.2.2.

Protecting existing wetlands and encouraging wetland restoration;

3.2.3.

Phasing out the use of fossil fuels for agricultural processes; and

3.2.4.

Phasing out synthetic nitrogen fertilisers.

Incentivise low greenhouse gas agricultural initiatives.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Agriculture Policy --- Reviewed: 2025 --- Version: 09 March 2026

3

<!-- page 4 -->

4.

Te rāngai aumangea | A resilient sector

Our Vision
The agricultural sector is resilient, diversified, and agile in the face of changing weather patterns,
markets, and consumer demands. The sector maintains its focus on sustainable and ethical
agriculture, and in the development and processing of crops and technologies to support that
focus.

Actions

5.

4.1.

Require imported foods to meet our own national growing and production
requirements.

4.2.

Support a transition to agroecological practices (such as regenerative and organic
approaches).

4.3.

Encourage the preservation and growing of heritage seeds for personal use as well as
commercial production.

4.4.

Strengthen the collective resilience of grassroots community collaborations such as
local catchment groups.

Te rāngai tōnui | A thriving sector

Our Vision
Agriculture is collaborative and farmers produce high quality products for good prices.
Community Supported Agriculture and farmers’ markets are thriving. Communities benefit from
local and seasonal food production that is nutritious, safe, fresh, and affordable. Our sustainable
agricultural practices create products that are in high demand globally. Agriculture is an
accessible and desirable career path for youth.

Actions

6.

5.1.

Provide startup funding for innovative systems and/or new food and fibre trials.

5.2.

Fund ongoing research to explore sustainable agricultural livelihoods that require
fewer energy, time, and cost inputs.

5.3.

Resource innovative projects that address the food and fibre needs of local
communities.

Tauutuutu | Reciprocity and honouring traditional practices

Our Vision
Mātauranga Māori is well recognised, and tangata whenua are supported to grow, forage, hunt
for, and exchange their products of the land. The mana of the people, their healthy food, and
their land are sustained through adapting traditional practices to a modern world.

Actions
6.1.

Prioritise iwi-based initiatives in the management and restoration of retired and/or
degraded agricultural land.

6.2.

Fund research and development that supports hapū and iwi Māori agribusiness.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Agriculture Policy --- Reviewed: 2025 --- Version: 09 March 2026

4

<!-- page 5 -->

7.

6.3.

Resource a Māori-led authority that oversees the distribution of start-up funding to
Māori agricultural initiatives that are locally led and sustainable.

6.4.

Protect and enhance the cultural, spiritual, historical, and other values of agricultural
land.

Tiaki kararehe | Caring for animals

Our Vision
The agricultural sector consistently uses an ethical and humane approach to managing animals.
Our approach is world-leading, and animals enjoy the highest animal welfare standards, with
their death managed as humanely as possible. Welfare standards are properly enforced and the
need for prosecution is rare.

Actions
7.1.

Ban the importation of animals and animal products when living conditions in their
country of origin have not met Aotearoa New Zealand’s animal welfare standards.

7.2.

Resource animal welfare inspectors and prosecutors to fully uphold the Animal
Welfare Act.

7.3.

Address the requirements of the Global Animal Protection Index to improve animal
welfare.

7.4.

Prohibit new, and phase out existing factory farming of animals, including highly
intensive outdoor facilities such as feedlots.

7.5.

Adopt fit-for-purpose animal-centric transport standards, specific to species and age.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Agriculture Policy --- Reviewed: 2025 --- Version: 09 March 2026

5

documents/ai-policy-2026-safe-sovereign-.title: Safe, sovereign AI — An AI Plan for Aotearoa
documents/ai-policy-2026-safe-sovereign-.text:
# Safe, sovereign AI — An AI Plan for Aotearoa

<!-- page 1 -->

Safe,
sovereign AI
An AI Plan for Aotearoa
Auth by M Ross, greens.org.nz

<!-- page 2 -->

AI policy 2026

AI regulation is needed to protect New Zealanders’
creativity, data and jobs and ensure that the benefits
of AI are shared and not captured by the massive
technology companies running the AI sector.
The Green Party will make sure the right
AI protections are in place.

The growing pressures to adopt
and embrace AI are unprecedented,
but AI is not a force of nature that we
have to surrender to. Government
has a role to safeguard the interests
of our creatives, our workers, our
environment, and the New
Zealand public.

This growing bubble presents risks
to jobs and economic stability.

New Zealanders are understandably
cautious about AI. The Green Party
shares this caution. When AI is
used thoughtfully and with
well-designed safeguards there
can be legitimate benefits, but the
rapid and unregulated explosion of
AI technologies presents significant
risks across our society and our
economy.

The best way to protect us, our
economy, and our sovereignty
from an uncertain future is to ensure
that AI is regulated properly. We
should and will implement the right
safeguards, before it’s too late to
put it back in the box.

We don’t have to surrender control
of our data, our privacy and the
things we create to massive overseas
tech companies that don’t support
the public interest.

The enormous investments
being made in AI are cause for
concern. Trillions of dollars have
been invested in new AI tools, and
companies cannot hope to see the
returns they expect.

greens.org.nz

01

<!-- page 3 -->

AI policy 2026

AI must serve people, not replace
human judgement or democratic
decision-making
Artificial intelligence should support human judgement, not
replace it. Decisions that affect people’s rights, welfare, health,
education, employment, or access to public services must remain
subject to meaningful human oversight and appeal.

Policy implications
• No fully automated decisions
for anything that could make a
substantive difference to people’s
lives in any public services. Humans
managing AI tools must be able to
make decisions with integrity and
appropriate workloads.
• People are accountable and will be
held accountable for AI decisions.

• Everyone has a right to challenge
AI-assisted decisions, and to opt
out of being subject to AI assisted
decision- making.
• New Zealand should refuse to
purchase or deploy autonomous
weapons systems and support
an international ban on these, in
the same way the international
community has banned chemical
and biological weapons.

• Require public registers of AI systems
used by government agencies – full
transparency around AI use, including
where in policy processes it has been
used, and where or how it has been
used to inform decisions.

greens.org.nz

02

<!-- page 4 -->

AI policy 2026

Data is a taonga: protect
data sovereignty and
community consent
The raw material of AI is data. New Zealanders, iwi, hapū,
communities, and creators should retain meaningful control over
how data about them is used. Language in particular is crucial to
identity and culture, and must be protected.

Policy implications
• Explicit consent standards for AI
training data.
• Appropriate remuneration for any
IP used for training AI models, and
genuinely deterrent fines for breaches.

• Strengthen the ability of the Privacy
Commissioner to enforce our privacy
laws, including codes relating to
biometric processing and facial
recognition technology, and introduce
penalties for serious privacy breaches.

• Strong protection of Māori data
sovereignty – specific regulation
requiring co-governance and codevelopment of Māori data and IP.
• Transparency regarding datasets used
by government AI systems.
• Neither people’s private information
which they have entrusted to
the government, nor classified
government data, shall be sent to third
parties, particularly for model training
or inference. Onshoring public data
should be prioritised.

greens.org.nz

03

<!-- page 5 -->

AI policy 2026

AI must operate within
environmental limits
AI is not a virtual technology. It consumes large amounts of electricity,
water, land, and materials. New infrastructure should only proceed
where environmental and community benefits are clear.

Policy implications
• Mandatory environmental impact
assessments for hyperscale AI data
centres.
• New AI facilities must provide new
renewable generation to cover full
energy use rather than competing for
existing electricity supply.
• Water-use limits and public reporting
requirements.
• Community consultation and local
consent requirements.
• A pause on consenting new hyperscale
data centres until the regulatory
framework is established.

greens.org.nz

04

<!-- page 6 -->

AI policy 2026

Ensure AI benefits are shared,
not concentrated
AI is creating unprecedented concentrations of economic power,
as well as enormous risks to the stability of the financial system.
Government should ensure gains benefit workers and communities
rather than being captured by global tech giants, and that the risks
are not socialised.

Policy implications
• Strong enforcement of tax law,
including application of withholding
tax rules so tech companies do not
offshore their profits.
• Update and pass the Fair Digital
News Bargaining Bill to ensure that
AI companies pay local media outlets
for data used in their AI summaries.
• Copyright and licensing protections
– in the first instance enforcing
current ones but look to develop
more if required.
• Use public-interest and open-source
alternatives wherever these are
available and viable.

• Worker participation in decisions
about workplace AI adoption.
• Children should not be forced to use
AI, particularly at school, and protect
the rights of children in line with the
UNCRC’s Joint Statement on Artificial
Intelligence and the Rights of the
Child.
• Collaborate globally with like-minded
countries to align AI regulation
and governance, establishing New
Zealand as a moral leader, building on
our work on the Christchurch Call.
• Government will encourage research
towards the development of Aotearoa
based and focused LLMs to avoid
dependence on foreign vendors.

• Prevent vendor lock-in by mandating
multiple and interchangeable AI
providers when using third-party
models.

greens.org.nz

05

<!-- page 7 -->

AI policy 2026

Require transparent, trustworthy,
and accountable AI
People have a right to know when they are interacting with
AI and how it is being used.

Policy implications
• Labelling requirements for
AI-generated content.
• Establish an AI office, in the first
instance sitting within DPMC, and
looking over time to establish an
independent AI Commission with
appropriate powers to conduct
assurance, audits, and education.
• Algorithm audits for high-risk systems
– public oversight of some algorithms
through the AI regulator.
• Align and cooperate with international
best practice, including key aspects
of the EU AI Act, around disclosure
requirements, labelling requirements,
and audits of AI systems.

greens.org.nz

06

<!-- page 8 -->

www.greens.org.nz

Authorised by M Ross, greens.org.nz

documents/animal-welfare-2025-2026.md.title: Animal Welfare Policy (Green Party policy document)
documents/animal-welfare-2025-2026.md.text:
# Animal Welfare Policy (Green Party policy document)

<!-- page 1 -->

Animal Welfare Policy
The Green Party will align regulation with animals’ rights to good nutrition, environment, health,
behaviour, and mental state, and provide strong oversight and accountability. We will minimise
the systemic exploitation of animals and require an ethical and humane approach to managing
animals. We will carefully balance the needs of indigenous species and introduced animals, and
uphold the Kaitiaki role and whakapapa connections of Māori to animals.

Vision
All animals are respected and their rights are upheld.

Values and Principles
- Aroha: All living things possess an inherent dignity and mauri. Animals are due respect,
love, and rights. Humans have a duty of care towards the animals they interact with. They
should not be violated or exploited, and their distress and pain should be minimised.

- Whanaungatanga: All living things are interconnected. We should live in reciprocal
relationships with animals. The deep, ancestral connection Māori have with the land and
its inhabitants must be respected.

- Tikanga: Societal systems, cultural practices, and traditional knowledge shape and are
shaped by our relationship with animals. Engagement with companion animals is a
privilege, not a right.

- Kaitiakitanga: Humans must interact with other animals in ways that support resilience
and ecosystem health. Indigenous species and ecosystems are essential for maintaining
supporting ecological balance so [they] must be paramount, with their interests prioritised
over invasive species.

- Mōhiotanga: Humans have an ethical obligation to make informed decisions on behalf of
animals, drawing on the best available knowledge of their needs and behaviours. Tikanga
and mātauranga Māori must be upheld alongside the evolutionary history and ecology of
animals.

Strategic Priorities
The Green Party’s strategic goals include:

“Our laws and practices will respect the biological integrity of all life, while prioritising the
health of indigenous species and ecosystems.”
Actions in this policy that work towards this goal include:
- Establish a Department of Animal Welfare, led by a Minister for Animal Welfare, with
responsibility for legislation, enforcement, hosting the NAWAC and NAEAC, and
advocating for the welfare of all animals. (1.5)

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Animal Welfare Policy --- Reviewed: 2025 --- Version: 09 March 2026

1

<!-- page 2 -->

- Require people who breed companion animals for sale, and rescue centres, to register and
hold a current license. (2.1)

- Develop local regulations around pet ownership to cater for the indigenous species
residing in that locale, such as requiring catios to keep cats safe and protect local
biodiversity. (5.1)

- Introduce national standards for desexing dogs and for registering, desexing, and
microchipping cats. (5.3)

Policy Positions
1.

Mōhiotanga:

Our Vision
Legal systems uphold an animal's right to a life worth living by recognising and promoting the 5
domains of animal welfare: positive nutrition, environment, health, behaviour, and mental state.
Animal welfare enforcement agencies and organisations are well supported through sufficient
funding and appropriate resources.

Actions

2.

1.1.

Ensure that the Animal Welfare Act 1999 and other related legislation are fit for
purpose, evidence-based, and enforced.

1.2.

Amend the Social Security Act 2018 to include companion animals in household need
assessments and financial assistance levels.

1.3.

Align Codes of Welfare with primary animal welfare legislation.

1.4.

Develop codes of welfare for home kills and support animals.

1.5.

Establish a Department of Animal Welfare, led by a Minister for Animal Welfare, with
responsibility for legislation, enforcement, hosting the NAWAC and NAEAC, and
advocating for the welfare of all animals.

1.6.

Establish a Parliamentary Commissioner of Animal Justice, and resourcing it to
monitor, investigate and make recommendations on animal welfare issues.

1.7.

Ensure central government adequately supports and funds local government to
uphold, monitor, and enforce local Animal Welfare bylaws.

Aroha

Our Vision
Animal breeders and rescue centres are well regulated, resourced, and supported to ensure
animals under their care thrive. Proper protection, education, and support are available for people
and animals in a companion relationship to ensure it is mutually beneficial and ownership is
responsible.

Actions
2.1.

Require people who breed companion animals for sale, and rescue centres, to register
and hold a current license.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Animal Welfare Policy --- Reviewed: 2025 --- Version: 09 March 2026

2

<!-- page 3 -->

3.

2.2.

Create national standards for the registered breeding of companion animals, including
limiting the number of litters an individual animal can have over a lifetime.

2.3.

Review the welfare standards of council pounds and animal rescue shelters to ensure
consistent practice and standards.

2.4.

Limit the number of companion animals an individual can have at once, with pathways
for exemptions, such as for owners who can demonstrate being able to uphold welfare.

2.5.

Ban prolonged close confinement and prolonged tethering or “life-chaining” of
animals, where it impacts wellbeing.

2.6.

Implement codes of welfare for highly social animals, such as guinea pigs, rabbits,
birds, rats, goats, horses and pigs, that require them to always be kept with others of
their species.

2.7.

Review the appropriateness of breed-specific legislation, and ban breeding of
lineages with high susceptibility to genetic welfare issues.

2.8.

Amend the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 to ensure that renters are able to own a
registered companion or support animal when the animal meets local bylaws.

Tikanga

Our Vision
Our culture is conscious of animals’ wellbeing. We effectively transition away from an economy
and culture reliant on the systemic exploitation of animals.
The agricultural sector consistently uses an ethical and humane approach to managing animals.
Our approach is world-leading, and animals enjoy a good life, with their death managed as
humanely as possible. The need for prosecution is rare. (See our Agriculture Policy)
Live animal imports and exports are rare, have strong protections, and only occur where there is
benefit to the animal or their species (see our Trade and Foreign Investment Policy).
Animal testing only occurs rarely, transparently, and has tangible benefits to people or animals
(see our Research, Science and Technology Policy).
Recreational activities that cause unnecessary distress or pain to animals or normalise cruelty
are prohibited (see our Recreation and Sport Policy).
Invasive species are managed using humane and effective methods, so that indigenous species
can flourish (see our Biodiversity and Environmental Regeneration Policy).
Fisheries and aquaculture are sustainably managed (see our Marine Policy).
4.

Maimoatanga:

Our Vision
The regulatory environment for animal welfare upholds Te Tiriti, and incorporates mātauranga
and tikanga Māori in design.

Actions
4.1.

Reform animal welfare legislation to recognise Māori concepts and values, in
partnership with tāngata whenua.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Animal Welfare Policy --- Reviewed: 2025 --- Version: 09 March 2026

3

<!-- page 4 -->

4.2.
5.

Ensure Māori representation in decision-making bodies for animal welfare, such as in
the Department of Animal Welfare.

Kaitiakitanga

Our Vision
Animal welfare and other relevant legislation help protect indigenous biodiversity.

Actions
5.1.

Develop local regulations around pet ownership to cater for the indigenous species
residing in that locale, such as requiring catios to keep cats safe and protect local
biodiversity.

5.2.

Fund free spaying and neutering for pets.

5.3.

Introduce national standards for desexing dogs and for registering, desexing, and
microchipping for cats.

5.4.

Regulate activities such as hunting and fishing where they have negative
consequences for indigenous species.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Animal Welfare Policy --- Reviewed: 2025 --- Version: 09 March 2026

4

documents/arts-culture-heritage-policy-2.title: Arts, Culture and Heritage Policy (Green Party policy document)
documents/arts-culture-heritage-policy-2.text:
# Arts, Culture and Heritage Policy (Green Party policy document)

<!-- page 1 -->

Arts, Culture and Heritage Policy
The Green Party will support the arts and cultural heritage sector to develop to its highest
standard and be properly resourced. A Green government will collaborate with funders, the
industry, and other stakeholders, including tangata whenua, who have the right to protect
traditional and contemporary Māori art. We will nurture talent in our communities by providing
educational opportunities in schools and communities and by expanding platforms for arts and
cultural heritage.

Vision
Creative, cultural and heritage work is integrated within our communities in myriad innovative
ways that empower people, spread happiness, and encourage intercultural appreciation and
understanding.

Values and Principles
- Honour Te Tiriti o Waitangi: Revitalising and celebrating toi Māori, tikanga Māori and te
reo Māori is key to ensuring a thriving arts industry. The Crown has a responsibility to
ensure the protection and return of taonga, including Māori arts, culture, intellectual
property and heritage sites. The Crown must support and contribute to but not determine
the revitalisation of toi Māori, tikanga Māori and te reo Māori.

- Ecological Wisdom: The arts play a part in enabling the transition to a life-sustaining
society by changing hearts and minds. Mātauranga Māori, as expressed through art and
cultural practice, is inextricably linked to the natural world.

- Social Responsibility: The arts foster community and improve our daily well-being,
empathy, equality and cultural diversity, as well as contributing economically.

- Appropriate Decision-Making: Those involved in arts and cultural heritage work must be
involved in developing guidelines for funding. Local communities must be given the ability
to protect places, buildings and heritage collections that are important to them historically
and culturally. The tino rangatiratanga of hapū and iwi over their taonga must be affirmed,
through Matike Mai mechanisms.

- Non-Violence: All art forms practised and recognised in Aotearoa New Zealand are
included in this policy and their interconnectedness is acknowledged. The art forms of
marginalised cultures and groups should be equitably supported.

- Resilience: Arts, culture and heritage are essential social infrastructure, not luxuries. The
Government should help build their resilience in our communities and at professional
levels.

- Professional: A vibrant and diverse professional arts sector contributes to all our lives, as
well as the identity of Aotearoa New Zealand on the international stage.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Arts, Culture and Heritage Policy --- Reviewed: 2014 --- Version: 17 June 2026

1

<!-- page 2 -->

Strategic Priorities
The Green Party’s strategic goals include:

“People will be part of caring communities with a strong heritage fabric”
Actions in this policy that will help achieve this include:
- Ensure cultural heritage infrastructure and funding provisions are sufficient to increase
participation in community arts, provide arts and cultural heritage education, and support
the professional arts to reach the highest standard. (1.2)

- Support and contribute to the revitalisation of toi Māori (2.1)

- Develop and resource the implementation of an ongoing arts education strategy from
early childhood to tertiary level. (3.3.1)

- Developing a network of Art Spaces and heritage equivalents in every community that are
accessible to all cultures and levels of ability, including programmes in prisons, and care
and refuge spaces. (3.11)

Connected Policies
Providing platforms through Media to celebrate the arts is important for arts, culture and
heritage to thrive. Ensuring sufficient income for those working in the arts, cultural and heritage
sectors is part of our Livelihoods and Workforce Policies. The Crown’s responsibility to ensure
the protection and revitalisation of natural and other taonga is explored in our Biodiversity and
Environmental Regeneration and Kaupapa Māori Policies.

Policy Positions
1.

Resourcing the arts, culture and heritage sector

Issues
Inadequate resourcing of the arts, culture and heritage sector risks a downward spiral in which
organisations close or cut back, long‑running programmes disappear, inequities deepen, and the
sector loses diversity and capacity it may not get back. The sector faces persistent structural
problems with few full-time jobs, low pay, and an expectation that creative professionals will
work for free or for ‘exposure’. Burnout and financial stress are common. Toi Māori has long been
structurally under‑resourced relative to its cultural significance and the scale of its activity especially considering language revitalisation, marae‑based arts, intergenerational teaching, and
community‑driven practice.

Actions
1.1.

Collaboratively establish effective systems of communication and coordination
between all those involved in arts, culture, and heritage, including government
ministries, funding agencies, local bodies, tangata whenua, and communities.

1.2.

Ensure cultural heritage infrastructure and funding provisions are sufficient to
increase participation in community arts, provide arts and cultural heritage education,
and support the professional arts to reach the highest standard, including by:
1.2.1.

Improving funding of local arts amenities, such as community galleries; and

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Arts, Culture and Heritage Policy --- Reviewed: 2014 --- Version: 17 June 2026

2

<!-- page 3 -->

1.2.2.

2.

Supporting the establishment of local arts trusts, especially where local arts are
currently not well supported.

Ngā toi Māori

Issues
National strategy and funding systems were not designed for kaupapa that are relational,
long‑horizon and whakapapa‑based, such as whare wānanga, customary arts, and iwi‑driven arts
infrastructure. They fail to uphold tino rangatiratanga or to represent the breadth and diversity
of te ao Māori, instead encouraging simplified, commodified, or misappropriated works.

Actions
2.1.

3.

Support and contribute to the revitalisation of toi Māori, including by:
2.1.1.

Establishing the legal ownership by tangata whenua of crafted taonga;

2.1.2.

Requiring commercial use of taonga to be based on informed consent, genuine
engagement, and reciprocity; and

2.1.3.

Redesigning arts-related Government processes and support systems to be
appropriate for Māori artists and arts practitioners.

Access to the Arts, Culture and Heritage

Issues
Access to arts, culture and heritage is growing, but uneven, with persistent gaps for rural
communities, disabled people, and low-income households. Arts, culture and heritage are too
often sidelined in education, in favour of other prioritised subjects, especially in under-resourced
schools.

Actions
3.1.

3.2.

Ensure equitable access to all aspects of the arts, culture and heritage for
marginalised communities, including by:
3.1.1.

Resourcing marginalised communities to fully participate and lead in the sector,
including through targeted funding and research;

3.1.2.

Providing sustainable funding to inclusive community arts, culture and heritage
organisations and those enabling access to the arts, culture and heritage; and

3.1.3.

Implementing safety frameworks to support marginalised groups in arts spaces.

Support, promote and protect the arts of Pacific and other communities of colour,
including by:
3.2.1.

3.3.

Developing and maintaining vocational pathways for tagata moana artists.

Ensure young people have access to appropriate arts training, both within and
external to their schooling, including by:

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Arts, Culture and Heritage Policy --- Reviewed: 2014 --- Version: 17 June 2026

3

<!-- page 4 -->

3.3.1.

Developing and resourcing the implementation of an ongoing arts education
strategy from early childhood to tertiary level;

3.3.2.

Provide secure funding for advisory services to schools in the performing arts,
culture and screen arts;

3.3.3.

Provide training to artists and other education providers to teach arts and
cultural heritage to young people, and encourage young artists; and

3.3.4.

Providing contestable funding for arts and cultural heritage organisations with
a proven commitment to arts education, to cover operational and management
expenses.

3.4.

4.

Encourage participation in and consumption of the arts, culture, and heritage,
including by:
3.4.1.

Resourcing regular community gatherings, festivals, and cultural events that
bring communities together;

3.4.2.

Developing a network of Art Spaces and heritage equivalents in every
community that are accessible to all cultures and levels of ability, including
programmes in prisons, and care and refuge spaces;

3.4.3.

Supporting the purchase of artworks for public buildings, especially hospitals
and schools, with an emphasis on locally-produced art;

3.4.4.

Encouraging the therapeutic use of the arts in long-stay care, and rehabilitation
facilities;

3.4.5.

Supporting the heritage collections of public museums and art galleries as
research and design resources for education, artistic, creative and community
history projects through public access, robust care, and management; and

3.4.6.

Supporting the purchase by public collecting institutions of nationally significant
heritage objects and collections at risk of export.

Economic Development and the Arts, Culture, and Heritage

Issues
Creative industries make a significant economic contribution. Rising economic disparities,
unstable income streams, and intergenerational knowledge gaps hinder creative start-ups and
innovation. Reliance on corporate funding risks eroding artistic autonomy and public trust.
Creative and cultural exporters face significant trade barriers, and there is a lack of scalable midsize businesses.

Actions
4.1.

Support the role of a high-quality arts, culture, and heritage sector in economic
development, by:
4.1.1.

Establishing an arts and cultural promotion unit within the Ministry of Foreign
Affairs and Trade;

4.1.2.

Funding research and development in the arts, culture, and heritage;

4.1.3.

Incentivising private sector investment in projects and initiatives focused on the
arts, culture, and/or heritage; and

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Arts, Culture and Heritage Policy --- Reviewed: 2014 --- Version: 17 June 2026

4

<!-- page 5 -->

4.1.4.
4.2.

5.

Promoting local craft practitioners using local ingredients, recycling, and
distributing products in sustainable ways.

Enable liveable incomes in the arts, culture, and heritage, by:
4.2.1.

Establishing that copyright of a commissioned work is retained by the artist by
default, not the commissioner, and that, when negotiated otherwise, copyright
of a redistributable work reverts to the artist when the commissioner of a work
ceases to distribute it; and

4.2.2.

Ensure that the Public Lending Right provides adequate compensation to
authors for the free public access New Zealanders have to their works through
public libraries.

Protecting and Preserving our Heritage

Issues
There are significant challenges in protecting and preserving built heritage, including cost,
seismic and climate risks, and pressures from urban development. Neglected buildings require
expensive fixes to avoid demolition. Negative and systemic biases towards built and colonial
heritage sideline and erode pre-colonial history, wāhi tapu, stories, and skills. Heritage losses are
irreplaceable.

Actions
5.1.

5.2.

Strengthen heritage policy and funding by:
5.1.1.

Establishing national direction for heritage, requiring local authorities to place
more weight on recognising and supporting heritage places in district plans; and

5.1.2.

Providing funding schemes for the maintenance and earthquake strengthening
of privately-owned heritage buildings.

Enhance Māori and community leadership and engagement in heritage protection by:
5.2.1.

Providing programmes that enable communities to safely explore the diversity
and tensions in local heritage and traditions;

5.2.2.

Increase the capacity of Te Papa's National Services to provide effective
assistance, training and other services to local museums and art galleries in the
care and management of heritage collections;

5.2.3.

Prioritising areas of cultural value to communities, whānau, hapū and iwi when
resourcing climate change adaptation; and

5.2.4.

Resourcing artistic and community activities that seek to challenge entrenched
harmful narratives and enhance understanding of a positive, sustainable and
climate-safe future.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Arts, Culture and Heritage Policy --- Reviewed: 2014 --- Version: 17 June 2026

5

documents/biodiversity-environmental-reg.title: Biodiversity and Environmental (Green Party policy document)
documents/biodiversity-environmental-reg.text:
# Biodiversity and Environmental (Green Party policy document)

<!-- page 1 -->

Biodiversity and Environmental
Regeneration Policy
In Government, the Green Party will take a holistic approach to conservation. We will make sure
Aotearoa New Zealand plays a leading part in protecting the biodiversity of planet Earth from
the global mass extinction that is currently underway. We will protect threatened indigenous
species from invasive species, diseases, and human activity, and support the kaitiaki role and
indigenous knowledge of tangata whenua.

Vision
Indigenous biodiversity thrives and there is a healthy relationship between people and te taiao |
the environment.

Values and Principles
Policy decisions relating to biodiversity regeneration must be consistent with the following values
and principles:
- Honour Te Tiriti o Waitangi: Regenerative efforts must recognise the kaitiaki role of
tangata whenua and the insight that mātauranga Māori brings.

- Ecological Wisdom: Regenerative efforts must recognise the inherent value of nature, and
work within its complex dynamics. We must actively safeguard and regenerate indigenous
ecosystems, Ki uta ki tai | from the mountains to the sea.

- Social Responsibility: Regenerative efforts must ensure future generations will inherit a
healthy environment, which is achieved alongside progress on social issues.

- Non-Violence: Regenerative efforts must cause minimal harm whilst preventing the harm
caused by inaction.

- Appropriate Decision-Making: Regenerative efforts must be adaptable, evidence-based,
and effective. Decision-making must be distributed equitably, engage with local
communities, and achieve co-benefits.

- Interconnectedness:

Regenerative efforts must recognise that humans are
interdependent with other species. Our survival requires a functional biosphere as we are
part of the circle of life and share a common descent and whakapapa.

Strategic Priorities
The Green Party’s strategic goals include:

“Human interaction with the rest of the natural world needs to be based on the principles
of ecological sustainability and circularity, underpinned by mātauranga Māori, and giving
life to our international commitments on indigenous knowledge and rights.”
Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Biodiversity and Environmental Regeneration Policy --- Reviewed: 2025 --- Version: 09 March 2026 1

<!-- page 2 -->

“All native species and their habitats will be thriving or on a path to recovery in terrestrial,
freshwater, and marine environments.
Our laws and practices will respect the biological integrity of all life, while prioritising the
health of indigenous species and ecosystems.
The customary and decision making roles of whānau, hapū, and iwi will be integral to
decisions about resource use."
Actions in this policy that work towards these goals include:
- Establishing a job guarantee programme focused on understanding, protecting, and
regenerating ecosystems. (2.1.1)

- Broadening legal protections and conservation strategies to cover indigenous fish, plants,
invertebrates, and fungi to recognise the importance of taxonomic diversity. (3.1.2)

- Investigating appropriate regulation that limits or suspends the harvesting of vulnerable
aquatic species, such as whitebait, to ensure populations regenerate. (3.1.3)

- Significantly increasing resourcing for bodies that eradicate and control invasive species
and weeds, prioritising the eradication of invasive species identified in Predator Free 2050
and other species with disproportionate effects on indigenous ecosystems. (3.2.3)

- Taking a collaborative, Tiriti-based approach to Government-led conservation, such as
co-governance and co-management (4.2.3)

- Establishing a Sovereign Biodiversity Fund to resource regenerative efforts. (2.1.3)

Connected Policies
See also our specific policies for the protection and regeneration of Land, Freshwater, and Marine
ecosystems, and our policies relating to:
- Establishing legal rights of nature and recognising the legal status of Papatūānuku
(Governance Policy) and a right to a healthy environment (Human Rights Policy)

- Ensuring economic activities uphold the wellbeing of the natural world (Government in
the Economy, Business, and specific sectors, e.g. Agriculture, Tourism, Forestry)

- Minimising the further loss of indigenous ecosystems to other land uses (Land Use and
Soils Policy)

- Adapting urban design to support environmental growth (Housing and Sustainable
Communities Policy)

- Collaborating with other countries, including strengthening international treaties (Global
Affairs Policy) and leveraging trade agreements (Trade and Foreign Investment Policy)

- Aligning ‘carbon farming’ with ecological resilience (Climate Change Policy)

Policy Positions
1.

Global Biodiversity Crisis - The urgent need for action

Issues
Rates of species extinction across the world have increased sharply due to pressures caused by
human activity. Global economic and political systems undervalue, exploit, and destroy nature.
Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Biodiversity and Environmental Regeneration Policy --- Reviewed: 2025 --- Version: 09 March 2026 2

<!-- page 3 -->

Rates of extinction are now as high as the five previous 'mass extinction events' in Earth’s history,
meaning we are facing the “Holocene mass extinction event”. The level of biodiversity is declining
to the point that it is threatening ecosystems, and the human systems reliant on them.This
means the need for action is critical.

Actions
1.1.

Implement and advocate for universal membership of international agreements that
support biodiversity, such as the Convention on Biological Diversity.

1.2.

Ensure that the need to act to prevent ongoing biodiversity loss and secure a viable
future is widely understood, including by:

1.3.

1.2.1.

Expanding the National Policy Statement for Indigenous Biodiversity to establish
clear targets within its implementation plan and demonstrate clear practical
pathways to achieving those.

1.2.2.

Supporting advocacy and education within the wider community regarding
biodiversity loss and the mass extinction event, including restoring and
adequately resourcing DOC's advocacy and education role; and

1.2.3.

Incorporating environmental education into curricula, from early to adult
education, and funding nature-based school activities.

Minimise the impact of climate change on biodiversity, including by:
1.3.1.

1.4.

2.

Considering climate change impacts and adaptation strategies when designing
conservation programmes.

Enable New Zealanders to strengthen their relationship with the environment and
conservation efforts, including by:
1.4.1.

Supporting traditions and practices that recognise the rights and wellbeing of
the natural world and its fundamental societal value;

1.4.2.

Exploring a refocus of DOC to be solely on conservation by allocating its tourism,
recreation, and heritage roles to other agencies; and

Environmental Growth and Ecosystem Regeneration

Issues
Human activity pressures ecosystem health and functioning through pollution, habitat loss,
resource extraction, and biodiversity loss, which is further accelerated by an economy that
incentivises exploitation for short-term gain. This has led to the loss and degradation of
ecosystems and their critical functions.

Actions
2.1.

Ensure that economic development and commercial activities support the
regeneration and growth of the environment, including by:
2.1.1.

Establishing a job guarantee programme focused on understanding, protecting,
and regenerating ecosystems;

2.1.2.

Exploring and supporting the criminalisation of 'ecocide' within domestic and
international law, incorporating a Te Tiriti o Waitangi perspective; and

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Biodiversity and Environmental Regeneration Policy --- Reviewed: 2025 --- Version: 09 March 2026 3

<!-- page 4 -->

2.1.3.

2.2.

2.3.

2.4.

2.5.

3.

Establishing a Sovereign Biodiversity Fund to resource regenerative efforts,
with:
2.1.3.1.

Incentives for government,
biodiversity; and

private,

and

iwi

investment

2.1.3.2.

Reliable funds from a new user-pays natural resources levy.

in

Resource landowners to regenerate and maintain indigenous biodiversity, including
by:
2.2.1.

Introducing a biodiversity credits system that incentivises private and Māori
landowners to establish indigenous biodiversity pockets and regenerate
indigenous ecosystems, particularly for important ecosystems disproportionally
being degraded, such as wetlands;

2.2.2.

Ensuring resource management legislation and plans take an ecosystem-based
approach and encourage the regeneration of indigenous ecosystems and
biodiversity; and

2.2.3.

Prohibiting further net loss of indigenous ecosystems to human land uses, and
requiring new developments to undergo thorough analysis on environmental
impacts, whilst bolstering the ability to gather and access data needed for these
analyses.

Ensure that Aotearoa New Zealand’s activity in Antarctica protects the region's
biodiversity, including by:
2.3.1.

Collaborating with other Antarctic Treaty signatories to uphold responsible
stewardship;

2.3.2.

Developing and funding a biodiversity and environmental regeneration plan for
the Ross Dependency; and

2.3.3.

Establishing a system to require environmental impact assessments for human
activities such as research and tourism in Antarctica.

Monitor and control air pollutants, including by:
2.4.1.

Introducing mandatory monitoring and controls for fine particulate matter; and

2.4.2.

Updating the National Environmental Standards for Air Quality to reflect
international standards.

Minimise light pollution, including by:
2.5.1.

Supporting research and development on efficient light technologies that
minimise light pollution; and

2.5.2.

Increasing and protecting dark sky reserves.

Indigenous Species

Issues
Aotearoa New Zealand is a known “hotspot” for its biodiversity. Due to its distinct evolutionary
history, it has many unique species and a distinct ecological composition. Unfortunately, this
uniqueness makes our endemic species particularly vulnerable to extinction and human
pressures. The majority of our vertebrate indigenous species, and many other indigenous
species, are now at risk of extinction due to habitat loss, invasive species, pollution, disease, and
Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Biodiversity and Environmental Regeneration Policy --- Reviewed: 2025 --- Version: 09 March 2026 4

<!-- page 5 -->

genetic bottlenecks. Growing pressures, such as climate change and human impacts on the
environment, increase the urgency to respond.

Actions
3.1.

3.2.

3.3.

3.4.

3.5.

Restore the population health of indigenous species so that they are safe from the
threat of extinction, including by:
3.1.1.

Broadening recovery plans to cover more threatened species across different
taxa and updating them regularly;

3.1.2.

Broadening legal protections and conservation strategies to cover indigenous
fish, plants, invertebrates, and fungi to recognise the importance of taxonomic
diversity; and

3.1.3.

Investigating appropriate regulation that limits or suspends the harvesting of
vulnerable aquatic species, such as whitebait, to ensure populations regenerate.

Ensure that invasive species are either exterminated or well managed and monitored,
and no longer prevent indigenous species from flourishing, including by:
3.2.1.

Expanding 'mainland islands' for intensive invasive species management;

3.2.2.

Strengthening regulation and enforcement around introducing, releasing, and
commercial use of invasive species;

3.2.3.

Significantly increasing resourcing for bodies that eradicate and control invasive
species and weeds, prioritising the eradication of invasive species identified in
Predator Free 2050 and other species with disproportionate effects on
indigenous ecosystems; and

3.2.4.

Developing and prioritising humane and effective biological, chemical, and
physical invasive species control options, while recognising and applying the
most effective options currently available (e.g. 1080, cyanide, glyphosate,
trappings).

Ensure that diseases that impair indigenous species (e.g. Kauri dieback, myrtle rust)
are well understood, monitored, and controlled, including by:
3.3.1.

Funding research to understand diseases that affect indigenous species; and

3.3.2.

Establishing strategies to combat the spread of disease in indigenous species.

Ensure that genetic diversity and variation of indigenous species are well protected,
including by:
3.4.1.

Researching and monitoring genetic bottlenecks, inbreeding depression, and
other declines in variation of indigenous species;

3.4.2.

Funding genetic rescue programmes to increase genetic variation of indigenous
species;

3.4.3.

Exploring ways to use eco-sourcing in nurseries and re-wilding programmes;
and

3.4.4.

Establishing genome and seed banks for indigenous species, prioritising
endemic species.

Ensure biosecurity measures that prevent the introduction of new species and
biological hazards are robust, well-resourced, and effective.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Biodiversity and Environmental Regeneration Policy --- Reviewed: 2025 --- Version: 09 March 2026 5

<!-- page 6 -->

3.6.

4.

Recloak Papatūānuku through the regeneration of indigenous forests, including by:
3.6.1.

Strengthening the existing restrictions and penalties on the harvesting and
export of indigenous logs and chips, including swamp kauri;

3.6.2.

Ensuring that any removal of windthrown trees on public conservation land is
ecologically and culturally sound; and

3.6.3.

Prioritising the control of introduced pests that contribute to forest collapse (i.e.
possums, pigs, and deer) over recreational hunting.

Te Tiriti and Conservation

Issues
Conservation that is disconnected from Māori fails to uphold Te Tiriti o Waitangi. Conservation
systems have exacerbated the disconnection of Māori from ancestral lands and undermined the
kaitiaki role of tangata whenua.

Actions
4.1.

4.2.

Ensure that all environmental protection and resource management legislation:
4.1.1.

Reflect Te Tiriti o Waitangi and values and understandings from te ao Māori; and

4.1.2.

Uphold the tino rangatiratanga of iwi and hapū to protect their land, water, and
other natural resources, in cooperation with local government.

Ensure that conservation efforts resource and uphold the tino rangatiratanga of Māori
as kaitiaki, including by:
4.2.1.

Enabling customary use of indigenous species and resources on public
conservation land by iwi and hapū Māori, in line with kaitiakitanga;

4.2.2.

Supporting Māori-led oversight of the customary management of tāonga
species by iwi and hapū Māori;

4.2.3.

Taking a collaborative, Tiriti-based approach to Government-led conservation,
such as co-governance and co-management; and

4.2.4.

Implementing recommendations of Ko Aotearoa Tēnei Waitangi Tribunal
(WAI262) report, such as establishing Māori advisory boards, improving support
for rongōa Māori, and reviewing patents of plant lineages.

4.3.

Build public awareness of the colonial history of public conservation land and how Te
Tiriti o Waitangi and conservation intersect.

4.4.

Ensure conservation efforts recognise native species as tāonga with whakapapa
connections to Māori, including by:
4.4.1.

5.

Developing strategies to preserve non-native tāonga animals and plants, such
as the kiore, in a way that would not threaten indigenous species.

Effectiveness of Conservation Efforts

Issues

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Biodiversity and Environmental Regeneration Policy --- Reviewed: 2025 --- Version: 09 March 2026 6

<!-- page 7 -->

Conservation efforts seek to protect biodiversity and halt its decline but they have so far been
insufficient. Despite decades of conservation, locally and nationally, biodiversity is continuing to
decline.

Actions
5.1.

5.2.

5.3.

Ensure that conservation efforts are accorded sufficient priority, funding, and tools to
achieve their goals, including by:
5.1.1.

Expanding DOC's core capacity by increasing funding for technology, data, and
employing many more field and research personnel;

5.1.2.

Enabling the purchase, protection, and regeneration of special places, including
by iwi and hapū, that are threatened or under-represented in the public
conservation estate; and

5.1.3.

Strengthening the role and funding of conservation boards as independent
advocates, speaking for the community.

Ensure that conservation efforts are evidence-based and reflect the drivers of
ecosystem health, productivity, and biomass, including by:
5.2.1.

Funding increased research into indigenous ecosystem functioning and species
population dynamics;

5.2.2.

Prioritising landscape-scale and ecosystem-based conservation projects that
will protect and restore the ecological niches of individual populations and
species that are at risk; and

5.2.3.

Developing a set of environmental indicators with meaningful tipping points and
limits, grounded in mātauranga Māori and Western science.

Support community efforts to regenerate urban biodiversity and incorporate better
indigenous ecology and greenspace into city design, including by:
5.3.1.

Including community-based biodiversity conservation initiatives in land-use
planning and local sustainable development strategies.

.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Biodiversity and Environmental Regeneration Policy --- Reviewed: 2025 --- Version: 09 March 2026 7

documents/business-policy-2025-2026.md.title: Business Policy (Green Party policy document)
documents/business-policy-2025-2026.md.text:
# Business Policy (Green Party policy document)

<!-- page 1 -->

Business Policy
The Green Party will deepen business relationships with communities, encourage innovation,
and regulate business to prevent both environmental and social harm. It will do this by
reforming regulatory agencies, requiring accessibility, supporting the Māori economy,
supporting new business models, promoting local business, co-investing in skills, and
increasing access to academic research and local institutions of learning.

Vision
Our businesses are locally celebrated, nationally valued, and internationally renowned for their
economically successful, environmentally sustainable, and socially responsible practices.

Values and Principles
Policy decisions relating to business must be consistent with the following values and
principles:
- Honour Te Tiriti o Waitangi: Te Tiriti o Waitangi and He Whakaputanga should actively
shape the practices of all businesses operating in Aotearoa New Zealand, including their
products, their practices, and their use of resources.

- Ecological Wisdom: Environmental sustainability is integral to business success and
economic stability. Short-term profit must not be prioritised over long-term
environmental health. Businesses and investors must prioritise accessible, regenerative,
and circular activity across all sectors.

- Social Responsibility: Businesses should be active participants in positively shaping and
supporting society. Businesses create value beyond profit and must focus on
stakeholders beyond shareholders.

- Appropriate Decision-Making: Staff and business owners flourish in a collaborative, safe,
accessible, and respectful environment.

- Non-Violence: Businesses should protect the wellbeing of their employees, customers,
and supply-chain, and prevent harm to affected communities and ecosystems.

- Fair Competition: Local businesses should be protected from threats from unfair
economic activity, including overseas activity.

- Collaboration: Businesses are vital in tackling complex challenges but cannot do it alone.
Working with others, including other businesses within a competitive environment, can
help address them.

- Innovation: Businesses should actively develop accessible, efficient, and sustainable
practices and technologies. Businesses should be adaptable and build resilience to a
changing business environment.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Business Policy –- Reviewed: 2025 —Version: 17 June 2026

1

<!-- page 2 -->

- Shared Benefits: The benefits derived from resource use should not be concentrated,
but shared across society.

- Responsibility for Harm: Businesses are responsible for fairly compensating for any
harm they cause or resources they use.

Strategic Priorities
The Green Party’s strategic goals include:

“Aotearoa will be in transition, creating green work and broad prosperity while moving
Aotearoa away from carbon-dependent, extractive, and resource-intensive industries.”
“All people will be empowered to shape the systems that affect them through
community engagement enabled by good evidence, co-design, and adequate
resourcing.”
Actions in this policy that will help achieve this include:
- Reforming market structures in industries that are consistently dominated by a few
large firms, making excessive profits, overcharging consumers, exploiting workers, or
having adverse social and environmental impacts. (1.1.2)

- Regulating businesses operating in Aotearoa New Zealand to be socially and
environmentally responsible throughout the lifecycle of their operations, including the
whole supply chain, repair and resource recovery, and remediations after close of
business. (2.1)

- Regulating and penalising marketing practices that misrepresent a company's social,
ethical, environmental, or economic commitments and practices. (2.4.1)

- Implementing strategies to connect specific industries with educational institutions,
technologies, and international expertise. (3.1.3)

- Supporting relationships between Māori businesses and non-Māori businesses as
suppliers and partners. (4.1.2)

Connected Policies
The Government makes many decisions in other policy areas that affect businesses. See, for
example, our Government in the Economy, Workforce, Trade and Foreign Investment, and
Research, Science, and Technology Policies.

Policy Positions
1.

Market dominance

Issues
Markets are increasingly dominated by just a few large firms, at home and overseas.

Actions

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Business Policy –- Reviewed: 2025 —Version: 17 June 2026

2

<!-- page 3 -->

1.1.

1.2.

2.

documents/childrens-2013-2026.md.text:
# Children’s Policy (Green Party policy document)

<!-- page 1 -->

Children’s Policy
The Green Party will reform social support services to enable equitable access for all whānau,
extend paid parental leave, reform Working for Families and lift minimum wage entitlements to
eliminate child poverty in Aotearoa. We will promote greater collaboration across Government
for the benefit of children and support effective solutions to keep children from harm.

Vision
All children experience a joyful childhood and the best possible start to life.

Values and Principles
- Care: Children have the best opportunities in life when their whānau can provide them
with aroha and emotional and material support. All children should be connected with
their whānau, surrounded by love and respect, generosity and care, and have every
opportunity to be healthy.

- Honour Te Tiriti o Waitangi: Tamariki Māori have the right to be respected as tangata
whenua and effective systems should be in place for their benefit. Their contribution
should be recognised and encouraged and their culture allowed to thrive.

- Ecological Wisdom: Children and future generations should all have access to clean air
and water, safe food and thriving ecosystems.

- Social Responsibility: Government has a crucial role in supporting parents and other
caregivers in providing for their children, and in creating policies that put children first.
The Government has a responsibility to protect the rights of marginalized and
disadvantaged children.

- Appropriate Decision-Making: Children have valuable perspectives, and should be
supported in their own initiatives and encouraged to participate in decisions that affect
their lives, future, communities, and the environment. Children should be supported to
develop to their full potential and become responsible, compassionate, engaged citizens.

- Non-Violence: All children have the right to be treated with respect and dignity, and they
must be protected from all forms of abuse.

- Diversity: The cultural and gender identities of our diverse tamariki should be honoured
and celebrated.

- Learning: Children should experience a childhood of exploration and discovery, including
through a quality formal education.

Strategic Priorities
The Green Party’s strategic goals include:

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Children’s Policy --- Reviewed: 2013 --- Version: 02 March 2026

1

<!-- page 2 -->

“As a Party we strive to create a more connected, compassionate and equal Aotearoa,
free from structural biases that discriminate against groups and individuals.”
Actions in this policy that will help achieve this include:
- Support the co-design with tangata whenua of an evidence-based nationwide child
wellbeing strategy that cements children’s rights, including the rights of tamariki and
rangatahi Māori under Te Tiriti o Waitangi. (1.2)

- Ensure that legislation, policy, and practice meet Aotearoa New Zealand’s human rights
obligations under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCROC) and that the
recommendations of the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child (CRC) are fully
implemented. (1.3)

- Work with marginalised people, including children, to uphold their rights. (1.7)

- Improve and ensure equitable access to social services for children with additional needs
and their whānau, focused on both early identification and ongoing support, including
adequate resourcing of and access to respite services for parents. (2.1)

- Support by Māori, for Māori solutions, that enable tamariki to stay with whānau (...). (4.1)

- Review and reform the Child Support system to ensure it operates in a way that best
benefits children and young people. (3.3)

Connected Policies
When whānau and communities thrive, children thrive. Improving children’s lives requires lifting
incomes at all levels (see our Livelihoods Policy), and supporting parents in and outside of work
(see our Workforce and Women’s Policies), as well as protecting the wellbeing of the natural
world and supporting their deep connection with it (see our Biodiversity and Environmental
Regeneration and Climate Change Policies). See also our Education, Health, Housing and
Sustainable Communities, Justice, and Youth Policies.

Policy Positions
1.

A Cross-Government Approach to Child Wellbeing

Issues
Policies and systems focussed on child wellbeing are fragmented across Government. The Green
Party supports a cross-governmental approach to child wellbeing, ensuring alignment between
plans and strategies prepared by all relevant agencies.

Actions
1.1.

Ensure that the Children’s Commissioner is adequately funded, retains their
independence and advocacy role, and takes on responsibility for promoting the
understanding of the rights of tamariki and rangatahi under Te Tiriti o Waitangi.

1.2.

Support the co-design with tangata whenua of an evidence-based nationwide child
wellbeing strategy that cements children’s rights, including the rights of tamariki and
rangatahi Māori under Te Tiriti o Waitangi.

1.3.

Ensure that legislation, policy, and practice meet Aotearoa New Zealand’s human
rights obligations under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCROC) and

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Children’s Policy --- Reviewed: 2013 --- Version: 02 March 2026

2

<!-- page 3 -->

that the recommendations of the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child (CRC) are
fully implemented.

2.

1.4.

Establish the use of child impact assessments in all government policy and planning.

1.5.

Protect the right of every child to their name, nationality, and preservation of identity.

1.6.

Establish effective systems for the development and coordination of services for
tamariki and rangatahi Māori, in partnership with tamariki and rangatahi, whānau,
hapū, and iwi.

1.7.

Work with marginalised people, including children, to uphold their rights.

1.8.

Oppose the incarceration of children, regardless of citizenship status

1.9.

Ensure that all children are able to engage with the natural world, including through
providing immersive environmental education activities in parks and reserves.

A Child-centred Approach to Services

Issues
Social services, such as early childhood education, are often unaffordable for parents. All children
should have equitable access to high-quality social services that enable them to have the best
educational and social start in life.

Actions

3.

2.1.

Improve and ensure equitable access to social services for children with additional
needs and their whānau, focused on both early identification and ongoing support,
including adequate resourcing of and access to respite services for parents.

2.2.

Recognise the social value of early childcare services, including care provided through
playcentres and kōhanga reo, including by developing a funding model that promotes
high standards of care, allows flexibility for parents, removes barriers to access for
families and ensures fair wages for early childcare teachers.

2.3.

Ensure all children have access to safe public spaces to play.

2.4.

Support local communities to provide a wide range of extracurricular activities to all
children.

2.5.

Support universal availability of effective parenting and child development
programmes, and ensure these are culturally appropriate and support connections
between whānau.

2.6.

Support the development of initiatives that promote children’s full citizenship and
participation in their communities.

Child Poverty Alleviation

Issues
Child poverty levels are at unacceptably high levels in Aotearoa. Poverty in childhood has longterm impacts on people’s wellbeing.

Actions
3.1.

Introduce a universal child payment, increase the minimum wage and base benefit
levels, extend paid parental leave, and increase benefit levels

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Children’s Policy --- Reviewed: 2013 --- Version: 02 March 2026

3

<!-- page 4 -->

4.

3.2.

Review and reform family assistance policies, and remove discriminatory policies to
ensure family assistance rates are related to family income rather than parental
employment status.

3.3.

Review and reform the Child Support system to ensure it operates in a way that best
benefits children and young people.

3.4.

Guarantee child support for children and young people in low-income families through
advanced payments.

3.5.

Support community-led provision of safe and healthy food in schools.

3.6.

Support free budgeting services for parents and primary caregivers.

Manaakitanga mō ngā Whānau Katoa - Care for all Families

Issues
The Green Party is concerned about the State removal of children from their whānau, and failures
to keep children safe. We need a new approach to children at risk of harm.

Actions
4.1.

4.2.

Support by Māori, for Māori solutions, that enable tamariki to stay with whānau,
including:
4.1.1.

Support hapū, iwi and Māori community organisations to provide effective social
support services for at-risk children and families, recognising the need for these
to be culturally appropriate and non-coercive; and

4.1.2.

Implement Waitangi Tribunal recommendations relating to Oranga Tamariki.

Invest in effective programmes and Government policies that aim to:
4.2.1.

Eliminate family violence;

4.2.2.

Establish positive parent support services
causes of harm; and

4.2.3.

Improve the outcomes of children removed from the care of their families,
recognising the additional needs of these children in recovering from trauma,
and the importance of ensuring they are safe and supported through to
adulthood.

that work to resolve underlying

4.3.

Implement the recommendations of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in
Care, in consultation with community organisations, iwi and hapū, and survivors.

4.4.

Provide easily accessible and timely redress to people who have suffered abuse in
care.

4.5.

Ensure that children who hold part-time jobs to contribute to their households are
provided with sufficient and timely support to continue their education.

4.6.

Overhaul adoption and other laws relating to the care of children to reflect the
diversity of Rainbow families.

4.7.

Ensure the rights of all adopted persons are upheld, including by:
4.7.1.

Implementing the recommendations of the 2022 Ministry of Justice Adoption
Law Reform initiative;

4.7.2.

Replacing the Adoption Act 1955 and the current system with one which:

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Children’s Policy --- Reviewed: 2013 --- Version: 02 March 2026

4

<!-- page 5 -->

- promotes openness and transparency;

- places the rights of the adoptee as paramount;

- ensures the preservation of, and connection to, culture and identity; and

- protects whakapapa and recognises the whanaungatanga responsibilities of
family, whānau, hapū, iwi and family group information, culture,
opportunities and property, as related to their biological heritage

4.7.3.

Incorporating knowledge from iwi-based organisations into the adoption
process;

4.7.4.

Creating systems for adopted Māori to reconnect with their whakapapa, whānau,
whenua and reo;

4.7.5.

Giving full legal recognition to whāngai; and

4.7.6.

Apologising and providing redress for failures to recognise whāngai and for the
forced displacement of tamariki Māori.

4.7.7.

Enabling adopted adults to have their adoption order reversed

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Children’s Policy --- Reviewed: 2013 --- Version: 02 March 2026
