documents/housing-and-sustainable-commun.title: Housing and Sustainable (Green Party policy document)
documents/housing-and-sustainable-commun.text:
# Housing and Sustainable (Green Party policy document)

<!-- page 1 -->

Housing and Sustainable
Communities Policy
The Green Party will ensure people’s right to healthy, secure housing. We will focus on:
launching a massive public housing project that is funded, managed and run by the
government; providing for a substantial increase in Māori housing and the removal of barriers
to Māori housing; making housing accessibility and safety for disabled people a high priority;
reducing building-related greenhouse gas emissions; and creating frameworks to ensure
regenerative urban development that connects people within their communities.

Vision
Accessible, healthy, secure and sustainable housing for all in thriving communities.

Values and Principles
This housing policy must be consistent with the following values and principles:
- Honour Te Tiriti o Waitangi: Article 2 of Te Tiriti o Waitangi guarantees tangata whenua
tino rangatiratanga over their taonga, which includes their whenua. Honouring this
guarantee is fundamental to enabling housing developments, including papakāinga.
Funding should be prioritised for Māori housing developments, with ownership and
decision-making by Māori. Mātauranga Māori principles of design for housing and
communities should be broadly applied across the whole housing sector to build
adequate housing for all.

- Ecological Wisdom: Our communities must be life-sustaining. They should be designed,
built or renovated using principles, materials and processes that are regenerative and
minimise negative environmental impacts.

- Social Responsibility: People should have access to healthy, affordable and secure homes
that support wellbeing and enable connected, inclusive communities. Housing needs to
be designed as universally accessible so that all groups in the community have equitable
access to appropriate and affordable housing.

- Appropriate Decision-Making: Communities should be actively involved in decisions that
affect the places they live. Decision-making should particularly consider the interests of
those who have been marginalised, and actively ensure their inclusion in community
engagement processes.

- Non-Violence: Vested private interests that seek to maintain control of housing should
be mitigated by the government through legislation and engagement to neutralise the
power imbalance. No one should be forced to move out of their home without a suitable
alternative being provided.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Housing and Sustainable Communities Policy --- Reviewed: 2022 — Version: 17 June 2026

1

<!-- page 2 -->

Decommodification: Housing should be seen as a fundamental human need and right,

- not something that is traded for capital gains and profits that serve to perpetuate
inequality. Basically, houses should be homes.

Housing security: People should be able to live in their home or community for as long

- as they wish, regardless of ownership. Having generations of family/whānau living
together contributes to stable and healthy communities.

Housing for disabled people: Disabled people have the right to live in accessible housing

- both wherever and with whomever they choose to live.

Strategic Priorities
The Green Party’s strategic goals include:

“Healthy homes within thriving neighbourhoods will be available to everyone. People will
be part of caring communities with a strong heritage fabric and easy access to the
natural environment.”
Actions in this policy that will help achieve this include:
- Sufficiently resourcing papakāinga and other Māori-led housing solutions and Māori
community housing providers (1.2.1)

- Establishing a right to housing in legislation that requires the State to ensure all New
Zealanders are adequately housed in safe, healthy, accessible, affordable housing. (2.1.1)

- Establishing a Ministry for Green Works to ensure supply of suitable housing for all New
Zealanders (...) (3.4.1)

- Establishing representative housing committees in all local communities that reflect both
homeowners and renters (4.6.2)

- Creating regulatory structures, including affordable housing requirements, that require
developers to provide for equitable developments. (4.3.2)

Connected Policies
To address the housing crisis, alongside the actions below the Government in the Economy must
incentivise productive Business investment and savings to support Livelihoods, and
disincentivise property speculation. Sustainable development is an important part of protecting
Biodiversity and Environmental Regeneration, including restoring urban Freshwater ecosystems.
Key to sustainable development are minimising suburban sprawl in favour of regenerative Land
Use and Soils, reducing the impacts of Climate Change, minimising Energy use, enabling and
prioritising low-carbon Transport, and focusing on Community in the Economy. See our Kaupapa
Māori Policy for pathways for returning Māori ancestral lands to Māori ownership.

Policy Positions
1.

Honouring Te Tiriti o Waitangi and Hoki Whenua Mai

Issues
Dispossession of land has created deep, intergenerational harm for many Māori communities
that goes far beyond the initial physical loss of whenua. Its loss underpins higher rates of Māori
Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Housing and Sustainable Communities Policy --- Reviewed: 2022 — Version: 17 June 2026

2

<!-- page 3 -->

poverty, unemployment, and insecure or overcrowded housing in many regions. Dispossession
often forced Māori to relocate, breaking up hapū and disrupting traditional support structures. It
also meant loss of decision-making power over the use of whenua. There are still barriers to and
breaches of tino rangatiratanga, which guarantees the right of Māori to build and house their
people on their own land.

Actions
1.1. Ensure all government agencies with responsibility for housing are fully responsive to
Māori housing priorities, including by:
1.1.1. Establishing a co-governance model at the Ministry of Housing and Urban
Development and Kāinga Ora, and promoting co-governance structures for all new
housing developments through Kāinga Ora;
1.1.2. Encouraging mātauranga Māori-informed designers to be involved from the
formative stages across all housing development to honour Te Tiriti; and
1.1.3. Partnering with Māori to determine the need for and implement a Māori Housing
Authority.
1.2. In partnership with Māori, empower Māori-led solutions for secure, affordable housing
in all areas of the country by:
1.2.1. Sufficiently resourcing papakāinga and other Māori-led housing solutions and Māori
community housing providers;
1.2.2. Providing easy-to-access pathways to housing ownership for all Māori, including
from the rental market;
1.2.3. Delivering targeted programmes providing culturally appropriate housing for
homeless tamariki and rangatahi Māori and hapū tāngata and their whānau;
1.2.4. Identifying and removing barriers to housing development by Māori for Māori,
especially those that affect building on Māori land; and
1.2.5. Reaching out to all Māori experiencing housing stress.
1.3. Seek to return whenua Māori to Māori ownership and restore the rights of Māori as its
kaitiaki, including by:
1.3.1. Returning Crown land reserved for Māori into Māori ownership, starting with land
that supports the resilience of our communities;
1.3.2. Including the return of Māori land in climate change adaptation and heritage
protection programmes;
1.3.3. Restoring the powers of the Waitangi Tribunal to make recommendations in relation
to privately owned land;
1.3.4. Establishing a fund, proportional to accumulated land value loss, to enable whānau,
hapū, and/or iwi to reacquire dispossessed Māori land when it becomes available;
1.3.5. Upholding the Right of First Refusal of purchase for Māori ancestral land that is
released by the Crown;
1.3.6. Ending perpetual leases of Māori-owned land;

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Housing and Sustainable Communities Policy --- Reviewed: 2022 — Version: 17 June 2026

3

<!-- page 4 -->

1.3.7. Amending the Public Works Act to prevent compulsory acquisition of Māori
customary land and Māori freehold land, as defined in the Te Ture Whenua Māori
Act; and
1.3.8. Support Māori to settle land disputes and challenges using tikanga Māori-led
processes.

2.

Housing as a Public Good and Basic Right

Issues
House buying and renting are increasingly unaffordable for many. Thousands of mainly lowincome and other housing-marginalised New Zealanders do not have adequate housing, living
unhoused or in cars, motels, camping grounds, or overcrowded or substandard housing. Housing
is often inappropriate for marginalised groups, including disabled people and people from
communities in which large, extended families live together. Inadequate housing leads to adverse
health outcomes. This housing crisis, rooted in the commodification of housing, is exacerbated
by land banking and vacant, underutilised housing stock.

Actions
A. Housing as a Human Right
2.1. Treat housing as a human right by:
2.1.1. Establishing a right to housing in legislation that requires the State to ensure all New
Zealanders are adequately housed in safe, healthy, accessible, affordable housing;
and
2.1.2. Supporting those at high risk of facing housing disadvantage to be fully housed in
the communities of their choice.
2.2. Ensure that homelessness is rare, brief, and non-recurring by:
2.2.1. Providing healthy, safe and accessible permanent housing to unhoused people in a
way that upholds autonomy and dignity;
2.2.2. In cases where permanent housing is not appropriate, providing adequate shelters
and facilities; and
2.2.3. Adopting a housing-first approach with wrap-around support for people who have
both housing needs and other complex needs, including those who have been
evicted or had to leave their home due to domestic violence.
2.3. Provide disabled people with equitable choices about where they live, including by:
2.3.1. Providing support to transition from residential services to living in the community;
and
2.3.2. Providing timely, transparent, needs-based funding for housing modifications,
including for people living in papakāinga.
2.4. Decommodify the housing market by:
2.4.1. Investigating capping the number of houses that may be bought by an individual,
private company, or family estate; and
2.4.2. Introducing a value uplift levy where rezoning, the provision of public transport
and/or other public works result in increased land development potential.
Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Housing and Sustainable Communities Policy --- Reviewed: 2022 — Version: 17 June 2026

4

<!-- page 5 -->

B. Public housing
2.5. Ensure that everyone who does not own their own home has access to adequate public
housing by:
2.5.1. Protecting, enhancing and expanding public housing stock;
2.5.2. Phasing out means-testing and background-testing for public housing as more
public housing stock is built;
2.5.3. Giving priority for public housing to people who are living in poor accommodation
and those at high risk of extremely poor outcomes;
2.5.4. Making Kāinga Ora a government department rather than a Crown entity to ensure
a focus on service to the public, and reorienting its activities to significantly increase
public housing supply;
2.5.5. Opposing any privatisation of public housing, including public housing land; and
2.5.6. Creating public, purpose-built, rent-assisted living units for older people in all areas
that maintain community inclusiveness.
2.6. Ensure the approach to developing new public housing:
2.6.1. Fully honours Te Tiriti;
2.6.2. Uses high-quality urban design and built environments, centering new housing
developments around pre-existing communities and enabling social connections in
public housing areas; and
2.6.3. Maximises the proportion of housing supply from public and Māori housing, by
increasing the availability of government, council, community and iwi-provided
housing, aiming for universal public housing for all.
2.7. Support and partner with community housing groups whose objectives and methods
align with the principles outlined in our policy, including by:
2.7.1. Providing direct government funding for public and community housing projects,
avoiding the use of private funding such as leveraging.

C. Rental housing
2.8. Expand the rights of renters by:
2.8.1. Requiring all rental tenancies to be offered as long-term or permanent tenancies;
2.8.2. Mandating that disabled people must have an accessible house to move into before
ending a tenancy;
2.8.3. Establishing a rental warrant of fitness system that guarantees affordable, healthy
rental homes; and
2.8.4. Allowing renters to have pets, subject to any restrictions aimed at protecting wildlife.
2.9. Improve oversight and compliance of landlords delivering on their obligations to tenants,
including by:
2.9.1. Creating a register for landlords and property managers;
2.9.2. Supporting and enabling efforts (such as renters’ unions and more legal protections)
for renters to take direct action against corporate and bad-acting landlords to
demand better conditions and affordable rents; and
Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Housing and Sustainable Communities Policy --- Reviewed: 2022 — Version: 17 June 2026

5

<!-- page 6 -->

2.9.3. Reviewing the Tenancy Tribunal system to ensure it is accessible and balanced for
renters and that their privacy is protected.
2.10. Ensure that rents are affordable, including by:
2.10.1. Expanding the Income-Related Rent Subsidy to councils;
2.10.2. Implementing rent controls that limit rent increases to whichever is lower of inflation
and average wage increases; and
2.10.3. Limiting the loss of rental accommodation to short-term visitor accommodation.

3.

Sustainable Buildings

Issues
Since the early 1990s, housing construction has trended toward larger, expensive homes, while
failing to provide enough affordable, accessible homes. Construction produces high carbon
emissions and waste, and supplier monopolies exacerbate supply and affordability issues. Land
has been used inefficiently, causing urban sprawl, rising land prices, and greater infrastructure
needs. Many of the 1.8 million existing houses, especially rentals, are substandard and lack
resilience to climate change, natural hazards and utility disruptions.

Actions
3.1. Ensure, through regulation and standards, that buildings and their surroundings are
designed, constructed, renovated and repurposed to provide:
3.1.1. Efficient and effective heating and cooling of buildings;
3.1.2. Water conservation;
3.1.3. Resilience against natural hazards, including identifying and preparing for climate
change-related threats, and outages of network utilities;
3.1.4. Universal access and design;
3.1.5. For the physical and mental wellbeing of communities and residents of buildings,
including the safety of disabled people in an emergency;
3.1.6. Safe access by active and public transport, including at night;
3.1.7. Minimal embodied and operational carbon and regenerative approaches towards
energy and waste; and
3.1.8. Long life expectancy for buildings and infrastructure, using regenerative
architectural principles.
3.2. Ensure that public financial support for the renovation and repurposing of existing
buildings and the construction of new buildings is efficient, equitable, and sufficient to
achieve the above goals, with priorities for funding being:
3.2.1. Māori and Pasifika housing solutions;
3.2.2. Providing healthy buildings;
3.2.3. Reducing climate change impacts;
3.2.4. Ensuring universal access and use for disabled people and older people;
3.2.5. Improving resilience against natural hazards (including managed retreat) and
network utility outages;

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Housing and Sustainable Communities Policy --- Reviewed: 2022 — Version: 17 June 2026

6

<!-- page 7 -->

3.2.6. Providing public housing to meet the needs of those who need to move due to
climate change effects; and
3.2.7. Providing affordable housing.
3.3. Encourage residential development that:
3.3.1. Differs between city centres, urban suburbs, provincial towns, villages and rural
areas;
3.3.2. Meets diverse housing needs in each neighbourhood;
3.3.3. Is adaptable to changing life stages and multi-generational living needs;
3.3.4. Reverses the trend of the increasing size and complexity of residential buildings;
3.3.5. Contributes to the vibrancy of the community;
3.3.6. Provides for food gardens and trees; and
3.3.7. Is oriented to the sun.
3.4. Improve oversight and coordination in the housing market by:
3.4.1. Establishing a Ministry for Green Works to ensure supply of suitable housing for all
New Zealanders (along with broader goals to address the infrastructure deficit and
the climate crisis) that, when building housing:
3.4.1.1. Acts with three arms: construction, design and oversight;
3.4.1.2. Sets a bold target for public housing that will achieve the urgent aim of
accessible, healthy, secure and sustainable homes for all, including in rural
towns and villages;
3.4.1.3. Works in conjunction with other areas of government to greatly increase
government capacity to respond to interconnected challenges such as the
housing and climate crises;
3.4.1.4. Has a board that ensures co-governance with Māori, prioritises the
involvement of disabled people and includes workers and local government;
3.4.1.5. Partners with Māori organisations to provide Māori housing;
3.4.1.6. Is set up so it cannot acquire new land itself but can recommend the return
of land to Māori;
3.4.1.7. Must take a long-term active role in solving the housing crisis, and not look
to continue the current market-based approach; and
3.4.1.8. Will delegate management to Kāinga Ora or, if requested, to local councils
with oversight from Kāinga Ora to ensure maintenance standards are met.
3.4.2. Creating an independent auditing body to ensure both new and existing buildings
meet minimum modern standards.
3.5. Improve the energy efficiency of buildings by:
3.5.1. Raising mandatory energy efficiency standards in line with international best
practices for new buildings, requiring all new builds to meet them, and developing a
mechanism, incentives and a timeframe for retrofitting existing buildings to meet
them;
3.5.2. Working with the building industry and research organisations to create a building
energy performance rating system.
Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Housing and Sustainable Communities Policy --- Reviewed: 2022 — Version: 17 June 2026

7

<!-- page 8 -->

3.5.3. Establishing a requirement for residential and commercial buildings to carry an
energy performance rating when put up for sale or rent.
3.5.4. Expanding advisory services and financial assistance to households to implement
energy efficiency and conservation measures, including retrofitting inefficient
homes and providing renewable energy options
3.6. Improve understanding of sustainable housing, by:
3.6.1. Researching effective ways to improve the sustainability and design of buildings,
including construction methods designed for deconstruction and the reuse of
building components;
3.6.2. Providing education and advocacy programmes on why and how to improve housing
through renovations, repurposing and new builds;
3.6.3. Modelling sustainable building principles and high-quality design in all government
buildings, including offices and public housing; and
3.6.4. Providing a low-cost public design and advice service for sustainable buildings.

A. Construction
3.7. Ensure that the market supplying building materials is working effectively in providing
affordable, locally-produced materials for sustainable buildings, including by:
3.7.1. Breaking up building material supply monopolies, where necessary, and setting up
publicly-run alternatives; and
3.7.2. Incentivising the use of wood and other construction materials low in embodied
carbon for housing and for mid-rise buildings, and disincentivising the use of
materials high in it.
3.8. Minimise construction waste by:
3.8.1. Removing barriers to reusing demolition materials in construction, including timber
for structural purposes; and
3.8.2. Encouraging the relocation and renovation of existing timber houses where sites are
being redeveloped and/or intensified, or where the existing house is at risk from
natural hazards.
3.9. Ensure high-quality construction work by:
3.9.1. Reviewing construction contract law; and
3.9.2. Investigating mandatory insurance cover for poor construction, work not being
completed, and to provide financial protection for subcontractors.
3.10. Enable the construction sector to deliver sufficient quality housing, including by:
3.10.1. Undertaking workforce planning and training for the construction sector; and
3.10.2. Building responsiveness to construction boom and bust scenarios into the public
housing and building programmes to provide continuity of work for building industry
workers.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Housing and Sustainable Communities Policy --- Reviewed: 2022 — Version: 17 June 2026

8

<!-- page 9 -->

4.

Sustainable Communities

Issues
Poor quality urban environments reduce mobility, community engagement and belonging, and
environmental sustainability. Gentrification of urban areas too often forces low-income residents
out of the area or into substandard housing.

Actions
4.1. Support urban development that:
4.1.1. Creates vibrant, connected streets and public spaces at a human scale1;
4.1.2. Equitably adopts universal urban design principles to ensure accessibility for
disabled people;
4.1.3. Prioritises active and public transport over cars by design, with walkable2 urban
fabrics;
4.1.4. Promotes ecosystem health and community access to green space; and
4.1.5. Protects the rural-urban boundary and valuable food-growing soils.
4.2. Protect and restore nature in and around our cities by:
4.2.1. Taking an ecosystem-based approach to urban development;
4.2.2. Planting and protecting urban trees and urban ngahere;
4.2.3. Establishing guidelines for indigenous planting in urban areas, such as unused road
strips, railway corridors, esplanade reserves and other areas;
4.2.4. Establishing green networks and ecological corridors through developed areas,
including waterways; and
4.2.5. Prohibiting covenants that undermine positive environmental or social outcomes.
4.3. Equitably increase urban density by:
4.3.1. Reviewing and reducing the extent, scope and significance of ‘special character
areas’, with a refocus that prioritises Māori heritage, natural heritage, and providing
a strong heritage fabric;
4.3.2. Creating regulatory structures, including affordable housing requirements, that
require developers to provide for equitable developments; and
4.3.3. Enabling a localised assessment of urban density and form with leadership by mana
whenua and local government organisations.
4.4. Ensure that all New Zealanders, regardless of where they live, have access to all basic
services in close proximity3 including by:
4.4.1. Developing regional networks of towns and villages that are well connected by rail
and have equitable internal transport;

1

‘Human scale’ means being readily relatable to the people who interact with it, and not being overbearing
or massive.
2
‘Walkable’ means that a wide range of things you may want or need are within walking distance.
3
‘Basic services’ are those that are essential for wellbeing and participation in society, and include food,
clothing, healthcare, education, training, phone/internet, community spaces, public transport
Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Housing and Sustainable Communities Policy --- Reviewed: 2022 — Version: 17 June 2026

9

<!-- page 10 -->

4.4.2. Encouraging equitable, mixed-use development of higher residential density close
to urban centres and around public transport routes and infrastructure corridors,
including through form-based zoning;
4.4.3. Supporting the use of redistributive policies such as inclusionary zoning4.
4.5. Coordinate development and the provision of infrastructure that supports sustainable
communities, including by:
4.5.1. Developing a National Policy Statement on Urban Design;
4.5.2. Developing proactive spatial plans for satellite cities with strong rail or rapid transit
connections to major centres;
4.5.3. Developing national standards on mitigating natural hazard risks and climate change
adaptation, such as managed retreat, for use when planning development in both
urban and rural areas;
4.5.4. Establishing and maintaining an overview of housing needs; and
4.5.5. Including housing in the National Infrastructure Development Plan.
4.6. Support local communities to be included in decision-making on housing issues,
especially minority or underserved groups, including by:5
4.6.1. Supporting the formation of regional housing forums as a means of collaboratively
developing, implementing and monitoring design policy at the local level;
4.6.2. Establishing representative housing committees in all local communities that reflect
both homeowners and renters;
4.6.3. Establishing public housing tenants’ committees to give a collective voice to those
living in public housing; and
4.6.4. When requested, allowing and resourcing regulated, non-profit community housing
providers to collaboratively manage public housing.
4.7. Ensure sufficient housing in rural towns and villages to meet the needs of all generations
over all life stages, including social, rental and assisted-living housing and papakāinga.
4.8. Support the development of co-housing and other communal housing approaches,
including by:
4.8.1. Amending laws around private land ownership to enable co-operative models of land
usage; and
4.8.2. Ensuring the Unit Titles Act remains up to date, promotes the sustainability of new
apartment and multi-unit builds, and provides fair ownership and decision-making
processes.

4

‘Inclusionary zoning policies’ are planning rules that require a given share of new construction to be
affordable by people with low to moderate incomes
5
‘Minority or underserved groups’ in the housing context include Māori; disabled people; Pacific peoples;
women; rainbow communities; migrant/ethnic communities; sole parents; renters; and low socio-economic
communities throughout Aotearoa New Zealand.
Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Housing and Sustainable Communities Policy --- Reviewed: 2022 — Version: 17 June 2026

10

documents/human-rights-policy-2024-2026..title: Human Rights Policy (Green Party policy document)
documents/human-rights-policy-2024-2026..text:
# Human Rights Policy (Green Party policy document)

<!-- page 1 -->

Human Rights Policy
The Green Party is committed to ensuring that everyone’s human rights are upheld. We will
honour Te Tiriti o Waitangi by strengthening the rights of Tāngata Whenua through a te ao
Māori lens. We will safeguard the rights of future generations. We will extend our laws to cover
more human rights, sign up to more international treaties, and give the courts and human
rights institutions more power to uphold human rights.

Vision
Everyone’s rights are safeguarded and actively upheld so that everyone can participate
equitably.

Values and Principles
Decisions relating to human rights must uphold the following values and principles:
● Honour Te Tiriti o Waitangi: Tino rangatiratanga must be fundamental to the human
rights framework of Aotearoa New Zealand and be upheld at all levels.
● Ecological Wisdom: Equitable access to a healthy environment is a fundamental human
right and essential to the rights of future generations.
● Social Responsibility: Everyone has a right to an adequate standard of living, and to take
part in social, economic and cultural activities.
● Appropriate Decision-Making: Everyone must be empowered to exercise their
democratic rights. Everyone has a right to live free from discrimination and groups that
currently face structural marginalisation have a right to equity.
● Non-Violence: Diversity must be not only celebrated, but actively protected. Everyone
must be able to live free from discrimination, fear, violence and abuse.
● International Cooperation: Aotearoa New Zealand must use our resources and voice to
support the human rights of other people and nations.

Strategic Priorities
The Green Party’s strategic goals include:

“As a Party we strive to create a more connected, compassionate and equitable Aotearoa,
free from structural biases that discriminate against groups and individuals.”
Actions in this policy that will help achieve this include:
● Establishing a human rights framework that enables human rights issues to be resolved
appropriately and implements the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of
Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP), informed by Tikanga Māori, Matike Mai, Mātauranga
Māori, He Whakaputanga, and Te Tiriti o Waitangi. (1.1.3)
● Developing enduring legal frameworks that explicitly protect the rights of future
generations. (2.1.3)
Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Human Rights Policy --- Reviewed: 2024 --- Version: 17 June 2026

1

<!-- page 2 -->

● Implementing the recommendations of the Royal Commission on the Christchurch
Mosque Attacks regarding hate speech and hate crimes, and extending hate speech laws
to cover religious or ethical belief, disability, gender (including gender identity and
gender expression), sexual orientation and sex characteristics. (3.1.1)
● Extending the prohibited grounds of discrimination in the Human Rights Act to cover
caste, union activity, appearance, genetic information, gender identity, gender
expression, sex characteristics, and all sexual orientations, and reviewing the exceptions
to the prohibitions on discrimination to ensure they do not harm or exclude marginalised
groups. (3.1.2)
● Extending the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act to cover other human rights recognised in
international human rights instruments, such as social, economic and cultural rights, the
right to privacy, the right to self-determination and children’s rights, and ensuring that
our laws and practices are consistent with them. (3.3.3)
● Making the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act supreme law and entrenching it. (3.4.3)

Connected Policies
All Green Party policies apply the concept of human rights, including upholding the rights of
tangata whenua under Te Tiriti o Waitangi. Our Workforce Policy upholds the rights of workers.
Our Immigration Policy upholds the rights of refugees and migrants. Our Justice Policy upholds
the right to justice and the rights of detainees. Our policy treats access to Housing and Health
as human rights. Our Governance Policy creates robust and effective legal rights for the natural
world. Our Disability Policy upholds the rights of disabled people. Other policies uphold the rights
of Children, Women, the Rainbow community and Tagata Moana.

Policy Positions
1.

Individual Rights and Te Ao Māori

Issues
The current legalistic view of human rights is a colonial one that focuses on individual civil and
political rights. It does not recognise interconnectedness, collective rights, or indigenous rights,
and does not balance rights with responsibilities. This undermines the rights of Tāngata Whenua
upheld by Te Tiriti o Waitangi and conflicts with Tikanga and Mātauranga Māori.

Actions
1.1.

Ensure that Māori communities are able to exercise their collective rights, including
by:
1.1.1.
Establishing a full-time Māori Rights Commissioner on the Human Rights
Commission.
1.1.2.
Amending or opposing any legislation that is found to be inconsistent with Te
Tiriti o Waitangi by the Waitangi Tribunal.
1.1.3.
Establishing a human rights framework that enables human rights issues to be
resolved appropriately and implements the United Nations Declaration on the
Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP), informed by Tikanga Māori, Matike Mai,
Mātauranga Māori, He Whakaputanga and Te Tiriti o Waitangi.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Human Rights Policy --- Reviewed: 2024 --- Version: 17 June 2026

2

<!-- page 3 -->

1.1.4.

2.

Resourcing the Waitangi Tribunal to reach consensus on the resolution of, and
restitution for, all outstanding breaches of Te Tiriti o Waitangi, broaden its
binding decision-making authority, and implement its recommendations to date.

Rights of Future Generations

Issues
Human activity is undermining the foundations that allow life on Earth to thrive. Climate change,
loss of biodiversity, and its other impacts are disrupting earth systems. This undermines the
rights of future generations of all species, including humans, to a liveable planet.

Actions
2.1.

3.

Ensure that the human rights of future generations are protected under the law,
including by:
2.1.1.
Adding a right to a clean, healthy, and sustainable environment to the New
Zealand Bill of Rights Act.
2.1.2.
Developing enduring legal frameworks that explicitly protect the rights of future
generations.

Intersectionality and Privilege

Issues
Human rights are not adequately protected by our laws and institutions. The rights of some
groups of people are undermined by many systems that are designed for or benefitting the most
privileged among us. Moreover, access to the resources necessary for legal defence of these
rights is not universally accessible.

Actions
3.1.

3.2.

Through human rights instruments, ensure equality for all groups and people, without
discrimination and prejudice, including by:
3.1.1.

Implementing the recommendations of the Royal Commission on the
Christchurch Mosque Attacks regarding hate speech and hate crimes, and
extending hate speech laws to cover religious or ethical belief, disability, gender
(including gender identity and gender expression), sexual orientation and sex
characteristics.

3.1.2.

Extending the prohibited grounds of discrimination in the Human Rights Act to
cover caste, union activity, appearance, genetic information, gender identity,
gender expression, sex characteristics, and all sexual orientations, and reviewing
the exceptions to the prohibitions on discrimination to ensure they do not harm
or exclude marginalised groups.

3.1.3.

Reviewing all laws to identify and remove any discrimination or human rights
breaches.

3.1.4.

Ensuring that all new laws do not discriminate or constitute a human rights
breach.

Ensure that remedies for human rights breaches are readily accessible to all, including
by:

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Human Rights Policy --- Reviewed: 2024 --- Version: 17 June 2026

3

<!-- page 4 -->

3.3.

3.4.

3.5.

3.6.

3.2.1.

Expanding the availability of damages and other redress for human rights
breaches

3.2.2.

Requiring all government agencies to publish regular, audited reports of
indicators which assess the human rights impacts of their activities and
implement programmes that remedy them

3.2.3.

Expanding the functions and powers of the Human Rights Commission to ensure
that it can address all human rights issues.

Ensure that all human rights are recognised and protected effectively by our laws,
including by:
3.3.1.

Amending or opposing any legislation that is found to be inconsistent with the
New Zealand Bill of Rights Act by the Attorney-General or the courts.

3.3.2.

Ratifying international human rights treaties to which New Zealand is currently
not a party and removing New Zealand’s reservations to international human
rights treaties;

3.3.3.

Extending the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act to cover other human rights
recognised in international human rights instruments, such as social, economic
and cultural rights, the right to privacy, the right to self-determination and
children’s rights.

Ensure that human rights institutions protect everyone’s rights effectively and
independently of government, including by:
3.4.1.

Ensuring that human rights institutions have sufficient funding to be effective
and prompt in their roles;

3.4.2.

Making Human Rights Commissioners Officers of Parliament, appointed by
Parliament rather than by Ministers;

3.4.3.

Making the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act supreme law and entrenching it.

Ensure that vulnerable communities are assisted to realise their human rights,
including by:
3.5.1.

Empowering the Ombudsman to close places of detention for failure to correct
repeated findings of non-compliance with inspections.

3.5.2.

Resourcing and supporting community organisations that advocate for human
rights or support people to raise human rights concerns.

3.5.3.

Teaching Human Rights in schools.

Ensure that Aotearoa New Zealand respects the human rights of everyone
everywhere, including by:
3.6.1.

Amending the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act to explicitly apply to the actions of
the New Zealand Government when it acts overseas.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Human Rights Policy --- Reviewed: 2024 --- Version: 17 June 2026

4

documents/immigration-policy-2017-2026.m.title: Immigration Policy (Green Party policy document)
documents/immigration-policy-2017-2026.m.text:
# Immigration Policy (Green Party policy document)

<!-- page 1 -->

Immigration Policy
For those who would like to come to live in Aotearoa New Zealand, the Green Party will ensure
that the process of selecting immigrants is fair, reasonable and flexible, and that immigrants are
treated with dignity and respect, including, for example, through family reunification and fair
employment conditions. The Green Party believes that Aotearoa New Zealand should remain firm
in our commitment and humanitarian responsibilities towards international refugees and asylum
seekers.

Vision
A progressive immigration system that is humane, fair, practical, sustainable, and sensitive to
the requirements and concerns of all migrants as well as tangata whenua and tangata Tiriti.

Values and Principles
- Honour Te Tiriti o Waitangi: The right for non-Māori to live in Aotearoa New Zealand
derives from Te Tiriti o Waitangi. Māori, as tangata whenua, should have a partnership
role in determining Aotearoa New Zealand's immigration policies.

- Ecological Wisdom: Immigration policy should consider the environmental impacts of
population changes and support climate goals.

- Social Responsibility: All immigration applicants, migrants, asylum seekers and refugees,
should be treated with dignity, compassion and respect in accordance with international
conventions on human rights.

- Appropriate Decision-Making: Immigration processes should be open, accountable and
responsive. Local communities should be involved in policy decision-making and
implementation.

- Non-Violence: All migrants and refugees should be welcomed and included in Aotearoa
New Zealand society, such that they feel a sense of belonging. Tolerance, acceptance and
understanding is important in a diverse and multicultural society.

- Responsibility: Aotearoa New Zealand should act as a responsible member of the
international community. Aotearoa New Zealand is a Pacific nation with a Pacific history
and its immigration policies and practices should reflect that.

- Distributed benefits: The positive contributions that migrants make to the social, cultural
and economic life of Aotearoa New Zealand should be shared across all regions, not just
in the main centres.

Strategic Priorities
The Green Party’s strategic goals include:

“As a Party we strive to create a more connected, compassionate and equal Aotearoa,
free from structural biases that discriminate against groups and individuals.
Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Immigration Policy --- Reviewed: 2017 --- Version: 19 January 2026

<!-- page 2 -->

“Comprehensive support for communities and individuals affected (...) by the impacts of
climate change within New Zealand and the Pacific will be well established.”
Actions in this policy that will help achieve this include:
- Actively support Māori aspirations for a Tiriti-based immigration system (...). (1.1)

- Advocate for a Pacific Passport to allow for free movement between the islands and
Aotearoa. (2.1.1)

- Make specific provision in immigration legislation for people displaced by climate change,
based on need. (2.1.2)

- Ensure that immigration policies do not discriminate based on applicants' countries of
origin, ethnicities, cultures, age, gender, sexual orientation, and all other prohibited
grounds of discrimination. (3.1)

- Increase our refugee quota and the resources required to provide adequate refugee
services. (4.1.2)

- Require employers to pay temporary workers no less than local workers, and to provide
them with the same working conditions as local workers. (6.9.1)

Connected Policies
Refugees are part of our Pacific-oriented and Human Rights-based approach to Global Affairs
and Climate Change. Migrant workers are part of our Workforce and contribute to Business
success. Migrants, including international students, must be well-supported in Education and by
other public services, such as Health and public Housing.

Policy Positions
1.

Immigration and Te Tiriti o Waitangi

The presence of non-Māori peoples in Aotearoa New Zealand is a result of Te Tiriti o Waitangi
but immigration systems do not reflect this.

1.2.

Devolving resources to whānau, hapū, and iwi to strengthen traditional

Initiating a Tiriti-based negotiation with tangata whenua to determine how Māori

Provide an initial orientation and ongoing education to all new immigrants that
includes information about Aotearoa New Zealand civics, culture, and

Support collaboration between resettlement programmes and interested

Aotearoa New Zealand in the Pacific Region

Immigration Applications and Selection

The process of selecting migrants is not always fair, reasonable, and flexible. This can influence

Migrants can struggle with culture shock and, especially people of colour, can be made to feel

6.2.

# Justice Policy (Green Party policy document)

<!-- page 1 -->

Justice Policy
The Green Party envisages a justice system based on Te Tiriti o Waitangi, tikanga Māori and te
ao Māori values. We will prioritise restorative justice, rehabilitation, and community responses to
offending. We will focus on prevention, early intervention, and addressing underlying issues such
as mental health. We will tackle bias, discrimination and inequalities in the justice system, while
removing barriers to access to justice and strengthening accountability to ensure that it upholds
everyone’s rights.

Vision
The justice system heals and protects people and communities equitably.

Values and Principles
Decisions relating to the justice system must uphold the following values and principles:
- Honour Te Tiriti o Waitangi: Tikanga Māori is the first law of Aotearoa. The justice system
should uphold tino rangatiratanga and ensure equity for Māori.

- Ecological Wisdom: Environmental justice is an integral part of justice. The legal system
should protect nature now and in the future.

- Social Responsibility: Everyone is entitled to equitable access to justice, to a fair hearing,
and to be treated with respect in the justice system. Everyone deserves an opportunity to
atone for past wrongs and to reintegrate into society.

- Appropriate Decision-Making: The rule of law and judicial independence are fundamental
to achieving justice. Transparency is necessary to ensure that justice is both done and
seen to be done.

- Non-Violence: The justice system should engage all participants with compassion, ensure
support is available, and seek to be transformative and restorative rather than punitive.

- International Obligations: Honouring international obligations and institutions is necessary
to ensure justice and peace, both internationally and in Aotearoa New Zealand.

Strategic Priorities
The Green Party’s strategic goals include:

“As a Party we strive to create a more connected, compassionate, and equal Aotearoa,
free from structural biases that discriminate against groups and individuals.“
Actions in this policy that will help achieve this include:
- Establishing a Mana Ōrite (equal power) governance model under which Māori and Crown
agencies share in justice sector decision-making. (1.1.2)

- Investing in a Tiriti-based primary prevention and early intervention model. (1.2.1)

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Justice Policy --- Reviewed: 2025 --- Version: 17 June 2026

1

<!-- page 2 -->

- Funding restorative and transformative justice initiatives, including through Rangatahi
and Matariki Courts. (1.3.1)

- Expanding legal aid eligibility to cover all people who need it, increasing payment rates,
and providing it as grants. (2.1.3)

- Enabling judicial discretion in sentencing, including by abolishing mandatory minimum
sentences, life sentences, preventive detention, limits on sentence discounts, and limits
on when home detention can be imposed instead of imprisonment. (3.6.2)

- Increasing funding for counselling and mental health support for victims, whānau,
witnesses, defendants, and legal professionals engaging in the justice system. (3.13.1)

- Replacing youth justice residences and boot camps with whānau and community-based
rehabilitation services for young people. (3.14.1)

Connected Policies
The justice system must uphold Human Rights and Te Tiriti o Waitangi. Prisoner voting and
constitutional issues are addressed in the Governance Policy, while the Global Affairs Policy
covers international law. Crime and justice issues are connected to social and economic
inequalities that are addressed in policies such as Livelihoods, Housing and Sustainable
Communities, and Education. Failure to provide timely and sufficient Disability and mental Health
support contributes to the overrepresentation of disabled people, including neurodivergent
people and people with mental health conditions, in the justice system. Drug laws are addressed
in the Drug Law Reform Policy. Pay equity and workers’ rights are covered in the Workforce Policy
and are relevant to workers in the justice sector.

The justice system does not honour the Crown’s obligations to tangata whenua under Te Tiriti o

Access to justice

Issues
Many people lack access to justice, including legal representation, services, and information. This
leads to inequities in civil, family, youth, and criminal courts. Barriers to justice prevent
participants in the justice system from achieving restoration and healing. Ultimately, inequities
in accessibility mean that some communities are served by the justice system, and others are
oppressed under it.

The justice system prioritises punishment over rehabilitation. It fails to respond to underlying

judges to grant bail; and

3.5.3.

Requiring bail to be granted unless remanding in custody is necessary to protect
the public from violence and this risk cannot be managed by bail conditions.

Ensure that sentencing prioritises rehabilitation over punitive approaches, including
by:
3.6.1.

Amending the purposes and principles of sentencing in the Sentencing Act to
prioritise rehabilitation;

3.6.2.

Enabling judicial discretion in sentencing, including by abolishing mandatory
minimum sentences, life sentences, preventive detention, limits on sentence
discounts, and limits on when home detention can be imposed instead of
imprisonment; and

3.6.3.

Prohibiting prison sentences from being imposed unless no other sentence can
protect the public.

Ensure that the criminal justice system prioritises community programmes and
facilities, including by:
3.7.1.

Increasing funding for community rehabilitation programmes and facilities;

3.7.2.

Ending the incarceration and detention of intellectually disabled, cognitively
impaired, and mentally ill people; and

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Justice Policy --- Reviewed: 2025 --- Version: 17 June 2026

5

<!-- page 6 -->

3.7.3.
3.8.

3.9.

3.10.

Replacing prisons with community programmes and facilities that reduce
reoffending.

Uphold and strengthen the rights of people in prison, including by:
3.8.1.

Strengthening complaints and monitoring processes for prisons, including
enabling independent monitoring institutions to enforce their recommendations;

3.8.2.

Enabling prisoners to challenge breaches of the United Nations Standard
Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (the Mandela Rules); and

3.8.3.

Extending employment rights to prisoners who are working, including the
minimum wage and rights under health and safety law.

Eliminate prison practices that undermine human rights and rehabilitation, including
by:
3.9.1.

Ensuring prisoners have access to facilities and resources to meet their needs;

3.9.2.

Ending double bunking and the use of spit hoods, and restricting the use of
solitary confinement; and

3.9.3.

Abolishing for-profit prisons.

Maximise the connection of people in prison with whānau and other support in the
community, including by:

3.10.1.

Supporting increased unlimited communications between prisoners and their
whānau and community;

3.10.2.

Minimising transfers between prisons and prioritising keeping prisoners near
their whānau and community; and

3.10.3.

Enabling monitored digital access to support rehabilitation and reintegration
programmes.

3.11.

Ensure that the justice system reduces reoffending through effective reintegration
into communities, including by:

3.11.1.

Improving access to, and levels of, financial, material, and practical support for
released prisoners;

3.11.2.

Only allowing employers to access or ask about criminal records of prospective
employees that are relevant to the particular job; and

3.11.3.

Ensuring rehabilitation programmes prepare prisoners to be released on parole
when they first become eligible, unless they have committed further offences.

3.12.

Ensure that the justice system fairly manages parole, home detention and bail,
including by:

3.12.1.

Enabling connection with whānau;

3.12.2.

Providing suitable housing where necessary to enable people to be granted bail,
home detention, or parole; and

3.12.3.

Replacing the practice of incarcerating people for breaching parole, home
detention, or bail conditions with community-based responses.

3.13.

Ensure that all participants in the justice system are able to access appropriate health
and wellbeing support, including by:

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Justice Policy --- Reviewed: 2025 --- Version: 17 June 2026

6

<!-- page 7 -->

3.13.1.

Increasing funding for counselling and mental health support for victims,
whānau, witnesses, defendants, and legal professionals engaging in the justice
system;

3.13.2.

Prioritising early trauma-informed mental health diagnosis and treatment for
people accused or convicted of crimes; and

3.13.3.

Establishing individual access for prisoners to counselling and trauma support.

3.14.

Ensure that youth justice recognises the developing nature of young people, including
by:

3.14.1.

Replacing youth justice residences and boot camps with whānau and
community-based rehabilitation services for young people;

3.14.2.

Prohibiting young people under the age of 18 from being detained and tried as
adults; and

3.14.3.

Raising the age of criminal responsibility to at least 14 years old and the youth
justice age to 25.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Justice Policy --- Reviewed: 2025 --- Version: 17 June 2026

7

documents/land-use-and-soils-policy-2022.text:
# Land Use and Soils Policy (Green Party policy document)

<!-- page 1 -->

Land Use and Soils Policy
The Green Party will improve the ways we use and care for land, for the sake of current and
future generations, other species, and ecosystem health. We will ensure that land use and land
cover are managed in accordance with Te Tiriti o Waitangi. Protecting soils and minimising the
impacts of mining will be priorities.

Vision
Land and soil ecosystems are protected and regenerated for present and future generations, to
nurture our wellbeing and livelihoods, and provide food, medicine, and spiritual fulfilment.

Values and Principles
- Honour Te Tiriti o Waitangi: We affirm tino rangatiratanga of iwi, hapū and whānau as
kaitiaki of this whenua. The perspectives, approaches, needs, and aspirations of tangata
whenua are embedded in the philosophy and approach to land and soil management.

- Ecological Wisdom: We must respect land and soil as part of the ecosystems we rely on.
Soil ecosystems have intrinsic value, and humanity needs to steward the natural world by
understanding and working within the carrying capacity of the land.

- Social Responsibility: The need for equity in the sustainable use of land and soil resources
is acknowledged.

- Appropriate Decision-Making: Good governance (i.e., the processes by which institutions
and other parties make and implement decisions in order to manage resources efficiently
and ensure human rights), and strong institutions should underpin land and soil
management.

- Non-Violence: Conflict resolution over land and soil management should ensure no
violence is felt by te taiao, the creatures that call it home, and always honour Te Tiriti.

- The mauri of land - its cultural, spiritual, historical, conservation and ecological aspects are prioritised. At the same time, agricultural land is valued for its ability to produce
healthy food, fibre and wood and is regenerated and managed sustainably to ensure that
its productive potential is protected and enhanced.

Strategic Priorities
The Green Party’s strategic goals include:

“All native species and their habitats will be thriving or on a path to recovery in terrestrial,
freshwater and marine environments.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Land Use and Soils Policy — Reviewed: 2022 — Version: 19 Sep 2025

1

<!-- page 2 -->

Our laws and practices will respect the biological integrity of all life, while prioritising the
health of indigenous species and ecosystems.
The customary and decision making roles of whānau, hapū and iwi will be integral to
decisions about resource use.
Decision-making about resource use will provide for community participation and
environmental justice.”
Actions in this policy that will help achieve this include:
- Upholding the right of tangata whenua to exercise customary practices regarding soil
sovereignty and māra kai on their land. (1.1.2)

- Using both mātauranga Māori and Western science in research and the development of
land and soil policies and practices. (2.1.3)

- Encouraging and resourcing landowners and communities to set marginal and erosionprone lands aside for permanent revegetation. (1.5.1)

- Encouraging and supporting the use of soil conservation and earthworks best practice,
including mechanical and biological control techniques (2.2.3)

- Ensure that the regulatory framework for mining avoids and mitigates harms (3.1)

- End the extraction of coal, oil, and gas, consistent with the urgency and necessity of
limiting global heating to 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels (3.5)

Connected Policies
This policy discusses land use and soils within the context of Biodiversity and Environmental
Regeneration, alongside our Freshwater and Marine Policies. Land health is impacted by human
activity, including Agriculture, Forestry, Housing and Sustainable Communities, Waste and
Hazardous Substances, and Climate Change. Resource extraction from land can be minimised
through resource and Waste management, including circular economy practices.
For our response to colonial land dispossession, please see our Kaupapa Māori and Te Tiriti o
Waitangi Policies.

Policy Positions
1.

Land Use Management

Issues
Extractive land uses that emphasise productivity and economic potential have dominated since
colonisation. Land used for farming and commercial forestry, urban areas, and infrastructure has
expanded by clearing or reclaiming vast areas of indigenous forest, wetlands, and other
ecosystems. This loss is ongoing, especially in lowland areas, as is the loss of highly fertile land
and soil to forestry and urban development. Water quality, watershed hydrology, habitat and
species composition, climate and carbon storage have all been negatively affected by changes
in land cover.
Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Land Use and Soils Policy — Reviewed: 2022 — Version: 19 Sep 2025

2

<!-- page 3 -->

Actions
1.1.

1.2.

1.3.

1.4.

Affirm the tino rangatiratanga of iwi, hapū and whānau when making decisions on
land use, including by:
1.1.1.

Facilitating strategic co-governance of ecological regions, informed by robust
assessment (including physical characteristics and risks), community
consultation, planning, and monitoring.

1.1.2.

Upholding the right of tangata whenua to exercise customary practices
regarding soil sovereignty and māra kai on their land.

1.1.3.

In partnership with tangata whenua, exploring a tikanga Māori-based system of
public access to Crown and private land.

Ensure that land use management systems:
1.2.1.

Protect wāhi tapu | sacred sites

1.2.2.

Reflect the urgency of climate change mitigation and adaptation

1.2.3.

Align with soil type, supports soil biodiversity, and prevent erosion

1.2.4.

Protect freshwater ecosystems, including water quality and flows

1.2.5.

Restore, connect, and protect native species and ecosystems

1.2.6.

Protect unique or vulnerable landscapes, including high-country property, from
uses that are outside the public interest.

1.2.7.

Recognise, protect, and support the restoration of significant indigenous
heritage and cultural landscapes, including within urban areas

1.2.8.

Recognise the interconnection of land use and animal husbandry methods with
ecosystem and human health, including zoonotic diseases

1.2.9.

Balance the rights and responsibilities of individual property owners against the
public good and collective responsibilities.

Mitigate green field development, and regenerate and protect valuable food growing
soils, including by:
1.3.1.

Identifying and mapping highly productive land and protecting it from urban
development.

1.3.2.

Protecting and enhancing greenbelts, and enhancing the legislative protection
of the rural-urban boundary

Ensure that land use patterns and functions in buffer zones adjacent to protected
areas and public conservation land are compatible with and complement conservation
objectives, including by:
1.4.1.

Establishing land use linkages and ecological corridors, including through
developed areas.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Land Use and Soils Policy — Reviewed: 2022 — Version: 19 Sep 2025

3

<!-- page 4 -->

1.4.2.

1.5.

2.

Improving processes for leasing and selling rural Crown land to protect
conservation values, public access to the conservation estate, rural
communities, and the interests of relevant iwi and hapū and the Crown.

Ensure all ecological regions in Aotearoa New Zealand have a minimum five percent
of the land area is in native vegetation or set aside for the restoration of nature, by:
1.5.1.

Encouraging and resourcing landowners and communities to set marginal and
erosion-prone lands aside for permanent revegetation.

1.5.2.

Devising and implementing a land cover strategy and action plan to rehabilitate
and restore degraded land cover systems of national concern, in partnership
with tangata whenua.

1.5.3.

Requiring all landowners and land developers to replace any displaced area of
ecological value with a comparable area of equal or greater ecological value.

Soil Protection

Issues
Soil quality and health is being degraded by intensive practices in primary industries and urban
development and pollution. Common issues include soil compaction and over-fertilisation. The
past use of hazardous substances in industry, agriculture, and horticulture has left a legacy of
soil contamination. Naturally high rates of erosion have accelerated due to deforestation, grazing
animals, intensive land use, and climate change, causing hundreds of millions of tonnes of soil
to enter rivers each year, valuable topsoil to be lost, and stored carbon to be released.

Actions
2.1.

2.2.

Establish a national soil management agency to:
2.1.1.

Develop and implement a National Soil Strategy that promotes soil health, soil
conservation, and carbon sequestration.

2.1.2.

Set direction on soil use, policies, and research, such as improving knowledge of
how the land responds to human pressures, understanding the potential limits
to land-use intensification and other development, and discovering what drives
natural resource management decisions.

2.1.3.

Use both mātauranga Māori and Western science in research and the
development of land and soil policies and practices.

2.1.4.

Promote objective assessment, monitoring and accountability among all
stakeholders.

2.1.5.

Prevent land from being used beyond its capabilities

Minimise soil erosion, including by:

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Land Use and Soils Policy — Reviewed: 2022 — Version: 19 Sep 2025

4

<!-- page 5 -->

2.3.

2.4.

2.2.1.

Requiring the soil surface to be protected with vegetation cover as soon as
possible after the harvest of trees and crops, earthworks, or other vegetation
clearance.

2.2.2.

Expanding soil protection programmes, such as the Hill Country Erosion
Programme, to improve environmental quality and reduce flooding.

2.2.3.

Encourage and support the use of soil conservation and earthworks best
practice, including mechanical and biological control techniques

Ensure soil pollution is effectively regulated and controlled, including by:
2.3.1.

Requiring treatment and remediation costs to be paid by the polluters.

2.3.2.

Preventing herbicides, fungicides, and pesticides from damaging soil system
integrity, including phasing out all that do.

Protect and enhance the role of soil in re-capturing or sequestering carbon and
retaining water.
2.4.1.

2.5.

3.

Develop a national wetland strategy that prioritises the establishment and
restoration of wetlands to accumulate carbon in areas that are otherwise
unsuitable for productive agriculture, such as boggy and flood-prone areas.

Support landowners to retain and regenerate soils and improve soil ecosystems,
including by:
2.5.1.

Providing soil mapping and soil quality information to land-use and farm
consultants, farmers, developers, and other land users.

2.5.2.

Monitoring and reporting on the loss and quality of soils, rates of soil carbon
sequestration, and soil biodiversity.

2.5.3.

Funding research and development to identify new innovations for building soil,
such as commercial-scale production and application of humus.

Mining1

Issues
Mining is an exploitative process, which adversely impacts the ecological, historical,
archaeological and/or cultural significance of the land and sea. These impacts arise not only from
the physical disturbance and noise caused by extraction, but also from toxic substances released
by the extraction process. Mining often extracts materials that directly contribute to the climate
crisis through their greenhouse gas emissions. Furthermore, the profits usually go to large
corporations, while local communities pay for the clean-up. Mined materials are too often
exported out of our country, representing a loss to current and future generations.

1

Mining: The term is used in the broad sense to include quarrying, well operations, beneficiating (e.g., crushing,
screening, washing, and flotation), and other preparation customarily performed at the mine site, or as a part of
mining activity.
Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Land Use and Soils Policy — Reviewed: 2022 — Version: 19 Sep 2025

5

<!-- page 6 -->

Actions
3.1.

3.2.

Ensure that the regulatory framework for mining avoids and mitigates harms,
including:
3.1.1.

Honouring Te Tiriti o Waitangi, including upholding the right of Māori to exercise
tino rangatiratanga over their lands and resources, including minerals and
ecosystems and species impacted by mining;

3.1.2.

Limiting mining to essential materials:

3.1.2.1.

that are required for our transition to a just and sustainable circular
economy, meet essential needs, or serve another socially essential
purpose (as determined by public consultation);

3.1.2.2.

for which renewable alternatives are not available; and

3.1.2.3.

for which maximum recovery and recycling of available materials has been
achieved, but is proven insufficient for the needs of Aotearoa New Zealand;
and

3.1.3.

Only allowing mining methods that minimise the risk of environmental and social
damage;

3.1.4.

Taking a precautionary approach to new mining technologies, especially for
offshore mining;

3.1.5.

Prioritising the needs of the natural world and future generations and providing
strict environmental protections relating to both the location of the extraction,
so that mining in significant ecological areas is avoided, and the environmental
impacts of extraction techniques; and

3.1.6.

Requiring those responsible to rapidly remedy any adverse effects.

Ensure that resource consent decision-making in relation to mining:
3.2.1.

Protects ecological, social, cultural, and landscape values;

3.2.2.

Ensures mining can only proceed within ecosystem baselines and other
acceptable environmental limits;

3.2.3.

Considers the greenhouse gas contribution of mining activities and other
downstream effects;

3.2.4.

Provides New Zealanders with equitable opportunities to be involved in decisions
about mining;

3.2.5.

Enables communities, whānau, hapū, and iwi to protect areas of historical,
archaeological, and/or cultural significance from mining, including the foreshore
and seabed; and

3.2.6.

Upholds the right of landholders, including Māori, to deny access for mining on
their land.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Land Use and Soils Policy — Reviewed: 2022 — Version: 19 Sep 2025

6

<!-- page 7 -->

3.3.

3.4.

3.5.

3.6.

3.7.

Ensure a Just Transition2 for communities impacted by new or declining mining
activities, including by:
3.3.1.

Developing a strategy for affected industries, regions and workers, in
partnership with tangata whenua, communities, unions and local economic
development associations; and

3.3.2.

Requiring decommissioned mining sites to be returned to hapū and iwi after
restoration by mining companies has been completed.

Ensure that the costs associated with the entire lifecycle of mining operations remain
with the operators, including by:
3.4.1.

Requiring bonds and/or minimum insurance for “worst case scenario” pollution
events caused by mining activities, on land and at sea;

3.4.2.

Establishing a levy on all mining operations in Aotearoa New Zealand, to fund
the decommissioning of mines and the clean-up and remediation of mining land
held by bankrupt or null companies; and

3.4.3.

Strengthening the regulatory regime for the existing oil and gas extraction
sector, to minimise greenhouse gas emissions from extraction processes.

End the extraction of coal, oil, and gas, consistent with the urgency and necessity of
limiting global heating to 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels, by:
3.5.1.

Prohibiting new coal, oil and gas prospecting, new exploration and mining
permits, the extension of expiring permits, and the expansion of existing permit
areas both offshore and onshore;

3.5.2.

Establishing a clear timeframe for phasing out coal, oil, and gas extraction
(onshore and offshore), including site remediation; and

3.5.3.

Working proactively to support other fossil fuel-producing countries to do the
same.

Phase out the extraction of other non-essential materials, by:
3.6.1.

Implementing sinking caps on sand mining that cover all sand types, in both
onshore and offshore areas; and

3.6.2.

Prohibiting industrial-scale hard-rock gold/silver mining.

Protect marine communities and ecosystems from the negative impacts of mining,
by:
3.7.1.

Amending the environmental management framework for offshore activities to
ensure better protection of the marine environment beyond the 12-mile limit;

2

A Just Transition requires a system transformation that applies principles of fairness, equity, and wellbeing to
uphold the rights and dignity of all involved. In this context, it is required to address our current climate, ecological,
and social crises.
Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Land Use and Soils Policy — Reviewed: 2022 — Version: 19 Sep 2025

7

<!-- page 8 -->

3.8.

3.7.2.

Prohibiting all seabed mining and seismic prospecting within Aotearoa New
Zealand’s territorial sea and Exclusive Economic Zone; and

3.7.3.

Supporting our Pacific Island neighbours in their leadership on the protection of
the marine environment from mining.

Protect public conservation land from the negative impacts of mining, by:
3.8.1.

Prohibiting new exploration, prospecting, and mining on or under all public
conservation land;

3.8.2.

Tightly controlling existing mining (including post-mining remediation) on public
conservation land and reserves, in partnership with tangata whenua, and
through consultation with environmental groups, local communities, and the
public;

3.8.3.

Requiring mining activities to stop immediately when rare, endemic species are
found to be present on the mining site;

3.8.4.

Gazetting areas of public conservation land that are deserving of schedule 4
(Crown Minerals Act) status but have been omitted from schedule 4 because of
their mineral potential; and

3.8.5.

Rejecting the notion of trading public conservation land for other land to
facilitate extractive activities.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Land Use and Soils Policy — Reviewed: 2022 — Version: 19 Sep 2025

8

documents/livelihoods-policy-2025.md.title: Livelihoods Policy (Green Party policy document)
documents/livelihoods-policy-2025.md.text:
# Livelihoods Policy (Green Party policy document)

<!-- page 1 -->

Livelihoods Policy
The Green Party will take a Tiriti-based approach to financial and material security. We will ensure
that the income support system is sufficient, accessible, and dignifying, and recognises unpaid
labour. We will support low-income households to minimise debt, including regulating lenders.
We will ensure that everyone has access to the services and resources they need to meet their
basic needs.

Vision
Everyone has enough income and resources to live a fulfilling life with dignity and participate
fully in society.

Values and Principles
Income support and other related policy decisions must be consistent with the following values
and principles:
- Honour Te Tiriti o Waitangi: Hapū and iwi Māori have the right to self-determination of
their livelihoods.

- Ecological Wisdom: We can choose to have a thriving society, where everyone has
enough, that works in harmony with the natural world.

- Social Responsibility: We have a responsibility to equitably support all those who live on
this land to flourish.

- Appropriate Decision-Making: Decisions must be made through appropriate engagement
with experts and those impacted by the decision, to find effective pathways forward.

- Non-Violence: Everyone has the right to livelihoods that are free from institutionalised
violence, coercion and discrimination.

Strategic Priorities
The Green Party’s strategic goals include:

“Poverty will be eliminated, everyone will have enough income and wealth will be held
more equally.”
Actions in this policy that will help achieve this include:
- Increasing main benefit levels to a liveable income and ensuring supplementary benefits
are sufficient. (1.2.1)

- Ensure that welfare service delivery is proactive, mana-enhancing, accessible, and
inclusive of a diverse range of people’s needs (1.3)

- Establishing a legal right to a minimum income and guaranteeing this income. (1.4.3)

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Livelihoods Policy — Reviewed: 2025 — Version: 04 August 2025

1

<!-- page 2 -->

- Pass legislation that prevents exploitative lending and debt collection, relating to both
currency and goods. (2.2)

- Resourcing underfunded basic services that support well-being, including preventative
and/or early intervention services. (3.1.1)

- Legislating clear rights, rooted in Te Tiriti o Waitangi, for basic resources, and legislating
the responsibilities of the Crown to provide them. (3.2.3)

Connected Policies
As well as income support, the role of the Government in the Economy includes taxation and
redistribution of wealth. Livelihoods are also affected by policy areas such as Workforce,
Education, Housing, and Climate Change. Some areas experience more livelihood challenges with
cascading impacts (see our Community and the Economy, Health and Justice Policy, for
example), as do different sectors (e.g. Agriculture and Arts).

Policy Positions
1.

Income equity and security

Issues
Increasing income and wealth disparity, high structural unemployment rates, low minimum wage,
and the poverty cycle continue to create long-term inequalities that disproportionately harm
vulnerable communities who cannot meet their own basic living costs.

Actions
1.1.

1.2.

Ensure that the welfare system:
1.1.1.

Provides an individualised income and basic services that are sufficient to meet
basic needs;

1.1.2.

Provides support in relation to unemployment, illness, disability, retirement,
bereavement or family breakdown, and emergency or crisis;

1.1.3.

Recognises and compensates unpaid labour, including caring and household
responsibilities;

1.1.4.

Equitably supports all New Zealanders, regardless of age, location, household
arrangements, disability, or any other factor;

1.1.5.

Supports, but does not require, participation in the paid workforce;

1.1.6.

Responds promptly to changes in circumstance and concerns raised; and

1.1.7.

Is informed by the Crown’s responsibilities under Te Tiriti o Waitangi and is
effective in improving outcomes for Māori.

Reform the welfare system, including by:
1.2.1.

Increasing main benefit levels to a liveable income and ensuring supplementary
benefits are sufficient; and

1.2.2.

Implementing the 2019 Welfare Advisory Group recommendations, including:

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Livelihoods Policy — Reviewed: 2025 — Version: 04 August 2025

2

<!-- page 3 -->

1.3.

Refining abatement considerations, rates, and thresholds to support
beneficiaries in transitioning into employment and avoid disincentivising
employment.

1.2.2.2.

Working with Māori to develop whānau-centred, simplified, strengthsbased welfare services based on kaupapa Māori values for all people.

Ensure that welfare service delivery is proactive, mana-enhancing, accessible, and
inclusive of a diverse range of people’s needs, including by:
1.3.1.

Resourcing outreach efforts to marginalised groups, through advocacy groups
and other relevant community organisations;

1.3.2.

Training and resourcing Work and Income staff to deliver high-quality,
empathetic, non-ableist, and culturally competent services; and

1.3.3.

Refocusing welfare service delivery on building supportive relationships and
coordinating services.

1.4.

Recognise and compensate unpaid labour, including by:
1.4.1.

Establishing a working group to explore the diverse needs of groups who do
unpaid labour;

1.4.2.

Legally recognising informal caregivers as part of the care system and
financially supporting informal carers to cover any reduced income or increased
expenses that result from caregiving; and

1.4.3.

Establishing a legal right to a minimum income and guaranteeing this income.

1.5.

2.

1.2.2.1.

Improve equity in retirement, including by:
1.5.1.

Contributing to the Kiwisaver or preferred retirement savings of those on low
incomes, including full-time informal carers and students on work placement,
regardless of their lack of employee contributions;

1.5.2.

Making financial advice accessible and useful for all, particularly marginalised
groups; and

1.5.3.

Indexing superannuation to the cost of living, enabling earlier eligibility to reflect
lower life expectancy.

Household Debt

Issues
High levels of household debt are a significant burden for many New Zealanders. Increased
borrowing to cover the cost of health, housing, education, and other expenses leaves families
vulnerable to economic shocks, predatory lending and financial instability, limiting their ability to
meet their needs.

Actions
2.1.

Minimise debt in low-income households, including by:
2.1.1.

Forgiving welfare-related debt, including recovery of overpayments; and

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Livelihoods Policy — Reviewed: 2025 — Version: 04 August 2025

3

<!-- page 4 -->

2.1.2.
2.2.

3.

Providing emergency and hardship grants, instead of loans.1

Ensure lenders behave fairly and transparently, including by:
2.2.1.

Passing legislation that prevents exploitative lending and debt collection,
relating to both currency and goods; and

2.2.2.

Requiring banks and other lenders to provide low-interest, consolidated debt
management facilities.

Meeting basic needs

Issues
Many people are forced to make unreasonable choices on what basic needs they prioritise (food
or rent, child-care or health, etc). They suffer material hardship that is linked to poorer health
and education outcomes, homelessness, and isolation.

Actions
3.1.

3.2.

1

Ensure that everyone has access to the services they need, including by:
3.1.1.

Resourcing underfunded basic services that support well-being, including
preventative and/or early intervention services; and

3.1.2.

Developing a comprehensive framework for the regulation, funding, and delivery
of basic services that guarantees access, regardless of one's location, capacity
to pay, or any other factor.

Ensure that everyone has access to the resources they need, including by:
3.2.1.

Resourcing organisations that provide basic resources to marginalised or hardto-reach communities;

3.2.2.

Providing everyone who needs it with basic amounts of food, water, shelter,
energy, and internet access; and

3.2.3.

Legislating for clear rights, rooted in Te Tiriti o Waitangi, for basic resources,
and legislating the corresponding responsibilities of the Crown to provide them.

These must be easy and quick to access.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
