Authorised by Miriam Ross, greens.org.nz

<!-- page 3 -->

Kaupapa Māori
By Māori, for Māori

The Green Party will support Māori to make decisions
about the destiny of their own whānau, hapū and iwi.
Tangata Whenua lived undisturbed for centuries as hapū, creating tikanga
and protocols unique to the whenua , with the central focus being the health
and sustainability of their whakapapa. Supporting ongoing kaupapa Māori
approaches for Māori to fulfil their aspirations was affirmed and guaranteed by
Te Tiriti o Waitangi and provides better outcomes for all who live in our country.
When Te Tiriti o Waitangi was signed, it was assured that the relationship
between Tangata Whenua and the Crown would mean no change in the way
Māori choose to live their lives. However, successive governments continue
to implement harmful actions which have eroded Māori social structures,
contributed to the loss of traditional knowledge, and created intergenerational
inequities across many key metrics in Aotearoa, New Zealand.
The current Governments legislative assaults have targeted tangata whenua
from all sides; Health, Justice, Tamariki, Education, Social services, and Te
Tiriti o Waitangi. They have consistently ignored independent experts, the
Waitangi Tribunal, and their own advisors, who have warned that their actions
will only deepen existing inequities for Māori and contribute to further racial
divide within the country.

Our plan
 Devolve power and redistribute resources back to tangata
whenua in recognition that Māori are the decision makers and
facilitators of the destiny of their own whānau, hapū and iwi.
 Invest in outcomes that minimise the disparities and inequities
tangata whenua face across the majority of social and economic
outcomes.
 Resource marae through a Marae Resilience Fund for Māori
to lead initiatives for their people, wāhi tapu, and whenua in
accordance with their own tikanga. Create ongoing funding for
provisions for civil emergencies in recognition of being consistent
community lifelines.
 End Perpetual Leases on Whenua Māori and amend the Public
Works Act 1981 to prevent the acquisition of Māori freehold land,
Māori Customary land, and lands within a reasonable proximity
to marae, urupā, and wāhi tapu.
 Expand the learning, speaking, and the promotion of te reo Māori
in both formal and informal settings to encourage the widespread
use of the language nationwide.

The Green Party support tangata whenua-led processes, actions and decisionmaking by devolving power and investing resources in all matters that affect
Māori. We know that Te Tiriti and democracy are not contradictory, they are
complementary. Decision-making with iwi, returning whenua to its kaitiaki,
and facilitating by Māori, for Māori solutions to target inequities and minimise
disparities are all ways we can uphold te Tiriti while honouring the democracy
this country should have been built on.

Kaupapa Māori

It is time to remove the burden from Māori to keep reminding the Crown of their
promises and for the Crown to take accountability for their ongoing injustices
against te Tiriti and using te iwi Māori as a political football.

6

<!-- page 4 -->

Children

Thriving tamariki and rangatahi
The Green Party will work to build a system that puts
tamariki, rangatahi and whānau first.
Tamariki Māori are disproportionately impacted by a child protection system
that excludes meaningful partnership and underinvests in culturally grounded,
whānau-led solutions. Whakapapa and identity must be centred with whānau
and hapū resourced to lead decisions affecting their tamariki. We reflect our
commitment to Te Tiriti o Waitangi by addressing the inequities tamariki Māori
face in everyday life and in the state care system.

Our plan
 Prioritise workforce safety by ringfencing training and workforce
development strategy prioritising Māori, Pacific, Rainbow,
Disabled, and community provider pathways.

Children

 Amend the Oranga Tamariki Act so that it protects tamariki Māori
and explicitly embeds whānau participation in decision-making
to exercise iwi/hapū authority.

8

<!-- page 5 -->

Bold action and solutions that hold
polluters to account

A Green Government would focus on Te Tiriti o
Waitangi-based solutions which address the climate
crisis by tackling its root causes and removing
economic incentives that encourage and enable climate
pollution.

Climate action: emissions reduction

Climate action:
emissions reduction

10

<!-- page 6 -->

Climate action:
resilience + adaptation
The Green Party will prepare all New Zealanders for the
impacts of climate change.
Climate change is one of the biggest challenges of our time and the impacts
are already being felt by communities all around the rohe. Severe weather,
with more frequent flooding, and more frequent droughts, already are having
devastating consequences. Often, marae and community groups are on the
front lines of the emergency and clean up response, but these groups are not
supported by the Government to adequately plan for adaptation. People who
are worried about rising insurance prices due to living in areas exposed to
floods or slips have not received any clarity from the Government as to the help
that will be provided when disaster strikes, or when the areas where they live
becoming increasingly unliveable.

Our plan
 Ensure climate adaptation planning affirms tino rangatiratanga
and upholds the mana motuhake of whānau, hapū and iwi over
whenua, wai, and taonga, by appropriately funding a Māori
Climate Resilience Fund.
 Establish a dedicated fund for central and local government
to implement climate adaptation and resilience measures,
including funding for partnerships with tangata whenua and
community organisations.

Climate action: resilience and adaptation

Keeping Aotearoa safe and prepared

12

<!-- page 7 -->

Conservation
+ biodiversity

Protecting and restoring plants,
animals and ecosystems
The Green Party will protect our precious whenua and
taonga species from corporate exploitation.
Over this term, the Luxon Government has made it easier for corporations to
plunder our moana and tear up the whenua—putting private profits ahead of
our precious native wildlife. Meanwhile, many of our native plants and animals
are on the brink of collapse, and without urgent action, we’re at risk of losing
them forever.
The Green Party are committed to protecting 30% of land and oceans by
2030 because we know the mauri and health of te taiao is foundational to the
wellbeing of our people, our climate, and our communities. We will achieve this
by giving effect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi and recognising tangata whenua as the
original and ongoing kaitiaki of Aotearoa.

Our plan
 Reform conservation and wildlife protection laws to give effect to
Te Tiriti o Waitangi, prioritise indigenous-led land stewardship,
and to ensure the conservation management system prioritises
halting and reversing nature loss in New Zealand.

Conservation and biodiversity

Aotearoa is home to natural taonga found nowhere else in the world, with our
ngahere, awa, and moana central to our national identity and way of life.

14

<!-- page 8 -->

Democracy

Politics for people, not big money
The Green Party is committed to a democracy that
upholds te Tiriti o Waitangi and the vision of Matike
Mai, creating a decision-making process that reflects
genuine partnership.

Our plan
 Resource a national conversation for constitutional
transformation that upholds He Whakaputanga me Te Tiriti o
Waitangi as our founding constitutional documents, utilising
Matike Mai to facilitate community discussions.

Democracy

 Entrench the Māori electoral seats to guarantee Māori
representation in Parliament and extend the time in which Māori
can switch rolls.

16

<!-- page 9 -->

Digital technology

Technology helping, not harming
The Green Party will hold digital platforms accountable
to protect us and our information.
Data centres running AI models are sucking the world’s energy and clean water
sources dry. Intellectual property is exploited by unaccountable platforms,
that for Māori are also a source of cultural theft and distortion. Companies
from social media giants to those storing our health records collect more
information about us while proving that they can’t be trusted with it.

 Adopt and implement Te Kāhui Raraunga’s Māori Data
Governance Model and Māori AI Governance Framework across
the public sector to protect Māori data sovereignty

Digital technology

Our plan

18

<!-- page 10 -->

Disability

An accessible Aotearoa for all
The Green Party will build an Aotearoa where disabled
people are valued, where they and their whānau live with
dignity and autonomy.
Our current laws, policies, and social norms mean disabled people are
often denied the same rights as others and are excluded from places and
activities non-disabled people take for granted. These barriers are often
worse for tāngata whaikaha Māori and for disabled people from marginalised
communities.
The current Government has made it harder for disabled people to access the
support they deserve and that enables them to participate equally in life and
their communities.
The Green Party is ambitious in its plan to create a more accessible Aotearoa
by building off the Enabling Good Lives framework and grounding our
approach in Te Tiriti o Waitangi. Our approach will operate on a high-trust
model and apply to all disabled people, including those with disabling
conditions that do not currently access support.

Our plan

Disability

 Introduce a Tiriti-based disability rights law with enforceable
accessibility standards.

20

<!-- page 11 -->

Drug law reform

Putting health first to keep people safe
The Green Party will take an evidenced, health-based
approach to alcohol and other drugs to reduce harm in
our communities.

Our plan
 Ramp up funding of harm reduction and addiction support for
people who want to reduce their drug intake, including through
kaupapa Māori, Rainbow, youth, and harm reduction programmes.

 Phase out all alcohol advertising and sponsorship, including at
sporting and cultural events and use funding from the alcohol levy
to establish a well-resourced national harm-reduction campaign.
 Implement stronger regulation for vape retailers to protect young
people and children, including by restricting maximum nicotine
concentrations, restricting flavours, and keeping vape stores out of
the vicinity of schools and kura.

Drug law reform

 Enable a licensing system for psychedelic treatment and recognise
taonga status of our native psylocibin species.

22

<!-- page 12 -->

Education

An Aotearoa where everyone
can reach their full potential
The Green Party will support an inclusive education
system that uplifts everyone.
The Green alternative is grounded in Te Tiriti o Waitangi and universal
human rights. A Tiriti centred education system honours tino rangatiratanga,
embraces te reo Māori and mātauranga Māori, and ensures Māori voices and
communities are central to decision making. Inclusion is not an add on but a
foundation. Disabled people, rainbow communities, migrants and refugees,
and others facing structural barriers are fully supported to learn, belong, and
thrive. Educators’ voices, and grounded expertise are central to decisions at
all levels.

Our plan
 Reset the government’s rushed and ideological curriculum and
assessment reforms, reverting to the original direction of Te
Mātaiaho and ensuring qualification reform follows curriculum
reform

 Support rangatiratanga to provide an education system driven by
whānau needs, allowing space for whakapapa-based decisions,
and working towards a Māori Education Authority governing and
funding all Māori Medium and Kaupapa Māori education.
 Support the workforce so all teachers and educators have fair
wages, staffing levels that support quality teaching, and codevelop a long-term workforce plan with the sector.

Education

 Expand Ka Ora, Ka Ako to 400 more schools, as a first step
towards providing a warm and nutritious locally made lunch to all
school children.

24

<!-- page 13 -->

Energy

Powering Aotearoa with
affordable renewable energy
The Green Party will fix our broken power
system so that people, not profits, come first.
The Green Party will speed up the electrification of our energy system and fix
the rules of the energy market so public wellbeing comes before corporate
profits. We will grow renewable generation, like wind and solar, support
community and Māori-led energy projects, and improve energy efficiency
so homes are warmer, bills are lower, and communities have more control of
their power.

Our plan
 Increase resilience by enabling greater distributed solar and
batteries for households, marae and suitable public buildings,
and supporting community-led energy planning

Energy

 Establish a single energy regulator, and a Ministry for Energy,
focusing on affordable, secure and sustainable energy with
equitable access and Tiriti-based frameworks that enable Māori
and community involvement, ownership, and leadership in
energy projects.

26

<!-- page 14 -->

Environmental
protection
Protecting and restoring nature
The Green Party stands for a healthy environment
as the foundation of healthy communities.

The Green Party stands for a healthy environment as the foundation of
healthy communities. The Green Party will strengthen environmental
protections, uphold Te Tiriti, and restore te taiao. Protection and restoration
of our environment is the foundation of our future.

Our plan
 Implement strong evidence-based limits for ecosystem health,
secure the role of Te Tiriti, and affirm the role of tangata whenua
as shared decision-makers and kaitiaki in the new resource
management system.
 Repeal the Fast-Track Approvals Act and revoke consents
for fast-track approvals for new coal, gold and seabed mining
projects.

Environmental protection

Luxon’s coalition has been the most environmentally damaging Government
in a generation. They have fast-tracked destructive mining projects in
wild places, scrapped our Ministry for the Environment, changed laws to
more easily allow the killing of native wildlife where it stands in the way of
development, and allowed rivers, lakes, and groundwater to become more
polluted. Environmental laws have been gutted, alongside the dismantling
of processes for shared decision making that honours Te Tiriti. Luxon’s
Government has prioritised private profit at the expense of our environment.

28

<!-- page 15 -->

Food, fibre and forestry
A regenerative approach that
puts people and nature first

The Green Party will support sustainable farming and
forestry that protects our environment, communities
and livelihoods.

Our plan
 Work with Māori led forestry organisations to support investment
in forestry and restoration of forests on whenua Māori and
recognise tangata whenua customary use rights in indigenous
forestry according to their tīkanga.
 Establish a biodiversity credits scheme that supports landowners
to undertake restoration and protection of land, as a voluntary
revenue alternative to the Emissions Trading Scheme, and
prioritise marginal whenua Māori where agreed by landowners.

Food, fibre and forestry

We can have a thriving, sustainable food and fibre sector that prioritises
mātauranga food production, creates food security, keeps our waterways
healthy and provides good jobs for our rural communities.

30

<!-- page 16 -->

Freshwater

Healthy water for drinking,
swimming and gathering kai

The Green Party will put the health of freshwater and
communities first.
Our rivers and lakes should be healthy, clean, and teeming with life.
Everyone should be able to turn on their tap knowing their water is safe to
drink, swim in their local awa without getting sick, and fish or gather kai from
waterways. Clean healthy freshwater is the foundation of the health of our
people and our environment.

Our plan

Freshwater

 Reinstate Te Mana o Te Wai to prioritise the health of freshwater
in decision-making and regulation and to give effect to Te Tiriti
o Waitangi.

32

<!-- page 17 -->

Gender equity

For a more equal Aotearoa
The Green Party will take action to advance gender
equality and ensure women and gender minorities are
respected and treated fairly.

Our plan
 Fund one-stop-shops that provides pā harakeke wrap-around
services for whānau throughout hapūtanga, after birth, first stages
of life, and navigating parenthood.
 Resource kaupapa Māori solutions and community-led solutions
to family and sexual violence, that have have been developed by
disproportionately impacted groups, including women, Pasifika,
rainbow, and disabled communities.

Gender equity

 Enact the recommendations from the Mana Wahine Inquiry when
they have been determined.

34

<!-- page 18 -->

Global affairs + trade
A safer, greener, fairer future for
people and planet

The Green Party will ensure that Aotearoa always
stands up for what’s right on the world stage.

Our plan
 Implement the Trade For All agenda, including democratic
scrutiny of trade agreements, and enforceable recognition of our
Te Tiriti o Waitangi obligations, workers rights, human rights and
climate commitments.
 Stand with decolonisation and democracy movements globally in
particular with indigenous peoples of our Asia Pacific region.

Global affairs + trade

 Support Pacific sovereignty and independence and oppose the
militarisation of the Pacific.

36

<!-- page 19 -->

Health

Accessible care to support
everyone’s health
The Green Party will ensure our health care system is
equitable, accessible and properly supported.
Undoing actions of redress for Māori such as the disestablishment of Te Aka
Whai Ora - The Māori Health Authority, removing requirements for culturally
safe care, and stripping power from iwi-Māori Partnership has not only reversed
decades of progress to provide equitable healthcare after decades of neglect,
but continues to force Māori into a health system that is known to underserve
them and is misaligned with their hauora aspirations.
Private provider costs are locking whānau out of accessible primary health care
which causes health issues to unnecessarily escalate because they are not
detected early. Meanwhile, Hauora Māori and social service providers that are
focused on whānau-wide holistic and preventative care remain underfunded
and restricted by overly prescriptive contracts.
Good health and dental care allow all of us to live enjoyable, meaningful lives.
Our plan will expand access to essential primary care and dental, and work with
and fund kaupapa Māori approaches to end health inequities in the system, and
prevent ill health and mental distress in the community.

Our plan

 Work towards a publicly delivered, fully free provision of dental
and primary care services, including by-Māori for-Māori
community clinics contracted through a redeveloped Te Aka
Whai Ora.
 Stop overly prescriptive Hauora service contracts and commit
to working with Iwi Māori Partnership Boards and Hauora Māori
to simplify and improve funding arrangements for providers of
health services for whānau, hapū iwi and hapori.

Health

 Fund mobile healthcare and mental health care clinics,
diagnostics services and dental vans to ensure rural
communities are able to access health services regularly,
including during and after civil emergencies.

38

<!-- page 20 -->

Housing

Safe, warm, affordable
homes for everyone
The Green Party is the only party with a credible plan
to ensure everyone can afford a warm and safe place
to call home.

Our plan
 Build tens of thousands of new public homes, significantly increase
accessible public housing stock, and fund more papakāinga to be
built on whenua Māori.

Housing

 Require Councils to collaborate with communities, including mana
whenua, to provide sustainable, walkable, mixed-use urban areas
and enable enough new affordable homes within existing urban
areas to meet the needs of the next generation.

40

<!-- page 21 -->

Immigration
+ refugees

Welcoming, safe and fair pathways
to make Aotearoa home

Our plan
 Implement Māori aspirations for a Tiriti-based immigration
system, including devolving resources and decision making
to hapū and iwi to strengthen traditional whanaungatanga
connections, and providing Tiriti education to new migrants and
refugees.

Immigration and refugees

The Green Party will make sure that everyone who
comes to Aotearoa is treated with respect and dignity.

42

<!-- page 22 -->

Justice +
community safety

The Green Party will make our communities safer
by addressing the drivers of crime.

Our plan
 Expand Te Ao Mārama to all Courts in Aotearoa and ensure
specialist youth courts including the Rangatahi and Pasifika
Courts, Alcohol and Other Drug Treatment Courts, and New
Beginnings Courts are available to all who wish to access them.

Justice and community safety

Keeping communities safe through
prevention and rehabilitation

44

<!-- page 23 -->

Local government
Empowering local democracy

The Green Party will back local government to deliver
community wellbeing.

Our plan

Local government

 Reinforce councils’ responsibility to Te Tiriti o Waitangi by making
the role of local government as a Tiriti partner explicit, and
reinstate their ability to keep Māori wards for their districts.

46

<!-- page 24 -->

Mental health
A safe, supportive and
accessible care system

The Green Party will work to address the drivers of
poor mental health, and ensure everyone can get safe,
culturally relevant care when they need it.
The Green Party will expand free services so cost is never a barrier to
accessing support, and provide more funding to kaupapa Māori and youth
services so support is culturally relevant to our communities. The mental
health workforce will receive more support, staffing and funding to reduce
burnout and allow for the phasing out of harmful practices like seclusion, to
ensure acute mental healthcare is rehabilitative, not harmful.

Our plan

 Implement the recommendations of Every Life Matters – He Tapu
te Oranga o ia Tangata suicide prevention strategy, together with
further actions identified as part of the kaupapa Māori response to
suicide prevention with particular focus on people under 24.
 Fund kaupapa Māori mental health and addiction programmes
and ensure rangatahi Māori voice is represented in policy.

Mental health

 Expand free mental health services to all communities so everyone
can access support when they need it, including expanding youth
services like Piki, Mana Ake and Youth One Stop Shops throughout
Aotearoa, Asian Family Services, and dedicated support for postnatal mental health.

48

<!-- page 25 -->

Oceans and fisheries
Abundant oceans teeming
with kaimoana

The Green Party will restore the mauri (life force) of our
moana through bold marine protection initiatives.
Aotearoa’s moana is a taonga and New Zealanders deserve to have healthy
and thriving oceans, with abundant marine life that provides for sustainable
kaimoana. Oceans are the lifeblood of our planet and our largest public
good—an abundant ocean belongs to all of us.
The Green Party will put Te Tiriti o Waitangi at the centre of our approach
to restoring the abundance of our moana, because when we invest in local
knowledge, we get closer to restoring the right of every New Zealander to
gather kaimoana and find abundant life in our seas for generations to come.

 Protect at least 30% of New Zealand’s ocean territory by 2030
through reforming marine protected areas legislation to ensure it
is fit-for-purpose and enabled Tiriti-consistent and tikanga-led
tools and approaches to improve ocean health outcomes.
 Ban seabed mining in the coastal marine area and the exclusive
economic zone; and maintain pressure for a moratorium on
seabed mining in international waters.
 Review the Quota Management System and move towards an
ecosystem-based fisheries management model, in line with the
Māori fisheries settlement.
 Resource iwi and hapū to lead ocean protection by embedding
kaitiakitanga, tikanga, and mātauranga in policy operational
management and ocean conservation projects.

Oceans and fisheries

Our plan

50

<!-- page 26 -->

Overseas
New Zealanders
Cultivating Kiwi connections
around the world

Our plan
 Enable a tikanga-based pathway for people who whakapapa Māori
to establish Aotearoa New Zealand citizenship, regardless of
country of residence or birth.

Overseas New Zealanders

The Green Party will ensure all New Zealanders living
overseas can feel connected to home.

52

<!-- page 27 -->

Public services
Strong essential services
accessible to everyone

The Green Party will make sure that public services
support the public good.
Strong public services also require a strong, capable, and independent
public sector anchored in its commitment to upholding Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
A Green Government would connect services to communities, ensure they
are grounded in equity, and able to look beyond short-term political cycles
to support the long-term public good.
Aotearoa has enough to properly invest in the services and infrastructure
everyone relies on and to ensure these services stay in public hands. With
political courage, an active state, and enhanced democratic accountability,
we can build public systems that support wellbeing, uphold Te Tiriti,
strengthen our national resilience, and give every community what it needs
to thrive.

 Uphold te Tiriti o Waitangi throughout the work of the public
service, and fund Māori organisations, iwi, hapū and marae to run
community and environmental initiatives that meet the needs
and aspirations unique to their rohe.
 Improve training in te Tiriti o Waitangi and te reo Māori for all
public servants, resulting in consistency across all agencies.

Public services

Our plan

54

<!-- page 28 -->

Rainbow communities
Rainbow communities thriving with
freedom, equality and respect

The Green Party will nurture an Aotearoa where
everyone belongs and enjoys a safe, healthy and
happy life.

Our plan
 Working with the different Rainbow communities to develop
appropriate healthcare services and strategies built on cultural
values and holistic models of care and wellbeing.
 Increase resourcing for Rainbow organisations, including
dedicated support for Māori and Pasifika-led organisations, to
support the development and delivery of services that reflect the
diverse needs, values, and strengths of Rainbow communities.

Rainbow communities

The Greens believe that rainbow healthcare should be shaped by
compassion, evidence, and aroha, not fear or political division. Rainbow
identities are connected to whakapapa and whānau and it is essential
that government enables these relationships to thrive. A fair society must
recognise and address the overlapping barriers to a healthy life faced by
Rainbow Communities, particularly where intersectional identities such as
Māori, Pasifika, disabled people, migrants and refugees further compound
those challenges.

56

<!-- page 29 -->

Seniors

Happy, healthy and supported

The Green Party will uphold the mana of seniors by
prioritising the support that enables equitable and
fulfilling lives.
Guided by manaakitanga, whanaungatanga, and led by Te Tiriti o Waitangi,
we envision communities where seniors are recognised and celebrated
as leaders and knowledge holders, actively shaping whānau, hapū and
iwi life. Homes are warm, accessible and designed for connection across
generations, while community spaces and marae-based centres foster
belonging, learning and support.
We believe those who work in aged care must be respected and rewarded,
with secure conditions that enable them to provide high-quality,
compassionate support. Care systems should be equitable, culturally
grounded, and responsive, ensuring Māori, Pacific Peoples and diverse
communities can access services that reflect their values and tikanga.

Our plan
 Launch a dedicated long-term strategy for the needs of an
ageing population which encompasses the holistic wellbeing of
kaumātua, elder abuse prevention, ensuring income is equitably
accessed and sufficient to live comfortably, and the establishment
of a state-owned, not-for-profit retirement village scheme.

 Resource Māori, Pacific and migrant organisations to provide
kaumātua care that is aligned with their values, cultural practices
and tikanga.

Seniors

 Expanding housing options by building more papakāinga,
prioritising kaumātua on social housing waitlists, and ensuring
housing designs are suitable for their needs — single-level and
warm, with mobility features and room for intergenerational living.

58

<!-- page 30 -->

Small businesses

Championing small, local enterprise
The Green Party will back local businesses, support
sustainable industries and ensure small businesses
have a fair shot.

Our plan

Small businesses

 Continue to invest in community-led regional development with
a focus on sustainable building, regenerative agriculture and
horticulture, improving low-carbon infrastructure, and iwi- and
hapū-led economic activity.

60

<!-- page 31 -->

Advancing an Aotearoa that
embraces Te Tiriti

The Green Party will put Te Tiriti o Waitangi at the heart
of a modern Aotearoa founded on real partnership.
We envision an Aotearoa where our governing structures uphold the rangatiratanga
of iwi and hapū, providing dignity for all. We can achieve this by demonstrating true
partnership between tangata whenua and the Crown as intended by Te Tiriti.
Successive governments have consistently breached Te Tiriti. The resulting harm,
lack of accountability and denial of Māori as equal partners mean that the Crown has
not upheld its side of the partnership. When Te Tiriti breaches are ongoing, apologies
for past harms are not enough.
It is our responsibility to acknowledge, take accountability and put right the
wrongdoings committed by the Crown. These have led to worse outcomes for Māori
in too many ways. We can’t allow government to pretend that everyone is equal in this
country when the exact systems that were created to oppress Māori are still operating.
The Green Party understands that He Whakaputanga and Te Tiriti are the foundation
for an enduring constitutional partnership. We acknowledge the need for ongoing
dialogue to build the awareness, understanding and vision that will give life to Te Tiriti
in Aotearoa.

Our plan
 Amend the Treaty of Waitangi Act to recognise that Te Tiriti is the
authoritative text and that Te Tiriti works in conjunction with He
Whakaputanga o te Rangatiratanga o Nu Tireni.
 Implement genuine Te Tiriti-based decision-making models across
government and resource iwi and hapū to participate as partners rather than
as advisors.
 Reform the Treaty Settlements process by amending the settlement policy
guide for negotiators to enable fair negotiations and just reparations without
cessation of sovereignty, removing any clauses that refer to ‘Full and
Final settlement’, ending the ‘large natural grouping’ approach to Treaty
settlements, and validating hapū rangatiratanga.
 Increase resourcing for the Waitangi Tribunal, providing them with the
power to make binding recommendations for the return of Crown and
Private land to iwi, whānau and hapū.
 Facilitate the return of whenua outside of Treaty Settlements that was
wrongfully alienated from tangata whenua, including through exploring a
right-of-first-refusal process that enables the return of private land to iwi,
hapū and whānau at point of sale.

Te Tiriti o Waitangi

Te Tiriti o Waitangi

62

<!-- page 32 -->

Tertiary education

Opportunities for everyone
to learn and grow

The Green Party will support student success by
overhauling tertiary education.

Our plan

Tertiary education

 Ensure all tertiary institutes uphold Te Tiriti o Waitangi and deliver
equitable outcomes for tauira Māori (Māori students). Expand the
Māori and Pasifika Trades Training programme, and fully resource
Whare Wānanga to increase opportunities for kaupapa Māori
education.

64

<!-- page 33 -->

Transport

Easy, sustainable ways
to get around
The Green Party will invest in modern, sustainable,
and affordable transport options.

Our plan

Transport

 Fund on-demand public transport, including by-Māori for-Māori
public transport to serve kōhanga reo and rural schools. Fund
affordable, reliable, interregional rural bus services.

66

<!-- page 34 -->

Violence prevention

Keeping whānau and communities safe
The Green Party will make sure everyone can live a life
free from violence and heal from trauma.

Violence prevention

The Green Party will invest in stopping violence before it starts. Our approach
will be safe, accessible and integrated, building on people’s strength and with
Te Tiriti o Waitangi at its heart. We will mobilise our communities to help and
ensure our workforce is skilled and culturally competent.

68

documents/marine-policy-2022-2026.md.text:
# Marine Policy (Green Party policy document)

<!-- page 1 -->

Marine Policy
Te Ao Tūroa helps us to care for all coastal and aquatic ecosystems through active kaitiakitanga
practice and precautionary, adaptive, integrated stewardship. Doing all we can to support a
naturally regenerating ocean is essential to protect its health, provide for us, and assist climate
stability. The Green Party will promote Te Tiriti-based governance of the seas of Aotearoa New
Zealand to regenerate mauri, prevent damage from human activities, increase resilience to
climate change, and support the thriving marine ecosystems that underpin a healthy, wellmanaged blue economy.

Vision
The ocean’s life force and life-supporting capacity are vibrant and vigorous. All human
relationships with the marine realm are mutually regenerative.

Values and Principles
- Honouring Te Tiriti o Waitangi: Kaitiakitanga, led by tangata whenua, should guide human
relationships with the sea, ensuring that it is better cared for. Māori regard all life forms
within Te Ao Tūroa as taonga that require appropriate consideration through kawa and
tikanga.

- Ecological Wisdom: Protecting the mauri, mana, and tapu - the intrinsic vitality, potency,
and sanctity of the ocean and of all who dwell within and around it - is fundamental to the
enduring life-support system of planet Earth.

- Social Responsibility: We should equitably provide for the sustainable livelihoods and
recreational and spiritual opportunities valued by New Zealanders that healthy oceans
and coasts offer.

- Appropriate Decision-Making: A range of interests at both local and national levels must
guide decisions concerning coastal and marine management. Decisions must include
consideration of the needs of future generations and of the wider environment and
ecology.

- Non-violence: Human activity should be restorative, not harmful, to the intrinsic mauri,
mana, and tapu of all life in the marine environment.

- Urgency: Given the biodiversity crisis, the declining health of ocean ecosystems, and
climate change impacts such as acidification and increasing sea temperatures, significant
increases in investment and pace of implementation are urgently needed to regenerate
coastal and marine ecosystems.

- Interconnection: Ki uta ki tai - from the mountains to the sea. Marine management
requires integrated management of terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems, including the vital
role of wetlands in coastal and estuarine zones. The health of people, land, and oceans
are inextricably linked.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Marine Policy — Reviewed: 2022 — Version: 02 March 2026

<!-- page 2 -->

Strategic Priorities
The Green Party’s strategic goals include:

“All our waters will be in transition to becoming clean and able to support healthy
ecosystems.
All native species and their habitats will be thriving or on a path to recovery in terrestrial,
freshwater, and marine environments.
Our laws and practices will respect the biological integrity of all life while prioritising the
health of indigenous species and ecosystems.
The customary and decision-making roles of whānau, hapū, and iwi will be integral to
decisions about resource use.
Decision-making about resource use will provide for community participation and
environmental justice.”
Actions from this policy that work toward these goals include:
- Establish a well-resourced and politically independent Ocean Commission to develop and
establish Te Tiriti-based ocean governance of the entire marine area, including the
Exclusive Economic Zone, and advise the Government on legislative, policy, and
institutional reform. (1.1)

- Reform fisheries and marine protection legislation, including establishing a national,
comprehensive, and coherent system of no-take marine protected areas. (2.1.1)

- Supporting the use of marine cultural health indices, shaped by mātauranga Māori, to
inform policy, management, and operations. (2.1.4)

- Ending bottom trawling, prioritising seamounts and areas with high levels of sequestered
carbon and biodiversity for protection. (5.1.2)

Connected Policies
This policy is one of several that focus on Biodiversity and Environmental Regeneration, alongside
Freshwater and Land Use and Soils. The mauri of the oceans is connected to human activity on
land, notably Agriculture, Forestry, Housing and Sustainable Communities, and Waste and
Hazardous Substances. Climate Change also impacts marine health. For acute marine crisis
response, see our Emergency Management Policy. See also our policies on coastal Transport and
wave and tidal Energy.

Policy Positions
1.

Te Mana o te Moana and Governance

Issues
Marine environmental management in Aotearoa New Zealand is complex legislatively,
regulatorily, and practically, and existing frameworks are inconsistently applied. The Māori
Fisheries Settlement underpins the Māori economy, but tangata whenua currently have no formal
leadership role in ocean management. A lack of up-to-date knowledge about the health of marine
environments undermines management planning and operations to address marine issues.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Marine Policy — Reviewed: 2022 — Version: 02 March 2026

<!-- page 3 -->

Marine environments face complex challenges, requiring a holistic understanding of the
interacting stresses on ecosystems and species.

1.2.

A. International Commitments
1.4.

2.

Support the leadership of Pacific Island nations on marine environment protection,
including international action on:
1.4.1.

Building resilience to climate change;

1.4.2.

Regenerating ocean ecosystems;

1.4.3.

Placing a moratorium on seabed mining in international waters;

1.4.4.

Halting seismic prospecting;

1.4.5.

Protecting at least 30% of Te Moana-nui-a-Kiwa from fishing and
extraction; and

1.4.6.

Protecting seamounts from bottom trawling.

1.5.

Ratify outstanding international marine agreements, including the Global Oceans
Treaty, in consultation with tangata whenua.

1.6.

Advocate for the international protection of endangered marine species on the
high seas, including expanding the membership and mandate of the International
Whaling Commission.

1.7.

Ensure all relevant national legislative and regulatory frameworks are aligned with
international marine commitments and obligations, and require and resource their
enforcement.

Marine Biodiversity, Regeneration and Resilience

Issues
The state of the environment and the pressures upon it indicate that humanity must
fundamentally reset its relationship with the natural world and foster regeneration in ourselves
and nature. Loss of coastal ecosystems, physical disturbance and damage, and fishing catch
levels that disrupt ecosystems and risk the health of marine realms for future generations,
livelihoods, and rural food security. They also risk undermining Māori fisheries settlement rights,
both customary and commercial, and therefore the Māori economy.
Actions
2.1.

Reform fisheries and marine protection legislation, including:
2.1.1.

Establishing a national, comprehensive, and coherent system of no-take
marine protected areas covering an area of at least 30% of the Aotearoa
New Zealand territorial sea and at least 30% of the EEZ, with the target
percentage and design founded on regenerating mauri and underpinned by
mātauranga Māori;

2.1.2.

Developing a nationwide mauri-based spatial design for marine and
estuarine ecosystem regeneration that incorporates mātauranga Māori and
indigenous ecosystem management tikanga, such as taiāpure, mātaitai, and
rāhui;

2.1.3.

Supporting the application of tikanga Māori and community-based
regenerative activities, aiming to restore mauri within marine and estuarine
ecosystems;

<!-- page 5 -->

Supporting the use of marine cultural health indices, shaped by mātauranga
Māori, to inform policy, management, and operations; and

2.1.5.

Amending the management framework for offshore activities to strengthen
protection of the marine environment outside the coastal marine area (12200 nautical miles offshore).

2.2.

Restore native marine flora (muka, salt marshes, mangroves, seagrass, seaweeds,
and marine sediments) for regeneration, customary use, and as ‘blue carbon’
initiatives.

2.3.

Collaborate internationally for the maximum possible protection of threatened
marine species, including by:

2.4.

3.

2.1.4.

2.3.1.

Developing international species recovery plans for all threatened marine
and migratory species;

2.3.2.

mammals;

2.3.3.

Opposing all commercial and research-oriented whaling, and supporting
South Pacific and regional whale sanctuaries; and

2.3.4.

Opposing marine mammals being held in captivity except as part of an
approved threatened species recovery strategy.

Ensure that commercial marine operations contribute to marine regeneration and
resilience, by:
2.4.1.

Establishing appropriate financial mechanisms (e.g., resource rentals) to
charge for private commercial use or occupation of public coastal and
marine space; and

2.4.2.

Requiring marine-based industrial activities to pay a bond covering
predicted and potential decommissioning and restoration costs, before
operations commence.

The Marine Environment in a Changing Climate

Issues
Climate change further threatens indigenous marine species and ecosystems. It shifts the
natural population range of some species, often with unpredictable and cascading ecological
consequences. Global warming causes algal blooms, deoxygenation, and species loss. In addition,
the increasing level of carbon dioxide absorbed by the ocean causes acidification, which affects
the ability of marine species to build shells and skeletons. This includes plankton, which are the
foundation of marine food webs, threatening entire ecosystems. Finally, melting Arctic and
Antarctic ice sheets are now affecting ocean currents critical to climate and temperature
moderation.
Actions

3.1.

Fully incorporate the role of a regenerating ocean in the national strategic
response to climate change, including by:

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Marine Policy — Reviewed: 2022 — Version: 02 March 2026

<!-- page 6 -->

3.1.1.

3.2.

4.

Developing a national blue carbon calculation and assessment capability
(including marine flora regeneration, marine permaculture, and polytrophic
aquaculture) for use in carbon pricing mechanisms.

Facilitate resilience and adaptation as marine ecosystems move and adapt to
climate change, including by:
3.2.1.

Researching and addressing the impacts of climate change on threatened
marine species, prioritising those endemic to Aotearoa New Zealand; and

3.2.2.

Protecting buffer areas from subdivision and development to leave room
for coastal and estuarine ecosystems to move inland with rising sea levels.

Marine Damage Prevention

Issues
Marine pollution ranges from micro- and macro-plastics to chemicals and wastewater carried
into the sea by rivers and failing water infrastructure. Bio-accumulation of microplastics, heavy
metals, and pollutants has been recorded in fish, shellfish, seabirds, marine mammals, and
humans. The long shape of the country, its position between significant oceans and the Tasman
Sea, soil types, and poor land-use practices all contribute to very high levels of coastal sediment,
which smothers coastal habitats. Sediment is also continuously resuspended by bottomcontacting fishing gear and sea-mining activities, choking marine life. This is exacerbated by
coastal and urban flooding.
Actions
4.1.

4.2.

Halt activities that significantly contribute to the degradation of marine and
estuarine habitats, including:
4.1.1.

Identifying and addressing coastal dumping and other sources of marine
pollution (point and non-point sources); and

4.1.2.

Prohibiting seabed mining and seismic prospecting for oil and gas within
Aotearoa New Zealand’s territorial sea and EEZ.

Reduce the risk of pollutants entering aquatic ecosystems by:
4.2.1.

Enforcing international maritime pollution legislation (MARPOL), to which
Aotearoa New Zealand is a signatory;

4.2.2.

Excluding from sensitive marine environments ships that carry significant
amounts of oil;

4.2.3.

Requiring oil and chemical tankers entering Aotearoa New Zealand’s
territorial waters to be double-hulled; and

4.2.4.

Resourcing marine biosecurity operations, including risk assessment,
surveillance, and incursion response.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Marine Policy — Reviewed: 2022 — Version: 02 March 2026

<!-- page 7 -->

5.

Fisheries and Aquaculture

Issues
Aotearoa New Zealand fisheries management is falling behind international developments.
Across many species, fish numbers and fish sizes are declining. Bottom trawling and dredging
destroy sensitive ecosystems and release carbon sequestered in ocean sediment.
Actions
5.1.

5.2.

5.3.

5.4.

5.5.

Reform the Fisheries Act 1996 and its subsequent amendments to enable Tiritiand ecosystem-based management of all fisheries, including:
5.1.1.

Transitioning the Quota Management System (QMS) to an ecosystembased approach that enables the interactions of all species, their
environment, and the interactions between trophic levels to be addressed
in management to ensure fish, shellfish, and associated and dependent
species populations are maintained at ecologically healthy, resilient levels;

5.1.2.

Ending bottom trawling, prioritising seamounts and areas with high levels
of sequestered carbon and biodiversity; and

5.1.3.

Ending the fishing-related mortality of marine mammals, turtles, seabirds,
and other protected marine species for all fisheries.

Ensure that commercial fishing occurs within agreed take areas and minimises
ecological impacts, including by:
5.2.1.

Supporting all commercial fisheries to transition to independently-verified
best practice methods and equipment.

5.2.2.

Implementing innovative, detailed, and effective incentives and penalties to
avoid bycatch of protected and threatened marine species.

5.2.3.

Strengthening the monitoring and enforcement of fishing regulations,
including recreational fishing and monitoring of commercial fisheries,

Ensure that recreational fishing regulations address cumulative and long-term
ecological effects and avoid harm to protected species, including by:
5.3.1.

Investigating recreational fishing licensing and innovative use of licensing
revenue; and

5.3.2.

Encouraging self-reporting of recreational fishing activity to inform bag
limits.

Minimise ghost fishing gear, including by:
5.4.1.

Mandating gear marking to promote responsible ownership;

5.4.2.

Providing adequate recovery and disposal facilities for old gear and
improving seabed mapping to help avoid broken gear; and

5.4.3.

Phasing out the use of synthetic plastic ropes.

Improve the viability of small commercial fishers in the inshore fleet, including by:
5.5.1.

Reviewing the operation of the QMS to improve the viability of small inshore
fishers to provide New Zealanders with verifiably sustainable seafood;

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Marine Policy — Reviewed: 2022 — Version: 02 March 2026

<!-- page 8 -->

5.6.

5.5.2.

Investigating opportunities for developing quota in a local pool that can only
be owned within a specific geographical area;

5.5.3.

Revising cost recovery and administration charges so that costs are more
proportional to the commercial benefit derived from the fishery; and

5.5.4.

Supporting responsible fisheries education, training and credentialing.

Enable the farming of marine species, including kelp, in ways that support
ecosystem health, including by:
5.6.1.

6.

Promoting the use of marine permaculture and polytrophic aquaculture,
without the introduction of artificial feed.

Connection with the Marine Environment

Issues
Much of the population of Aotearoa New Zealand lives close to the ocean, and it plays a
significant role in national identity. However, access to the marine environment is inequitable
and not readily possible for many children. There are too few protected places where New
Zealanders can experience the marine ecosystem in an undamaged and natural state. As a result,
knowledge of the past abundance of the moana is being lost over time.
Actions
6.1.

Support programmes to build a connection with the marine environment and
ocean, including:
6.1.1.

Developing and delivering cross-cultural ocean literacy so that all people of
Aotearoa can learn to understand, care for, and love the ocean;

6.1.2.

Supporting adult and child learn-to-swim and diving programmes, learn-tosail programmes, and opportunities to visit marine reserves;

6.1.3.

Enhancing and promoting education, training, and research in marine
sciences, and other capability-building opportunities;

6.1.4.

Supporting non-extractive marine-based recreation and tourism activities;
and

6.1.5.

Investing in mātauranga Māori as it pertains to the moana.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington

# Media Policy (Green Party policy document)

<!-- page 1 -->

Media Policy
The Green Party will support an independent media and enable community-based media. We will
support publicly owned broadcasting services and fund locally produced content, prioritising
those communities that are not well served by commercial interests, including Māori and
children.

Vision
A strong, diverse and independent media contributes to the maintenance of effective
democracy, and to our social, cultural, economic and environmental wellbeing.

Values and Principles
Decisions relating to broadcasting and media must uphold the following values and principles:
- Honour Te Tiriti o Waitangi: Māori media should be prioritised and recognised as a
platform to uphold the culture of tangata whenua in Aotearoa New Zealand.

- Ecological Wisdom: The environmental impact of the production and storage of media
content should be minimised.

- Social Responsibility: The media should be accessible to people of all abilities, and used
to inform, educate and entertain in a manner that supports citizens to participate
effectively in democracy and appreciate each others’ needs, interests and aspirations.

- Appropriate Decision-Making: The right to broadcast or publish is balanced with
expectations to act in a responsible and inclusive manner.

- Non-Violence: Non-violent resolution of political and social conflict is based on the
knowledge, acceptance and understanding of diverse communities, and of their needs,
interests and aspirations. Media should act as a means of checks and balances against
the misuse or abuse of social, economic and political power.

- Independence: A vigorous, independent and diverse media is the cornerstone of a free
society: Public broadcasting and community-based media initiatives should be supported;
and directives by the state, or ownership and control by international media
conglomerates, or domination by local commercial monopolies should be avoided.

Strategic Priorities
The Green Party’s strategic goals include:

“As a Party we want to see Te Ao Māori and Te Reo Māori flourish in Aotearoa.
“All people will be empowered to shape the systems that affect them.”
Actions in this policy that will help achieve this include:

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Media Policy --- Reviewed: 2014 --- Version: 11 March 2026

1

<!-- page 2 -->

- Establish, monitor and enforce obligations attached to the right to broadcast and stream
content online, including honouring the rights and interests of tangata whenua under Te
Tiriti o Waitangi. (1.1)

- Support quality public service broadcasting and streaming, and digital media commons,
that nurture and promote our own talent and creativity as a nation, reflecting the unique
social and cultural diversity of Aotearoa New Zealand. (1.3)

- Protect the political independence and public ownership of Radio New Zealand, Television
New Zealand and the Māori Television Service and iwi radio. (1.3.2)

- Secure long term funding and support for dedicated Māori language media, including the
Māori Television Service and iwi radio stations, to be independent, secure and successfully
play a major role in revitalising language and culture. (2.4.2)

Connected Policies
A freely available and politically independent media makes a significant contribution to the
effectiveness of Governance, Research, Science and Technology, and Education, through the
provision of political debate, diverse perspectives and information about the world we live in. It
is a key mechanism for celebrating the Arts, Culture and Heritage of Aotearoa New Zealand. It is
increasingly entwined with the development of Digital technologies. Its Workforce must be
protected.

Policy Positions
1. Free and Independent Media
Issues
Ownership of media in Aotearoa New Zealand is dominated by transnational mediacommunication conglomerates and private financial organisations. National media is not immune
to global trends that threaten free and independent media, leading to a shift of audiences and
advertising revenue from traditional mass media to social media, and the purchased influence of
far-right populists. This risks undermining public knowledge and increasing the polarisation of
views.

Actions
1.1.

Establish, monitor and enforce obligations attached to the right to broadcast and
stream content online, including honouring the rights and interests of tangata whenua
under Te Tiriti o Waitangi.

1.2.

Ensure responsible self-regulation of national media, by:
1.2.1.

Establishing a Tiriti-based framework for responsible self-regulation, covering
the Advertising Standards Authority, the Broadcasting Standards Authority and
the Press Council;

1.2.2.

Creating an organisational structure to monitor and report on media selfregulation organisations, and support an accessible appeals process; and

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Media Policy --- Reviewed: 2014 --- Version: 11 March 2026

2

<!-- page 3 -->

1.2.3.
1.3.

2.

Issuing minimum codes or regulations in the event that self-regulation can be
demonstrated to have failed.

Support quality public service broadcasting and streaming, and digital media
commons, that nurture and promote our own talent and creativity as a nation,
reflecting the unique social and cultural diversity of Aotearoa New Zealand, including
by:
1.3.1.

Ring-fencing public revenue, including for New Zealand on Air, and facilitating
additional sources of revenue, to ensure sustainable funding for public
broadcasting and streaming;

1.3.2.

Protecting the political independence and public ownership of Radio New
Zealand, Television New Zealand and the Māori Television Service and iwi radio;

1.3.3.

Establishing a Digital Media Commons that, in partnership with public television,
public radio, community broadcasters, and website media providers, provides
access to public-interest content and publicly funded resources (such as the
Public Archives, museums and libraries); and

1.3.4.

Resourcing all national media to support Māori language and culture, offer Te
Reo Māori services, and use correct pronunciation for Māori words and place
names.

Inclusive and accessible media

Issues
New Zealanders are heavily exposed to commercial and imported content. By comparison, locally
made content that shows Aotearoa New Zealand’s cultures, languages and values is relatively
limited. This reduces opportunities for children to see themselves and their communities, and
Māori as tangata whenua, positively reflected on screen. It is hard for Māori to exercise
rangatiratanga and be heard in the media. Expressions of the indigenous culture of Aotearoa
New Zealand, which is the birthright of every Māori, and the heritage of every New Zealander,
are diluted. Access gaps for disabled people and speakers of minority languages, for example,
can deepen social exclusion and limit participation as audience or creator. Meanwhile, access to
harmful content has impacts on mental health, attitudes to relationships, and discrimination especially for young people.

Actions
2.1.

Ensure and incentivise the production of music, films and programmes for
broadcasting and streaming by diverse Aotearoa New Zealand artists, producers,
writers and directors, including by:
2.1.1.

Requiring Government-funded broadcasters and streaming services to employ
a workforce that reflects the communities it serves, and employ best practice
for media coverage of marginalised communities;

2.1.2.

Investigating minimum Aotearoa New Zealand content quotas for public
broadcasters and streaming services and incentives for commercial
broadcasters and streaming services to provide higher levels of local content;
and

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Media Policy --- Reviewed: 2014 --- Version: 11 March 2026

3

<!-- page 4 -->

2.1.3.
2.2.

2.3.

2.4.

2.5.

2.6.

Ensure that New Zealand on Air enables local stories, songs and perspectives to reach
audiences by:
2.2.1.

Prioritising the local production, broadcasting and streaming of educational,
interactive children's media content;

2.2.2.

Permitting New Zealand on Air to require less of a financial contribution from
local broadcasters when generating content in specific priority genres; and

2.2.3.

Implementing criteria for New Zealand On Air funding decisions that increase
the quality of content for niche audiences who are underserved by commercial
programming.

Enable community broadcasting to grow and develop in a manner that reflects ethnic
and cultural diversity, and changing interests, needs and aspirations, including by:
2.3.1.

Providing a regulatory framework for broadcasting and streaming that offers
community-based broadcasters and streaming services ongoing security over
both broadcasting rights and funding; and

2.3.2.

Investigating establishing a network of community media hubs to share content
and contribute to the Digital Media Commons.

Support a strong voice for Māori as media content producers and broadcasters, by:
2.4.1.

Reviewing funding rates to achieve full equivalence with English language media
ensure Māori content producers can continue to provide varied genres of quality
content;

2.4.2.

Securing long term funding and support for dedicated Māori language media,
including the Māori Television Service and iwi radio stations, to be independent,
secure and successfully play a major role in revitalising language and culture;
and

2.4.3.

Working with the Māori media industry to develop and enhance services for a
multimedia, multi-platform environment.

Minimise harmful media content, by:
2.5.1.

Updating, monitoring and enforcing the codes of broadcasting practice on the
portrayal of violence on television, and developing an appropriate equivalent for
online content and social media;

2.5.2.

Monitoring and regularly reporting on the amount of harmful content viewed by
New Zealanders in all media formats; and

2.5.3.

Incentivising media platforms to counter harmful narratives and promote
diverse role models.

Enable caregivers and educators to minimise young people’s exposure to harmful
content, including by:
2.6.1.

2.7.

Increasing support for Pasifika media and services to the Pacific, such as Radio
New Zealand International.

Investigating removing commercial advertising from broadcasts and streaming
services aimed at pre-school and school-age audiences.

Ensure that media is accessible to all by:

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Media Policy --- Reviewed: 2014 --- Version: 11 March 2026

4

<!-- page 5 -->

2.7.1.

Enacting legislation to require broadcasters and streaming providers to provide
media in an accessible format, including captioning, audio-description and New
Zealand Sign Language content; and

2.7.2.

Adopting an ongoing monitoring and evaluation process, co-designed with the
disabled community, around captioning standards and quality of access.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Media Policy --- Reviewed: 2014 --- Version: 11 March 2026

# Overseas New Zealanders Policy (Green Party policy document)

<!-- page 1 -->

Overseas New Zealanders Policy
Vision
The Green Party celebrates the large and diverse diaspora of Aotearoa New Zealand, fosters
mutually-beneficial and meaningful links to home, and safeguards our rights and well-being.

Values and Principles
Waiho i te toipoto, kaua i te toiroa
Let us keep close together, not far apart
This policy is grounded in the Green Party charter, international Green values and elementary
policies of fairness, equity and human rights.
- Honour Te Tiriti o Waitangi: Tangata whenua should lead all kaupapa related to Māori living
overseas.

- Ecological Wisdom: Overseas New Zealanders should be supported with sustainable and
environmentally-conscious connections with home.

- Social Responsibility: Overseas New Zealanders should have human rights, democratic
rights and access to the principles of citizenship, regardless of where we live.

- Appropriate decision-making: Overseas New Zealanders should have the opportunity to
contribute to our home country and have their voices heard.

- Non-violence: States have a basic duty of care to their citizens. This must include overseas
New Zealanders and be free of political bias, favouritism or status based on perceived
worth to our home country.

Connected Policies
The Aotearoa New Zealand diaspora is impacted by policy in several areas including Governance,
Disability, Health, Global Affairs, Immigration, Livelihoods, Education, Te Tiriti o Waitangi, and
Workforce.

Policy Positions
1.

Te Tiriti o Waitangi and the Aotearoa New Zealand Diaspora

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Overseas New Zealanders Policy --- Reviewed: 2022 --- Version: 26 February 2026

1

<!-- page 2 -->

Issues
Māori hold a distinct and special status as the indigenous people, or tangata whenua, of Aotearoa
New Zealand. The particular rights of Māori living overseas, outlined by the articles of te Tiriti o
Waitangi, must be fully explored and upheld, enabling Māori leadership in supporting the Māori
diaspora.

Actions
1.1.

Guaranteeing Aotearoa New Zealand citizenship to all individuals with Māori
whakapapa living or born overseas; and

1.2.

Establishing a tikanga pathway to citizenship that allows for hapū and iwi to assess
whakapapa evidence, as recommended in Waitangi Tribunal’s “He Tangata, he
Whenua: The Citizenship Report” (Wai 3513)."

2.

Services, Support and Human Rights

Issues
Our interconnected world creates situations where many migrants do not have access to services,
support, or basic rights in either their country of residence or country of origin. New Zealanders
living overseas are no exception, and their basic needs must be met, including in times of crisis.
Our ability to return home must be equitable and accessible.

Actions
2.1.

Affirm the right of New Zealanders to hold multiple nationalities.

2.2.

Affirm the rights of New Zealanders to access pathways to citizenship in other
countries, including by advocating against health and disability cost-based
discrimination.

2.3.

Ensure that measures to address risks from current and future crises protect the
rights of New Zealanders to return home and do not impose additional costs on
them.

2.4.

Provide adequate resources to allow diplomatic staff to act as advocates or provide
support for New Zealand citizens in emergency situations.

2.5.

Investigate digital or embassy-based health services for New Zealanders living
overseas.

2.6.

Allow New Zealanders living overseas to claim a one-off emergency loan payment
in the event they have to leave their country of residence due to hardship or other
circumstances.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Overseas New Zealanders Policy --- Reviewed: 2022 --- Version: 26 February 2026

2

<!-- page 3 -->

2.7.

Pursue reciprocal healthcare support arrangements with more states and widen
existing agreements to include fixed-term residents.

2.8.

Pursue new and extended reciprocal working visa programmes with other states.

2.9.

Pursue reciprocal welfare arrangements with other states.

3.

Meaningful Connections

Issues
The relationship between New Zealanders living overseas and our home is affected by
Government policy and must be strengthened and supported. The government must be
responsive and represent the interests of the diaspora by understanding our unique and diverse
characteristics.

Actions

4.

3.1.

Establish a government institution with responsibility for the Aotearoa New Zealand
diaspora.

3.2.

Establish a formal channel for overseas New Zealanders to communicate with the
government directly on all issues relevant to them.

3.3.

Ensure that demographic data collection for New Zealanders overseas gives an
accurate understanding of our diaspora.

3.4.

Remove the requirement for people to be physically present in Aotearoa New
Zealand to renew or replace government-issued documentation and ensure renewal
processes are accessible, including to disabled people.

3.5.

Lengthen the repayment holiday for overseas student loan borrowers.

3.6.

Abolish border arrests for student loan repayment violations.

3.7.

Restore the ten-year eligibility-threshold for time spent in Aotearoa New Zealand
to be eligible for a full or partial superannuation.

3.8.

Ensure that people who leave Aotearoa New Zealand intending to return within six
months, but are unable to do so for exceptional reasons, remain eligible for
superannuation.

3.9.

Ensure that assessment of applications to be paid superannuation while overseas
for more than 26 weeks takes full account of financial position, family obligations,
and cultural considerations.

Participation in Society

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Overseas New Zealanders Policy --- Reviewed: 2022 --- Version: 26 February 2026

3

<!-- page 4 -->

Issues
Our ability to participate in the democracy of Aotearoa New Zealand must be upheld and
improved. We must have a voice and both ourselves and our families should feel part of Aotearoa
New Zealand society.

Actions
4.1.

Lengthen the time spent outside Aotearoa New Zealand before losing voting
eligibility.

4.2.

Establish accessible, secure enrolment and voting mechanisms for overseas voters.

4.3.

Ensure that sufficient accessible voting options are available so that all overseas
voters can vote, regardless of barriers (such as disability).

4.4.

Make it easier for overseas partners and immediate family members of New
Zealanders to become residents.

4.5.

Hold New Zealanders accountable for any international crimes committed at home
or overseas, while:
4.5.1.

Upholding the fundamental protections provided by international and
Aotearoa New Zealand’s criminal and human rights laws; and

4.5.2.

Ensuring prosecutions are not undertaken for partisan purposes.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Overseas New Zealanders Policy --- Reviewed: 2022 --- Version: 26 February 2026
