documents/te-waonui-a-tane-policy-2026.m.title: Te Waonui a Tāne — Thriving Marae for Thriving Communities
documents/te-waonui-a-tane-policy-2026.m.text:
# Te Waonui a Tāne — Thriving Marae for Thriving Communities

<!-- page 1 -->

Te Waonui a Tāne
Thriving Marae for Thriving Communities

Auth by Marama Davidson and Chlöe Swarbrick, Green Party Co-leaders.
Parliament Buildings, Wgtn. Funded by Parliamentary Services.

<!-- page 2 -->

The Green Party

When marae are strong,
communities are stronger.
At marae cultures thrive,
partnerships grow, communities
become more resilient, and
local solutions are developed
by the people who know their
communities best.
The Green Party policy Te Waonui a Tāne
will recognise and resource marae as the
critical social and cultural infrastructure
they are, to keep our communities
connected, safe and welcomed.

01

greens.org.nz

<!-- page 3 -->

Thriving Marae policy 2026

Te Waonui a Tāne, the Green Party policy
for thriving marae and communities,
recognises that marae are not simply
buildings—marae are living ecosystems
of people, whenua, culture, knowledge,
and communities.
For many New Zealanders, Māori and non-Māori
alike, marae are part of the shared cultural
landscape that shapes our national identity
and contributes to what makes Aotearoa
unique in the world. Marae are essential and
intergenerational community partners to local
councils, government agencies, schools,
community and health organisations, to
improve outcomes for all whānau.
Marae have also repeatedly demonstrated
their importance during times of crisis.
Time and again, marae have opened their
doors to support entire communities at the
worst of times.
Marae have played a vital role in civil
defence and community responses from the
Christchurch and Kaikōura earthquakes, to the
severe weather events impacting Te Tai Rāwhiti,
Te Tai Tokerau, Canterbury, and other regions
affected by states of emergency.
Despite their importance, marae across
the motu continue to face a compounding
number of challenges that threaten both their
operational capability and cultural integrity.
Funding programmes are often short-term,
capped, and prescribed rather than communityled. Many are fragmented across multiple
agencies, and difficult to access for marae
without the resources to navigate complex
application and reporting processes.
This makes it difficult for marae committees
to undertake long-term planning, restore
important infrastructure, build capability,
or invest in projects that strengthen their
communities for future generations.
Despite the enduring wealth and advantage
the Crown has obtained through historic

greens.org.nz

injustice and dispossession of Māori, the Treaty
Settlement process makes the Crown the
wrongdoer, the negotiator, and the rule maker.
The Crown continues to set the terms of
negotiations – deciding which resources may
be returned, which assets are available, and
how much compensation iwi can receive. This
does not reflect natural justice or a partner
acting in good faith.
Many marae are managing ageing buildings
and failing infrastructure, financial constraints,
limited opportunities to generate sustainable
income, and declining numbers of ahikā to
uphold tikanga and care for marae.
By restoring and sustaining marae, we
strengthen the foundations that allow
communities to thrive.

Together, we can ensure future
generations inherit a vibrant,
resilient, and self-determining
community and Aotearoa.
Marae should have the support to plan for
generations, not election cycles. Te Waonui a
Tāne creates a permanent solution to access
funding for short-term and long-term needs,
while building local capability, and providing
outcomes that benefit everyone in Aotearoa.
The Green Party will establish
Te Rangatiratanga Trust with an initial
funding commitment that will be transferred
into the ownership of hapū and iwi of
Aotearoa to create the capital base for the
permanent trust.
Te Rangatiratanga Trust will restore and
sustain marae as the living heart of our
communities by creating a permanent,
independent source of funding for the full
marae ecosystem—the people, whenua,
buildings, culture, and relationships
that keep marae and their surrounding
communities thriving.

02

<!-- page 4 -->

The Green Party

Closer partnerships,
better outcomes

Marae resilience for
safer communities

Many community services in rural
and regional areas such as education,
housing support, food security, health
and youth programmes operate in
isolation from one another.

During and after times of crisis such
as climate charged weather events,
marae have repeatedly demonstrated
their importance for keeping people
safe, connected, and cared for. Time
and again, marae have opened their
doors to welcome and support entire
communities.

Funding contracts are often short-term,
fragmented, and tied to different agencies
with separate reporting requirements. This
makes it difficult for marae, councils, and
community organisations to work together
in a coordinated way, even when they are
serving the same whānau.
How Te Waonui a Tāne responds: Flexible
funding through Te Rangatiratanga Trust
would support marae-led, cross-sector
community initiatives that bring together
local councils, service providers, schools
and social service organisations. Regional
commissioning bodies would help reduce
administrative burden, align funding
requirements and support shared planning,
delivery, and evaluation. The long-term
feature of Te Tōtara Haemata ensures
successful partnerships can continue and
scale over time.
The outcome: Marae become reliable
partners for coordinated community action,
where services work together rather than in
isolation. Whānau experience more seamless
support across health, education, and social
needs, while local organisations achieve
better outcomes through shared resources
and reduced duplication.
Importantly, Māori-led approaches
strengthen outcomes for the whole
community, not only Māori. When services
are designed around holistic wellbeing,
non-Māori also benefit from more
accessible healthcare, stronger emergency
preparedness, improved social support,
and better connection to local services. This
creates more resilient, cohesive communities
where improved wellbeing is shared across
everyone living in the area.

03

But one in three marae are at risk of flooding,
one in three are situated in landslide-prone
areas, one in five are in tsunami evacuation
zones and two in five are susceptible to
liquefaction in the event of an earthquake. At
the same time, marae are increasingly relied
upon as emergency response hubs, despite
often lacking resilient power, water supplies
and emergency infrastructure.
How Te Waonui a Tāne responds:
Te Rākau Whakarauora Restoration
Fund would provide immediate funding
for projects such as solar power and battery
storage, emergency water supplies,
communication systems, and secure
storage for emergency equipment. It could
also support climate adaptation initiatives
including flood mitigation, erosion control,
vulnerable infrastructure relocation,
improving stormwater management, and
other projects that strengthen the long-term
resilience of marae and surrounding whenua.
Regional commissioning bodies would assist
with planning, technical advice, and project
delivery, while Te Tōtara Haemata would
provide an ongoing source of funding to
maintain and enhance resilience
options over time.
The outcome: Marae are better prepared to
withstand the impacts of climate change and
natural disasters while continuing to provide
shelter, food, coordination and support when
communities need them most. Investing in
resilience before disasters occur helps reduce
future costs, protects places of cultural
significance, and strengthens the safety and
wellbeing of the wider community.

<!-- page 5 -->

Thriving Marae policy 2026

Rural health hubs for
local wellbeing
Many rural communities face long travel
times, limited transport options, and
limited access to healthcare. Marae have
become trusted locations for delivering
drive-through, pop-up, and mobile
health services during times of need, yet
many lack the facilities needed to provide
regular, preventative healthcare.
As a result, many people delay seeking
treatment until their health needs become
more serious and require hospital care.
How Te Waonui a Tāne responds: Funding
from Te Rākau Whakarauora or Te Tōtara
Haemata would support marae to establish or
upgrade spaces where they can host regular
primary healthcare services, including GP
clinics, nurses’ services, mental health

greens.org.nz

support, screening programmes, midwives,
immunisation clinics, and kaupapa Māori
health providers. Regional commissioning
bodies would support marae to coordinate
with healthcare providers and deliver these
projects.
The outcome: Whānau can access
preventative healthcare closer to home,
helping to identify and address health
concerns before they develop into more
serious conditions. This strengthens the
health and wellbeing of communities,
reduces pressure on the healthcare system,
and supports marae in continuing to serve
as trusted, locally led centres that support
healthier futures for all of us.

04

<!-- page 6 -->

The Green Party

The Green
Party will:
• Uphold tino rangatiratanga and
self-governance
• Facilitate nationwide wānanga to
establish the trustee body, two funds,
and governance mechanisms.
• Create Te Rangatiratanga Trust,
owned and governed by hapū and iwi
of Aotearoa.
• Establish Te Rangatiratanga Trust
• Dedicated Crown funding of $2.44
billion total for Rangatiratanga Trust.
• The Trust will govern immediate
investment and long-term
sustainability via two complementary
funds.
• Build a restoration fund
that provides for urgent and
immediate needs

• Implement Te Rākau
Whakarauora Restoration Fund for
immediate and urgent priorities.
• Allocate $400 million for
immediate and urgent projects
over four years.
• Build an intergenerational fund
that provides for generations to
come

• Implement Te Tōtara Haemata
Intergenerational Fund for long
term investment in marae and
community development.
• Invest $2 billion in a diversified
portfolio to generate returns for
annual distribution.
• Preserve the investment fund’s
capital for the benefit of future
generations.

05

Tino rangatiratanga
and self-governance
Before the Trust is established, the Green
Party will work with key groups to outline
and timeline the move from aspiration to
reality. We will facilitate nationwide wānanga
informed by constitutional transformation
processes, such as Matike Mai, to support
collectively designing the Trust’s governance
structure. The outcome of this process will
become the foundation of the Trust Deed.
This process will facilitate hapū
and iwi to determine:
• How collective ownership is exercised
• How trustees are appointed and removed
• Regional representation
• Tikanga alignment
• Dispute resolution process
• Succession arrangements
The governance model can draw from
successful Māori-led arrangements already
operating across Aotearoa, including Whānau
Ora commissioning approaches, hapū and
iwi governance structures, and Māori-owned
organisations that manage significant
resources while remaining accountable to
their communities and tikanga.
Once established, Te Rangatiratanga
Trust will operate independently through
governance arrangements designed to
protect its intergenerational purpose,
maintain transparency, and ensure
accountability to marae, hapū, iwi,
communities, and the public.
The role of the Crown will be limited to
establishing the Trust, supporting the
collective design process, and transferring
the agreed capital contribution to
establish the Trust.
The Crown will have no authority to direct
investments, appoint trustees, alter funding
decisions, or interfere with the operation
of the Trust beyond ordinary law applying
equally to all trusts.

greens.org.nz

<!-- page 7 -->

Thriving Marae policy 2026

Te Rangatiratanga Trust
Te Rangatiratanga Trust will govern a
permanent source of funding for marae,
hapū, and the communities they serve.
A $2.44 billion Crown funding input will
establish the Trust and its two
complementary funds:
Te Rākau Whakarauora Restoration Fund,
which provides for urgent and priority needs,
and Te Tōtara Haemata Intergenerational
Fund, which protects and grows capital for
future generations.
Together, these funds will provide immediate
and long-term support for the marae
ecosystem, remedy inequities derived
from historic and ongoing Crown actions,
enhance marae capability and community
partnerships, and create intergenerational
wellbeing independent of political cycles.
Te Rangatiratanga Trust is designed as a
permanent capital base for a funding model
that provides both immediate support for
marae and long-term funding certainty for
future generations. Instead of relying on
short-term funding cycles, the Trust creates
a permanent source of funding that grows
over time and supports marae, hapū, and
communities to lead their own aspirations.
The Trust combines immediate restoration
investment with an intergenerational
investment fund that protects and grows
wealth for the future.
Unlike traditional government funding
programmes, decisions about how funding
is invested and distributed will be made
independently of Ministers and successive
governments. This provides certainty for
marae and communities while ensuring
investment decisions remain focused on
long-term aspirations rather than changing
political priorities.
Te Rangatiratanga Trust is separate from
the Treaty settlement framework. It does not
replace, affect, or extinguish any existing
rights or obligations under

greens.org.nz

Te Tiriti o Waitangi. Rather than providing
Treaty settlement redress, the Trust
establishes a forward-looking investment
mechanism that supports the long-term
resilience and prosperity of marae and the
communities they serve.

Te Rākau Whakarauora
Restoration Fund
Intergenerational funds take time to mature,
but many marae and communities require
investment now.
Te Rākau Whakarauora Restoration Trust is a
time-limited establishment fund that provides
immediate investment in marae resilience
and restoration while Te Tōtara Haemata
Intergenerational Fund is established. It will
address urgent priorities such as restoring
buildings and infrastructure, strengthening
capability, improving climate resilience, and
supporting projects that support marae and
their surrounding communities to thrive.
Funding can support projects such as:

• Restoring marae buildings, fixtures,
and infrastructure.
• Strengthening emergency preparedness
and response capability.
• Improving climate resilience and
adaptation.
• Supporting capability development
and project delivery.
• Protecting taonga, wāhi tapu, and
cultural heritage.
• Enabling marae-led partnerships that
improve community wellbeing.
Te Rākau Whakarauora will also provide
an opportunity to establish and refine the
Trust’s funding pathways, ensuring future
investment through Te Tōtara Haemata
is effective, accessible, and responsive to
community aspirations.

06

<!-- page 8 -->

The Green Party

Te Tōtara Haemata
Intergenerational Fund
At the heart of Te Waonui a Tāne is Te Tōtara
Haemata Intergenerational Fund, a permanent
intergenerational fund designed to preserve
and grow the Trust’s capital through
long-term investment.
Rather than spending the capital itself,
investment returns will be distributed to
support the aspirations of hapū and iwi of
Aotearoa, while protecting the capital for
future generations. This creates an enduring
source of funding that grows over time and
provides long-term certainty independent
of political cycles.
Through responsible investment, Te Tōtara
Haemata will create enduring intergenerational
prosperity and strengthen Māori economic
capacity while aligning with environmental
sustainability, social wellbeing, and the longterm success of future generations.
Investment opportunities may include:
• Renewable energy and climate transition
• Investment in whenua Māori
• Housing and regional development
• Māori enterprise and business growth
• Emerging industries and technologies

Decisions made closer
to communities
The Green Party recognises that marae,
hapū, and local communities are best placed
to determine their own priorities and define
what success looks like.
Funding distribution can follow a similar
approach to Whānau Ora models, using
regional commissioning bodies to ensure
decisions remain close to communities.

07

This approach reduces barriers to
accessing funding, supports smaller
marae that may have limited administrative
capacity, and allows communities to
determine their own priorities.
Funding criteria can also be broadened to
support a wide range of aspirations that are
usually not accounted for when determined
by Government, including:
Te Pūtake – Acknowledging the Past:
Supporting projects that recognise
whakapapa, protect cultural heritage,
and acknowledge the achievements and
contributions of tūpuna.
Te Puāwai – Acting Today and Investing
in Tomorrow: Supporting the holistic
revitalisation of marae and the aspirations
of hapori Māori, hapū, and iwi.
Te Poipoi – Community Partnership
Projects: Supporting marae to partner
with wider communities, councils, and
organisations on projects that benefit
the rohe.
Accountability can be maintained through
transparent reporting and whānaucentred outcome measures developed
with communities. Instead of quantitative
reporting, success can be measured
through outcomes including:
Cultural wellbeing – strengthening
whakapapa, tikanga, mātauranga Māori,
and identity.
Social wellbeing – supporting whānau
resilience, connection, and community
strength.
Commercial activity – employment
and training opportunities, tourism levels,
cost of living.
Environmental resilience – protecting
whenua and supporting kaitiakitanga.
Long-term wellbeing – number of
generations that have benefitted from
the funding.

greens.org.nz

<!-- page 9 -->

Thriving Marae policy 2026

Funding the future

The funding is allocated in the first two years
from the Crown, and the Trust will determine
the investment and expenditure based on its
priorities. We have modelled that the Trust
will for the first four years spend $10 million a
year on establishment and associated costs,
$100 million a year on Te Rākau Whakarauora
Restoration Funding, and invest $2 billion in
seed funding for Te Tōtara Haemata.

The Green Party proposes an initial Crown
funding commitment of $2.44 billion with any
further Crown contributions to be determined
during the negotiation process. This amount
is aligned with other comparable long-term
public funds, including the New Zealand
Superannuation Fund’s initial $2.4 billion
contribution in 2003 and the Aboriginal and
Torres Strait Islander Land and Sea Future
Fund’s $2 billion contribution in 2019 in
Australia.

Using the Treasury investment return
assumptions in the 2026 Budget Economic
and Fiscal Update we can also estimate:
• The $2 billion invested through Te Tōtara
Haemata to grow to approximately $3.8
billion by 2039/40 before distributions.

The $2.44 billion investment is intended for the
establishment and maintenance of the Trust’s
components including Te Rākau Whakarauora
Restoration Fund and the seed funding for Te
Tōtara Haemata Intergenerational Fund for at
least 4 years until it has matured enough to
access returns.

• Annual distributions could provide between
$47 million and $118 million in ongoing
support once the fund has initially matured,
while maintaining the long-term capital base.

documents/tourism-policy-2025.md.text:
# Tourism Policy (Green Party policy document)

<!-- page 1 -->

Tourism Policy
The Green Party supports tourism that is sustainable, inclusive, and enhances the well-being of
people and the environment. For Māori, this means protecting and sharing culture through
tourism that upholds tikanga and tino rangatiratanga. Aotearoa New Zealand needs a national
strategy that supports low-impact tourism, reducing emissions, protecting nature, and
strengthening local communities. When tourism is managed responsibly, it creates meaningful
connections, supports local economies, and ensures future generations can enjoy our natural
and cultural heritage.

Vision
Tourism enhances cultural connections and delivers an experience to visitors that protects
communities and the natural world.

Values and Principles
Decision-making in relation to tourism must uphold the following interconnected values and
principles:
- Kaitiakitanga: Tourism activities must protect and nurture our natural environment, which
has more value than just an attraction or experience for visitors.

- Āhua o te rangi: Tourism is dependent on a stable climate, and must transition to lower
emissions and greater resilience.

- Manaakitanga: Tourism is a form of hospitality that must enhance the well-being of
tourists and communities.

- Kotahitanga: Tourism should work collaboratively to help achieve collective goals.

- Rangapū: Partnering with Māori provides unique, culturally authentic, non-exploitative
tourism.

- Tauutuutu: Tourism should build reciprocal, long-term relationships that involve a
mutually beneficial sharing of culture, experience, and resources.

Strategic Priorities
The Green Party’s strategic goals include:

“...regenerative practices in all areas of economic activity, including land use and food
production, will predominate.”
Actions in this policy that will help achieve this include:
- Phasing out permits and subsidies and introducing disincentives for high-emission
tourism activities, and providing resources for a just transition. (1.1.1)

- Establish a regulatory framework for limiting international tourism, based on the
environmental impacts of international flights. (1.1.3 )

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Digital Policy --- Reviewed: 2025 --- Version: 04 August 2025

1

<!-- page 2 -->

- Ensure fairness and justice in tourism development decision-making, by considering the
impacts of tourism on communities. (2.1.1)

- Removing barriers to equitably accessing domestic tourism experiences. (3.1.1)

- Reorienting the Aotearoa New Zealand tourism strategy around domestic tourism,
coordinating regional bodies, and enabling informed decisions by regional bodies. (3.1.1)

- Resourcing Māori Tourism to oversee and, if necessary, restrict tourism operators who
are misappropriating Māori taonga, guided by local iwi and hapū. (4.1.1)

Connected Policies
Tourism falls under our wider Business Policy. Tourism benefits from Te Tiriti o Waitangi, vibrant
Arts, Culture and Heritage, suitable active and public Transport options and other infrastructure
(see also our Government in the Economy Policy), and healthy ecosystems (see our Biodiversity
and Environmental Regeneration Policy), and must reciprocate. Tourism must adapt to the
realities of Climate Change and the needs of communities (see our Housing and Sustainable
Communities, Rural Communities, Workforce, and Community and the Economy Policies). For
more on upholding mātauranga Māori as intellectual property belonging to Māori, see our
Research, Science and Technology Policy.

Policy Positions
1.

Environmental impacts of tourism

Issues
High energy consumption is embedded in most tourism activities, especially transport. The
tourism industry contributes to environmental damage through, for example: the volume of
visitors in eco-sensitive places; activities that change land use and pollute air, land and water;
inefficiencies and waste in infrastructure and other systems that accommodate tourists; and
noise and light pollution, especially in rural areas. Tourism also contributes to the crisis of climate
change, including through high levels of greenhouse gas emissions from long-haul cruise ships
and air travel. Aotearoa New Zealand may lose its clean green reputation, which will directly
impact the tourist economy.

Actions
1.1.

1.2.

Restrict tourism sectors with a high environmental impact, including by:
1.1.1.

Phasing out permits and subsidies and introducing disincentives for highemission tourism activities, and providing resources for a just transition;

1.1.2.

Developing environmental standards for cruise ships that stop their emissions,
waste, and impacts on marine and coastal environments; and

1.1.3.

Establishing a regulatory framework for limiting international tourism based on
the environmental impacts of international flights.

Alleviate tourism’s environmental impact on tourist hotspots, including by:
1.2.1.

Regulating tourist numbers and activities in areas of high ecological sensitivity,
and developing alternative tourist destinations and opportunities, including
digital exploration; and

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Digital Policy --- Reviewed: 2025 --- Version: 04 August 2025

2

<!-- page 3 -->

1.2.2.
1.3.

2.

Introducing a dynamic, data-driven visitor management system covering all
areas of tourism to inform the sector about environmental and other impacts.

Support the development of tourism that is both low-impact and actively restorative,
including by:
1.3.1.

Strengthening 'freedom camping' legislation to minimise damage to the local
environment;

1.3.2.

Incentivise the electrification of tourist activities that are powered by fossil
energy;

1.3.3.

Establishing and monitoring a certification scheme for low-impact tourism
operators; and

1.3.4.

Developing and implementing a Tiriti-based, low-impact tourism strategy,
integrated with the value of the Mauriora System Framework.

Social impacts of tourism

Issues
The tourism industry impacts communities with an overly heavy presence. Impacts include
housing occupation, traffic congestion, increased cost of living in tourist hotspots, safety
concerns, changes in community character, a lack of social license, social tensions, overcommercialisation of Māori culture; and inappropriate behaviour of some international tourists.

Actions
2.1.

2.2.

2.3.

Ensure communities can minimise and are resilient to the social impacts of tourism,
including by:
2.1.1.

Requiring tourism development decision-makers to consider the impacts of
tourism on communities;

2.1.2.

Improving standards and protections for workers in the tourism industry,
especially seasonal and migrant workers; and

2.1.3.

Providing legal recourse for communities adversely impacted by over-tourism.

Enable Tiriti-based, community-led and differentiated decision-making in the tourism
sector, including by:
2.2.1.

Encouraging community-based ownership of and local employment in tourism
ventures;

2.2.2.

Facilitating the development of community-centred networks for tourism
operators to advocate and collaborate; and

2.2.3.

Implementing long-term, destination management plans by regional tourism
bodies, in partnership with iwi, hapū, and other local communities.

Manage the impacts of high tourist numbers in communities with popular tourist
sites, including by:
2.3.1.

Increasing the international visitor levy and distributing it fairly, reflecting the
impacts and distribution of costs associated with managing tourism’s impacts;
and

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Digital Policy --- Reviewed: 2025 --- Version: 04 August 2025

3

<!-- page 4 -->

2.3.2.
2.4.

3.

Establishing local strategies to discourage unmanageable visitor numbers, such
as bed taxes or restrictions on the use of housing for tourist accommodation.

Restrict tourism activities that have a high negative social impact, including by:
2.4.1.

Requiring tourism operations based on high-risk gambling to prove ongoing
community consent to operate;

2.4.2.

Prohibit the promotion of activities with a high risk of social impacts; and

2.4.3.

Enabling community-led decision-making to impose local restrictions on
harmful tourism activities.

Resilience of tourism

Issues
Businesses that provide services designed for tourists are vulnerable to a range of factors, both
local and global. These include over-tourism, pressure on infrastructure, supply chain
vulnerabilities, and overreliance on international tourists.

Actions
3.1.

4.

Support a resilient domestic tourism sector that enables New Zealanders to enjoy the
cultural and natural environment of Aotearoa New Zealand, including by:
3.1.1.

Reorienting the Aotearoa New Zealand tourism strategy around domestic
tourism, coordinating regional bodies, and enabling informed decisions by
regional bodies; and

3.1.2.

Removing barriers to equitably accessing domestic tourism experiences.

Te Tiriti in tourism

Issues
Despite many successful Māori-owned and -operated tourist initiatives, there are still too many
instances within the tourism sector and its governance where the value of Indigenous
perspectives is not fully appreciated and the rights of Māori in relation to tourism are
undermined.

Actions
4.1.

4.2.

# Trade and Foreign Investment Policy (Green Party policy document)

<!-- page 1 -->

Trade and Foreign Investment Policy
The Green Party will work toward a global trade regime that respects ecological limits and local
cultures, and which contributes to sustainable development. This should encourage good global
citizenship and corporate responsibility, including through enforceable international law to
protect human rights and the environment. Economic decision-making should be democratic and
transparent.

Vision
Trade and foreign investment prioritise social, economic, cultural, and environmental justice in
the pursuit of sustainability.

Values and Principles
Trade and foreign investment agreements and policies must be underpinned by the following
values and principles:
- Honour Te Tiriti o Waitangi: Māori as Treaty partners and the indigenous people of
Aotearoa New Zealand, should have their rights and interests upheld in all trade
negotiations between Aotearoa New Zealand and the rest of the world.

- Ecological Wisdom: The purpose of trade and foreign investment should be to achieve
environmental and social objectives that keep us within our planetary boundaries, and
ensure the equitable, sustainable, and responsible use of natural resources.

- Social Responsibility: Equity and intergenerational responsibility should be cornerstones
of trade and foreign investment, and exploitation rejected.

- Appropriate Decision-Making: Trade and investment agreements should be transparently
and democratically mandated, negotiated, agreed upon, and reviewed.

- Non-Violence: Human rights and fair labour standards must be upheld, and the
precautionary principle should be adopted where there is uncertainty or concern about
potential harm.

- Global citizenship: The specific needs, sovereignty, biodiversity, and cultural differences
of emerging economies should be respected.

Strategic Priorities
The Green Party’s strategic goals include:

“Sustainable transport, renewable energy and regenerative practices in all areas of
economic activity [...] will predominate.”
Actions in this policy that will help achieve this include:

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Trade and Foreign Investment Policy --- Reviewed: 2011 --- Version: 20 May 2026

1

<!-- page 2 -->

- Ensure that all international trade agreements to which Aotearoa New Zealand is a
signatory give full effect to Aotearoa New Zealand's Te Tiriti o Waitangi responsibilities,
and give effect to the values and principles of this policy (...) (1.3)

- Ensure all new international trade agreements are open to public scrutiny, including by
requiring a vote in Parliament before signing. (1.4.1)

- Retaining or imposing tariffs, quotas or bans where useful to prevent unfair competition
caused by unjust or unsustainable production practices in the country of origin. (2.4.3)

- Strengthening controls on speculative and other non-productive foreign investment (e.g.
land banking) to minimise its negative effects. (3.1.1)

Connected Policies
Managing trade activity is one role of the Government in the Economy, as part of Global Affairs.
Trade and foreign investment must support Biodiversity and Environmental Regeneration
(including addressing biosecurity), Climate Change responses, and Human Rights. Dependence
on trade can be mitigated with self-sufficiency in Food and Energy, and reorientation of key
sectors such as Agriculture, Tourism, and high-emitting industries. Any foreign-owned Business
operating in Aotearoa New Zealand must be held to the same standard as those that are locally
owned.

Policy Positions
1.

Sovereignty, International Trade Governance, and Global Citizenship

Issues
The large power imbalances among states engaging in consensus decisions in international trade
governance often leads to slow or stalled processes that protect the most powerful and so erode
trust. Trade agreements enhance international market access but can undermine national
decision-making through shared regulations, opaque dispute mechanisms, and strong investor
protections.

Actions
1.1.

Advocate for the World Trade Organisation to be replaced with a new international
trading organisation aligned with the values and principles of this policy.

1.2.

Advocate for strengthened powers for international environmental organisations,
labour and human rights organisations, and development organisations to enforce
their mandate and restrain unfair and unsustainable trading practices.

1.3.

Ensure that all international trade agreements to which Aotearoa New Zealand is a
signatory give full effect to Aotearoa New Zealand's Te Tiriti o Waitangi
responsibilities, and give effect to the values and principles of this policy, including
respecting and upholding:
1.3.1.

Positive sovereignty, the autonomy of communities and nations in decisions
relating to production, trade, and consumption, local values and cultures, and
the need for each country to be resilient to global changes;

1.3.2.

All international agreements to which Aotearoa New Zealand is a signatory,
including climate, environmental, and human rights agreements;

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Trade and Foreign Investment Policy --- Reviewed: 2011 --- Version: 20 May 2026

2

<!-- page 3 -->

1.3.3.

Environmental standards, ecologically sustainable practices, and the need to
reduce our global ecological footprint, including the need for developed
countries to reduce consumption;

1.3.4.

The need for mechanisms to reduce the importation of products that have a
heavy environmental impact through their lifecycle (e.g., border pricing relating
to embodied greenhouse gas emissions, disposal, or resource recovery costs)
and to prioritise circular economic activity;

1.3.5.

Human rights and labour standards;

1.3.6.

Indigenous cultural values, including the right of tangata whenua to protect
themselves and their taonga from trade- and investment-related exploitation;

1.3.7.

Animal rights and welfare;

1.3.8.

The importance of food sovereignty and food security, which includes the right
of all communities to have secure access to food and water, to prioritise growing
and producing their own food, and the wellbeing of small-scale organic and
regenerative food producers in emerging economies. This includes Māori food
sovereignty;

1.3.9.

The rights of peoples and governments over those of financial or corporate
investors;

1.3.10.

Global inequity, including by providing an appropriate means of exchange, such
that transaction costs no longer skew the value of goods and services to the
detriment of the countries with emerging economies; and

1.3.11.

Democratic principles embraced by all parties.

1.4.

Ensure all new international trade agreements are open to public scrutiny, including
by:
1.4.1.

1.5.

Advocate for a fair international intellectual property rights regime that includes:
1.5.1.

Guaranteed access to essential medicines by, for example, enabling generic
production of life-saving drugs; and

1.5.2.

Protection of indigenous knowledge and biodiversity from exploitation by, for
example, requiring disclosure of its use in patent applications.

Trade and Ecological Sustainability

Issues
The current regime of global trade compromises the health of our natural world. Prioritising
economic growth and efficiency over environmental safeguards increases resource extraction,
displaces pollution, and accelerates biodiversity loss.

Actions
2.1.

Advocate for multinational environmental agreements to take precedence over
international trade rules and trade agreements.

2.2.

Advocate for and collaborate in the development of international environmental
impact standards and certification processes for products and services

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Trade and Foreign Investment Policy --- Reviewed: 2011 --- Version: 20 May 2026

3

<!-- page 4 -->

2.3.

Regulate trade with Aotearoa New Zealand in goods that have a significant impact on
wellbeing and sustainability, including:
2.3.1.

Restricting or prohibiting imported products and services that fail to meet
international environmental impact standards;

2.3.2.

Requiring environmental impact labelling for internationally traded goods, with
regard to both contents and country of origin;

2.3.3.

Prohibiting the export of low-quality waste for recycling, and requiring any
exports of high-quality materials to be to certified, highly efficient overseas
systems;

2.3.4.

Prohibiting the export of hazardous wastes except for recycling, reprocessing,
or safe storage, and requiring this to be tracked;

2.3.5.

Prohibiting the trade of biofuels or biomass for energy;

2.3.6.

Implementing the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of
Wild Fauna and Flora;

2.3.7.

Prohibiting trade in unsustainable or illegal wild harvests, such as tropical
hardwoods;

2.3.8.

Prohibiting trade in viable genetically modified organisms, including seeds,
except under strict biosecurity controls

2.3.9.

Requiring imported mined materials to be ethically and sustainably sourced;

2.3.10.

Ending the import and export of coal and phasing out all other fossil fuel imports;

2.3.11.

Prohibiting the import of new and used combustion vehicles, with limited
exceptions.

2.3.12.

Limiting the trade of live animals for breeding and animal products to countries
that have equivalent standards of animal welfare and prohibiting the import and
export of live animals for slaughter.

2.3.13.

Prohibiting the importation of goods made or produced by forced, compulsory,
or child labour, as defined by the International Labour Organisation.

2.3.14.

Opposing deregulation of trade in public goods, services and utilities (e.g. health,
education, water, electricity, telecommunications)

2.3.15.

Rolling back commitments to liberalise trade under the World Trade
Organisation’ General Agreement on Trade and Services treaty, as needed to
achieve the above

2.4.

Reorient domestic trade strategies towards sustainable and fair production and
distribution and encouraging international trading corporations to be good corporate
citizens, pay fair taxes, safeguard the environment, and employ sound labour
practices, including by:
2.4.1.

Prioritising value-based export measures and targets over those based on
quantity or volume.

2.4.2.

Discouraging the long-distance transportation of equivalent goods in opposite
directions.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Trade and Foreign Investment Policy --- Reviewed: 2011 --- Version: 20 May 2026

4

<!-- page 5 -->

2.5.

2.4.3.

Retaining or imposing tariffs, quotas or bans where useful to prevent unfair
competition caused by unjust or unsustainable production practices in the
country of origin.

2.4.4.

Placing a carbon tax on energy-intensive imports from OECD countries that
have not adopted binding greenhouse gas emission reduction targets consistent
with our global obligation to restrict global warming to within 1.5°C of preindustrial levels with no overshoot.

Curb import spending, when urgently needed, by:
2.5.1.

3.

Imposing temporary across-the-board tariffs, where they align with the values
and principles of this policy

Foreign Investment in Aotearoa New Zealand

Issues
Foreign investment, especially when it is directly into businesses, assets, or projects in Aotearoa
New Zealand, while offering economic opportunities, also presents economic and democratic
risks. A foreign investor or multinational company could transfer profits out of the country,
thereby draining foreign exchange, reducing the funds available for local reinvestment, and
limiting the domestic benefits of foreign investment. Foreign ownership of assets, such as land
and infrastructure, erodes the national benefit from and influence over those assets, risking
decisions that ignore domestic priorities and democratic decision-making that reflects the
economic influence of foreign vested interests. These risks must be mitigated.

Action
3.1.

3.2.

Ensure that foreign investment in Aotearoa New Zealand is ethical, appropriate, and
supports sustainability, by:
3.1.1.

Strengthening controls on speculative and other non-productive foreign
investment (e.g. land banking) to minimise its negative effects

3.1.2.

Prioritising investment into sustainable enterprises;

3.1.3.

Strengthening the approval criteria to consistently limit profit repatriation,
protect the rights of tangata whenua, support community sovereignty, protect
ecosystems, and support a stable climate

3.1.4.

Requiring international businesses conducting significant operations here to
establish local subsidiaries that are incorporated within Aotearoa New Zealand
or otherwise create a local ownership stake in their activities;

3.1.5.

Reserving land ownership for Aotearoa New Zealand citizens and permanent
residents;

3.1.6.

Applying the national interest test to all foreign investment proposals

3.1.7.

Reducing the threshold for oversight and review of approved investments where
the purchasing entity is 10% or more foreign-owned

Advocate for an international charter of responsibilities for overseas investors.

# Waste and Hazardous Substances (Green Party policy document)

<!-- page 1 -->

Waste and Hazardous Substances
Policy
This policy seeks to transform all sectors of the Aotearoa New Zealand economy into a circular
economy in which the production of unnecessary waste and hazardous substances is eliminated
and, where this is not possible, they are effectively managed through reuse and recycling, safely,
effectively, and responsibly, to ensure the wellbeing of current and future generations.

Vision
All activities eliminate waste, circulate resources, and regenerate nature.

Values and Principles
- Honour Te Tiriti o Waitangi: Tangata whenua have primary decision-making power over
the elimination and reduction of waste and hazardous substances production, as well as
their management and disposal, and all decisions in this area show respect to the taonga
of te taiao.

- Ecological Wisdom: Material growth should be limited, such that waste production is
avoided or redirected for use in a circular economy.

- Social Responsibility: The management of waste and hazardous substances should not
further disadvantage or burden marginalised groups within or outside Aotearoa New
Zealand.

- Appropriate Decision-Making: Decisions regarding the management of waste should be
based on mātauranga Māori and western science, and determined in partnership with
whānau, hapū and iwi.

- Non-Violence: A precautionary approach to hazardous material should be taken to ensure
that no person, ecological environment or native species is harmed by the production,
management or disposal of hazardous materials.

Strategic Priorities
The Green Party’s strategic goals include:
“Our nation will be in transition to a zero waste economy, where single use plastics are
largely eliminated, wasteful consumption is ended, and all-of-lifecycle product
stewardship is in place across the economy.”

Actions in this policy that will help achieve this include:
- Establishing a Tiriti-based national circular economy strategy that sets out a clear
pathway for the phasing out of landfills (1.2.3)

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Waste and Hazardous Substances Policy — Reviewed: 2022 — Version: 17 December 2025

1

<!-- page 2 -->

- Promoting thoughtful and moderated consumption and restricting advertising that
promotes hyperconsumption (1.5.2)

- Resourcing the implementation of zero-waste strategies and associated legislation (1.2.1)

- Prohibiting most single-use plastic products and non-recyclable and non-homecompostable packaging, with necessary exceptions (2.2.1)

- Developing a national resource recovery network that resources existing local solutions
and replicates them in other areas (2.4.1)

- Requiring all products that include plastics and rare earth metals to be readily recyclable
(2.5.1)

- Leading international efforts to clean up plastic and other harmful waste from the Pacific
Ocean (2.9.5)

Connected Policies
Waste management is one role of the Government in the Economy and part of protecting
Biodiversity and Environmental Regeneration, Freshwater, Land Use and Soils, and Marine
ecosystems. See also our policies on waste minimisation in Agriculture, Health, Housing and
Sustainable Communities, and Business, and the use of waste for Energy and Trade.

Policy Positions
1. Towards A Circular Economy
Issues
Aotearoa New Zealand currently has a linear economic structure, where the production of waste
and the end life of products are often not considered when making decisions about production,
distribution, and use. This leads to an excessive focus on the extraction of new resources rather
than the repair of products and the reuse of already available resources. It generates waste that
could have been avoided, and inappropriate management and disposal of waste products.
Redefining “waste” and moving towards a circular economy and closed-loop systems can create
jobs and reduce our impacts on nature.

Actions
1.1.

Ensure that decision-making and operational arrangements enable a Tiriti-based, just
transition to a circular economy1, by:
1.1.1.

Resourcing the implementation of zero-waste strategies and associated
legislation;

1.1.2.

Establishing a Tiriti-based coordinating agency with a circular economy and
zero-waste focus; and

1

A circular economy is designed to keep materials in use and eliminate waste to landfill, guided by lifecycle and end-of-life analysis, so that products are either repaired, reused, sustainably recycled, or
composted.
Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Waste and Hazardous Substances Policy — Reviewed: 2022 — Version: 17 December 2025

2

<!-- page 3 -->

1.1.3.
1.2.

1.3.

1.4.

1.5.

2.

Establishing a Tiriti-based national circular economy strategy that sets out a
clear pathway for the phasing out of landfills.

Affirm the tino rangatiratanga of iwi, hapū, and whānau in:
1.2.1.

Decisions regarding waste elimination, management and disposal; and

1.2.2.

Their role as kaitiaki, including in their efforts to protect sites such as customary
food gathering areas and wāhi tapu from the negative impacts of pollution.

Legislate to increase circular economic practices, including:
1.3.1.

Expanding product stewardship requirements to all products with a significant
resource- and/or waste-related impact, including solar panels and batteries;

1.3.2.

Requiring and supporting key sectors to work within a zero-waste, circular
economy model, including food waste, health, construction, fishing, and textiles;
and

1.3.3.

Requiring companies to communicate to investors how, through their circular
economy activities, they can provide a return on investment.

Support research and development that enables a transition to a circular economy,
by:
1.4.1.

Promoting innovation and investment in resource efficiency, reuse and recovery;

1.4.2.

Provide business and organisational support for innovative circular economy
and zero waste businesses;

1.4.3.

Gathering accurate information on the volume, composition, management, and
disposal of waste and hazardous substances in New Zealand; and

1.4.4.

Increasing assessments of chemicals that are used in land and water
ecosystems (e.g. biocides), to ensure their safety for human use, and preventing
their use until such assessments have been undertaken.

Facilitate community-led circular economy initiatives and a zero-waste-to-landfill
cultural shift, including by:
1.5.1.

Resource Māori organisations working to support a circular economy, including
kaupapa Māori-based zero waste initiatives such as Para Kore;

1.5.2.

Promoting thoughtful and moderated consumption and restricting advertising
that promotes hyperconsumption; and

1.5.3.

Increase awareness of the role of waste management in climate change
mitigation, including the contributions of different sectors.

Waste Streams

Issues
Resource recovery is often seen as inefficient, with recyclable or reusable products and materials
sent to landfill due to cost and difficulties associated with more appropriate streaming. Waste is
not yet treated as a valuable resource for use in a circular economy.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Waste and Hazardous Substances Policy — Reviewed: 2022 — Version: 17 December 2025

Actions
2.1.

2.2.

2.3.

2.4.

Ensure that the management and disposal of waste and hazardous substances
protect ecosystems, including:
2.1.1.

Treating land, soil, and water as taonga and protecting them from the discharge
or inappropriate storage of waste and hazardous products;

2.1.2.

Protecting wild foods in terrestrial, freshwater, and marine environments from

2.1.3.

Minimise the use of inherently polluting substances at the production and import

Maximise the useful life of purchased products by:

Establishing quality, efficiency, and recycling standards for all products entering
or made in Aotearoa New Zealand;

2.3.2.

Prohibiting planned obsolescence;

2.3.3.

Legislating a right to repair;

2.3.4.

Requiring manufacturers of goods sold in Aotearoa to make replacement parts,

2.3.5.

Funding community-based repair services.

Redirect waste streams for reuse and repurposing wherever possible across the
economy, including by:

Developing a national resource recovery network that resources existing local

2.4.2.

Providing rural communities with local composting, repair, and reuse facilities
and ensuring access to centralised or mobile waste collection services;

2.4.3.

Expanding refill systems for safely collecting and reusing containers; and

2.4.4.

Enabling EV batteries to be repurposed as energy storage devices.

Authorised by Miriam Ross, Level 5, 108 The Terrace, Wellington
Waste and Hazardous Substances Policy — Reviewed: 2022 — Version: 17 December 2025

2.5.

2.6.

2.7.

2.8.

Maximise the recycling and composting of materials that cannot be reused, including
by:
2.5.1.

Requiring all products that include plastics and rare earth metals to be readily
recyclable;

2.5.2.

Providing residential and commercial composting facilities and services for

2.5.3.

Requiring clear product labelling using common standards for “compostable”

2.5.4.

Enabling and encouraging the use of composting toilets, where practicable;

Ensure that communities exposed to hazardous substances:

Are fully involved in the investigation and reporting of any health, community,

Receive appropriate treatment and compensation.

Manage the legacy of stored waste and hazardous substances by:

2.9.

Take responsibility for the impact of Aotearoa New Zealand’s waste on other countries

Participating in and supporting a strong global plastics treaty;

Prohibiting the export of low-quality waste for recycling, and requiring any

Policy announcement

# Affordable food for all of us. Reforming the food system.

Read our policy

Our policy will reform the food system so that everyone has easy and affordable access to good, nutritious kai.

[View our policy](affordable_food_full_policy)

The price of groceries

Food should be affordable for everyone. But do you know how much grocery staples have gone up in the last 10 years?

[Find out here](https://www.greens.org.nz/how_much_is_butter)

Stay in the know

Stay up to date with our latest policy announcements.

[Sign up now](https://www.greens.org.nz/sign_up)

Please allow a moment for this embedded form to load.

Please allow a moment for this to load.

## The Problem

We’re a nation of 5 million people, producing enough to feed 40 million people. Our food system could ensure that every New Zealander has access to affordable and nutritious kai.

Despite this, one in five children live in households that run out of food, food costs have increased by 29% over the last five years, and demand for food banks and emergency food grants is the highest it has been at any time, except during the pandemic.

Two big supermarket chains exploit their market power to prioritise their exorbitant profits, often for their overseas shareholders, crushing our farmers and growers at one end, and ripping off the rest of us at the other.

Only the two big corporate giants – and their shareholders – are winning in this system.

The lack of competition means growers and producers have few options but to accept rock-bottom prices and conditions, risking their commercial viability and stripping the country of farming and horticulture resilience and expertise.

This model is structured to leave people hungry, growers operating on the edge of viability, and competitors unviable, while delivering massive profits to two enormous corporations. The current system is harming our health and our bank balances and is undermining our national food independence.

**Our plan will reform the food system to give all of us lower prices, more choice, and greater security.**

> Our country produces enough food to feed 40 million people. There is no shortage of food in Aotearoa, but it's somehow becoming too expensive for too many New Zealanders.

— Chlöe Swarbrick

## Our Solution

Break up the duopoly and create competition with KiwiMart

Require Woolworths and Foodstuffs to divest at least 120 stores and distribution centre capacity into public ownership.

Create KiwiMart, a publicly owned supermarket chain with a single mandate - keep prices down.

Protect people from unfair pricing in supermarkets and other sectors

Immediately ban excessive supermarket prices.

Require supermarkets to be transparent about their price margins.

Extend the ban on price gouging to other uncompetitive sectors, including energy and fuel.

Empower the Commerce Commission to enforce the rules

Introduce a mandatory supermarket pricing accuracy code, including automatic compensation requirements when shoppers are overcharged.

Increase funding for the Commerce Commission, increase fines, and empower the Commission to issue binding directions.

Empower the Commerce Commission to regulate loyalty schemes and store brands, strengthen rules on incorrect pricing, and give consumers control over their shopping data.

Create a National Food Strategy for the whole food system

Introduce a National Food Strategy in collaboration with producers, distributors, public health experts, Māori, and the community food sector.

Prioritise local food in public procurement.

Ensure that food regulations are proportionate to scale.

Establish a legislative right to adequate and nutritious food.

Require large food distributors to reduce or donate surplus food.

Support community food security so no one goes hungry

Establish a $150m Fair Food Fund to expand community-led food security initiatives.

Increase funding for food banks from $8m to $25m and double the cap on food grants from Work and Income.

Provide better lunches for more children through Ka Ora, Ka Ako

Restore the Ka Ora, Ka Ako programme so nutritious lunches are provided through schools and local providers.

Fund the programme permanently to provide certainty for schools, whānau and local providers.

Expand the programme to around 400 more schools, ensuring 150,000 more children enjoy a nutritious lunch every day.

Click here to read the full policy

[View our policy](affordable_food_full_policy)

[View the Full Policy](https://assets.nationbuilder.com/beachheroes/pages/65102/attachments/original/1778624623/Policy-Greens_Agriculture_Policy_2025-2026.pdf)

## Summary

The Green Party will support all parts of the agricultural sector to look after our environment so that it sustains our communities and builds our resilience to multiple impacts, including climate and market instability. This policy shows that everyone in Aotearoa New Zealand can eat good food that is more affordable for our local consumers and gets a fair price for our food and fibre producers. Our sustainable agricultural practices will create products that are in high demand globally. Farmers will be supported to keep innovating and improving, and good data collection will ensure that agencies provide real-time feedback to inform that progress.

OUR VISION

> The agricultural sector upholds the mana of the land, people, and animals.

## Values and Principles

Agriculture policy must be guided by the following values and principles:

##### Kawanatanga:

Governance of the agricultural sector recognises the unique expertise and rights of Māori. Māori participation in shaping the future of agriculture is equitable.

##### Tiakina te taiao, tiakina te iwi e:

The agricultural sector protects our diverse ecosystems to sustain our communities using a precautionary approach for future generations. Mātauranga Māori guides our agricultural practices and environmental standards.

##### Ka mua, ka muri:

The agricultural sector recognises its impact on climate change and commits to reduced emissions.

##### Te Rāngai aumangea:

The agricultural sector is supported to adapt to a changing environment, including the land and weather patterns.

##### Te Rāngai tōnui:

The agricultural sector is supported to be financially viable. This viability includes ecological health and egalitarian human systems.

##### Tauutuutu:

Agriculture depends on relationships. Where these relationships have been undermined or damaged, they must be repaired.

##### Tiaki kararehe:

Farm animals are sentient beings deserving of our care and protection.

## Strategic Priorities

The Green Party’s strategic goals include:
“...regenerative practices in all areas of economic activity, including land use and food production, will predominate.”
Actions in this policy that will help achieve this include:

- Implement the recommendations of the Waitangi Tribunal to ensure that governance of the agricultural sector upholds Te Tiriti o Waitangi. (1.2)
- Establish an Agricultural Standards Framework that includes… sustainability standards for all food and fibre sectors. (2.1.3)
- Incentivise low greenhouse gas agricultural initiatives. (3.3)

- Strengthen the collective resilience of grassroots community collaborations, such as local catchment groups. (4.4)
- Provide startup funding for innovative systems and/or new food and fibre trials. (5.1)
- Resource a Māori-led authority that oversees the distribution of start-up funding to Māori agricultural initiatives that are locally led and sustainable. (6.3)

Full Policy Link

[View the Full Policy](https://assets.nationbuilder.com/beachheroes/pages/65102/attachments/original/1778624623/Policy-Greens_Agriculture_Policy_2025-2026.pdf)

## Connected Policies

Agriculture is an important [Business](https://www.greens.org.nz/sustainable_business_policy) and [Food](https://www.greens.org.nz/food_policy)-producing activity that is shaped by the [Government in the Economy](https://www.greens.org.nz/government_in_the_economy_policy). It is important for [Rural Communities](https://www.greens.org.nz/rural_communities_policy), [Animal Welfare](https://www.greens.org.nz/animal_welfare_policy), and [Trade and Foreign Investmen](https://www.greens.org.nz/trade_and_foreign_investment_policy)t. It is interconnected with and key to safeguarding the natural world, including [Climate Change](https://www.greens.org.nz/climate_change_policy), [Land Use and Soils](https://www.greens.org.nz/land_use_and_soils_policy), and [Freshwater](https://www.greens.org.nz/freshwater_policy). A range of risks, including exotic organisms and emerging technologies, are addressed in our [Biodiversity and Environmental Regeneration Policy](https://www.greens.org.nz/biodiversity_environmental_regeneration_policy), and [Research, Science and Technology Policy](https://www.greens.org.nz/research_science_and_technology_policy). Also related are our policies on [Forestry](https://www.greens.org.nz/forestry_policy) and [Marine](https://www.greens.org.nz/marine_policy) aquaculture.

# Animal Welfare Policy

[View our Priorities](https://www.greens.org.nz/animal_welfare_policy#animal_welfare_policy_strategic_priorities)
[View the Full Policy](https://assets.nationbuilder.com/beachheroes/pages/64486/attachments/original/1778624593/Policy-Greens_Animal_Welfare_2025-2026.pdf)

## Summary

The Green Party will align regulation with animals’ rights to good nutrition, environment, health, behaviour, and mental state, and provide strong oversight and accountability. We will minimise the systemic exploitation of animals and require an ethical and humane approach to managing animals. We will carefully balance the needs of indigenous species and introduced animals, and uphold the Kaitiaki role and whakapapa connections of Māori to animals.

OUR VISION

> All animals are respected and their rights are upheld.

## Values and Principles

Decisions relating to animal welfare should uphold the following values and principles:

##### Aroha:

All living things possess an inherent dignity and mauri. Animals are due respect, love, and rights. Humans have a duty of care towards the animals they interact with. They should not be violated or exploited, and their distress and pain should be minimised.

##### Whanaungatanga:

All living things are interconnected. We should live in reciprocal relationships with animals. The deep, ancestral connection Māori have with the land and its inhabitants must be respected.

##### Tikanga:

Societal systems, cultural practices, and traditional knowledge shape and are shaped by our relationship with animals. Engagement with companion animals is a privilege, not a right.

##### Kaitiakitanga:

Humans must interact with other animals in ways that support resilience and ecosystem health. Indigenous species and ecosystems are essential for maintaining supporting ecological balance so [they] must be paramount, with their interests prioritised over invasive species.

##### Mōhiotanga:

Humans have an ethical obligation to make informed decisions on behalf of animals, drawing on the best available knowledge of their needs and behaviours. Tikanga and mātauranga Māori must be upheld alongside the evolutionary history and ecology of animals.

## Strategic Priorities

The Green Party’s strategic goals include:
“Our laws and practices will respect the biological integrity of all life, while prioritising the health of indigenous species and ecosystems.”
Actions in this policy that work towards this goal include:

- Establish a Department of Animal Welfare, led by a Minister for Animal Welfare, with responsibility for legislation, enforcement, hosting the NAWAC and NAEAC, and advocating for the welfare of all animals. (1.5)
- Require people who breed companion animals for sale, and rescue centres, to register and hold a current license. (2.1)

- Develop local regulations around pet ownership to cater for the indigenous species residing in that locale, such as requiring catios to keep cats safe and protect local biodiversity. (5.1)
- Introduce national standards for desexing dogs and for registering, desexing, and microchipping cats. (5.3)

Full Policy Link

[View the Full Policy](https://assets.nationbuilder.com/beachheroes/pages/64486/attachments/original/1778624593/Policy-Greens_Animal_Welfare_2025-2026.pdf)

## Connected Policies

Other policies contribute to our vision for animal welfare.

- [Agriculture Policy](https://www.greens.org.nz/agriculture_and_rural_affairs_policy): The agricultural sector consistently uses an ethical and humane approach to managing animals. Our approach is world-leading, and animals enjoy a good life, with their death managed as humanely as possible. The need for prosecution is rare.
- [Trade and Foreign Investment Policy](https://www.greens.org.nz/trade_and_foreign_investment_policy): Live animal imports and exports are rare, have strong protections, and only occur where there is benefit to the animal or their species.
- [Research, Science and Technology Policy](https://www.greens.org.nz/research_science_and_technology_policy): Animal testing only occurs rarely, transparently, and has tangible benefits to people or animals.

- [Recreation and Sport Policy](https://www.greens.org.nz/recreation_and_sports_policy): Recreational activities that cause unnecessary distress or pain to animals or normalise cruelty are prohibited.
- [Biodiversity and Environmental Regeneration Policy](https://www.greens.org.nz/biodiversity_environmental_regeneration_policy): Invasive species are managed using humane and effective methods, so that indigenous species can flourish.
- [Marine Policy](https://www.greens.org.nz/marine_policy): Fisheries and aquaculture are sustainably managed.

# Arts, Culture and Heritage Policy

[View our Priorities](https://www.greens.org.nz/arts_culture_and_heritage_policy#arts_culture_and_heritage_policy_strategic_priorities)
[View the Full Policy](https://assets.nationbuilder.com/beachheroes/pages/64500/attachments/original/1781650645/Policy-Greens_Arts_Culture_Heritage_Policy_2014-2026.pdf?1781650645)

## Summary

The Green Party will support the arts and cultural heritage sector to develop to its highest standard and be properly resourced. A Green government will collaborate with funders, the industry, and other stakeholders, including tangata whenua, who have the right to protect traditional and contemporary Māori art. We will nurture talent in our communities by providing educational opportunities in schools and communities and by expanding platforms for arts and cultural heritage.

OUR VISION

> Creative, cultural and heritage work is integrated within our communities in myriad innovative ways that empower people, spread happiness, and encourage intercultural appreciation and understanding.

## Values and Principles

Decisions relating to arts, culture, and heritage should uphold the following values and principles:

##### Honour Te Tiriti o Waitangi:

Revitalising and celebrating toi Māori, tikanga Māori and te reo Māori is key to ensuring a thriving arts industry. The Crown has a responsibility to ensure the protection and return of taonga, including Māori arts, culture, intellectual property and heritage sites. The Crown must support and contribute to but not determine the revitalisation of toi Māori, tikanga Māori and te reo Māori.

##### Ecological Wisdom:

The arts play a part in enabling the transition to a life-sustaining society by changing hearts and minds. Mātauranga Māori, as expressed through art and cultural practice, is inextricably linked to the natural world.

##### Appropriate Decision-Making:

Those involved in arts and cultural heritage work must be involved in developing guidelines for funding. Local communities must be given the ability to protect places, buildings and heritage collections that are important to them historically and culturally. The tino rangatiratanga of hapū and iwi over their taonga must be affirmed, through Matike Mai mechanisms.

##### Social Responsibility:

The arts foster community and improve our daily well-being, empathy, equality and cultural diversity, as well as contributing economically.

##### Non-Violence:

All art forms practised and recognised in Aotearoa New Zealand are included in this policy and their interconnectedness is acknowledged. The art forms of marginalised cultures and groups should be equitably supported.

##### Resilience:

Arts, culture and heritage are essential social infrastructure, not luxuries. The Government should help build their resilience in our communities and at professional levels.

##### Professional:

A vibrant and diverse professional arts sector contributes to all our lives, as well as the identity of Aotearoa New Zealand on the international stage.

## Strategic Priorities

The Green Party’s strategic goals include:
“People will be part of caring communities with a strong heritage fabric”
Actions in this policy that will help achieve this include:

- Ensure cultural heritage infrastructure and funding provisions are sufficient to increase participation in community arts, provide arts and cultural heritage education, and support the professional arts to reach the highest standard. (1.2)
- Support and contribute to the revitalisation of toi Māori (2.1)

- Develop and resource the implementation of an ongoing arts education strategy from early childhood to tertiary level. (3.3.1)
- Developing a network of Art Spaces and heritage equivalents in every community that are accessible to all cultures and levels of ability, including programmes in prisons, and care and refuge spaces. (3.11)

Full Policy Link

[View the Full Policy](https://assets.nationbuilder.com/beachheroes/pages/64500/attachments/original/1781650645/Policy-Greens_Arts_Culture_Heritage_Policy_2014-2026.pdf?1781650645)

## Connected Policies

Providing platforms through [Media](https://www.greens.org.nz/broadcasting_policy) to celebrate the arts is important for arts, culture and heritage to thrive. Ensuring sufficient income for those working in the arts, cultural and heritage sectors is part of our [Livelihoods](https://www.greens.org.nz/household_livelihoods_policy) and [Workforce](https://www.greens.org.nz/workforce_policy) Policies. The Crown’s responsibility to ensure the protection and revitalisation of natural and other taonga is explored in our [Biodiversity and Environmental Regeneration](https://www.greens.org.nz/biodiversity_environmental_regeneration_policy) Policy.

# Biodiversity and Environmental Regeneration Policy

[View our Priorities](https://www.greens.org.nz/biodiversity_environmental_regeneration_policy#biodiversity_environmental_regeneration_policy_strategic_priorities)
[View the Full Policy](https://assets.nationbuilder.com/beachheroes/pages/64514/attachments/original/1778624595/Policy-Greens_Biodiversity_Environmental_Regenration_Policy_2025-2026.pdf)

## Summary

In Government, the Green Party will take a holistic approach to conservation. We will make sure Aotearoa New Zealand plays a leading part in protecting the biodiversity of planet Earth from the global mass extinction that is currently underway. We will protect threatened indigenous species from invasive species, diseases, and human activity, and support the kaitiaki role and indigenous knowledge of tangata whenua.

OUR VISION

> Indigenous biodiversity thrives and there is a healthy relationship between people and te taiao | the environment.

## Values and Principles

Policy decisions relating to biodiversity regeneration must be consistent with the following values and principles:

##### Honour Te Tiriti o Waitangi:

Regenerative efforts must recognise the kaitiaki role of tangata whenua and the insight that mātauranga Māori brings.

##### Ecological Wisdom:

Regenerative efforts must recognise the inherent value of nature, and work within its complex dynamics. We must actively safeguard and regenerate indigenous ecosystems, Ki uta ki tai | from the mountains to the sea.

##### Social Responsibility:

Regenerative efforts must ensure future generations will inherit a healthy environment, which is achieved alongside progress on social issues.

##### Non-Violence:

Regenerative efforts must cause minimal harm whilst preventing the harm caused by inaction.

##### Appropriate Decision-Making:

Regenerative efforts must be adaptable, evidence-based, and effective. Decision-making must be distributed equitably, engage with local communities, and achieve co-benefits.

##### Interconnectedness:

Regenerative efforts must recognise that humans are interdependent with other species. Our survival requires a functional biosphere as we are part of the circle of life and share a common descent and whakapapa.

## Strategic Priorities

The Green Party’s strategic goals include:
“Human interaction with the rest of the natural world needs to be based on the principles of ecological sustainability and circularity, underpinned by mātauranga Māori, and giving life to our international commitments on indigenous knowledge and rights.”
“All native species and their habitats will be thriving or on a path to recovery in terrestrial, freshwater, and marine environments.
Our laws and practices will respect the biological integrity of all life, while prioritising the health of indigenous species and ecosystems.
The customary and decision making roles of whānau, hapū, and iwi will be integral to decisions about resource use."
Actions in this policy that work towards these goals include:

- Establishing a job guarantee programme focused on understanding, protecting, and regenerating ecosystems. (2.1.1)
- Broadening legal protections and conservation strategies to cover indigenous fish, plants, invertebrates, and fungi to recognise the importance of taxonomic diversity. (3.1.2)
- Investigating appropriate regulation that limits or suspends the harvesting of vulnerable aquatic species, such as whitebait, to ensure populations regenerate. (3.1.3)

- Significantly increasing resourcing for bodies that eradicate and control invasive species and weeds, prioritising the eradication of invasive species identified in Predator Free 2050 and other species with disproportionate effects on indigenous ecosystems. (3.2.3)
- Taking a collaborative, Tiriti-based approach to Government-led conservation, such as co-governance and co-management (4.2.3)
- Establishing a Sovereign Biodiversity Fund to resource regenerative efforts. (2.1.3)

Full Policy Link

[View the Full Policy](https://assets.nationbuilder.com/beachheroes/pages/64514/attachments/original/1778624595/Policy-Greens_Biodiversity_Environmental_Regenration_Policy_2025-2026.pdf)

## Connected Policies

See also our specific policies for the protection and regeneration of [Land](https://www.greens.org.nz/land_use_and_soils_policy), [Freshwater,](https://www.greens.org.nz/freshwater_policy) and [Marine](https://www.greens.org.nz/marine_policy) ecosystems, and our policies relating to:

- Establishing legal rights of nature and recognising the legal status of Papatūānuku ([Governance Policy](https://www.greens.org.nz/governance_policy)) and a right to a healthy environment ([Human Rights Policy](https://www.greens.org.nz/human_rights_policy))
- Ensuring economic activities uphold the wellbeing of the natural world ([Government in the Economy](https://www.greens.org.nz/government_in_the_economy_policy), [Business](https://www.greens.org.nz/sustainable_business_policy), and specific sectors, e.g. [Agriculture](https://www.greens.org.nz/agriculture_and_rural_affairs_policy), [Tourism](https://www.greens.org.nz/tourism_policy), [Forestry](https://www.greens.org.nz/forestry_policy))
- Minimising the further loss of indigenous ecosystems to other land uses ([Land Use and Soils Policy](https://www.greens.org.nz/land_use_and_soils_policy))
- Adapting urban design to support environmental growth ([Housing and Sustainable Communities Policy](https://www.greens.org.nz/housing_policy))
- Collaborating with other countries, including strengthening international treaties ([Global Affairs Policy](https://www.greens.org.nz/global_affairs_policy)) and leveraging trade agreements ([Trade and Foreign Investment Policy](https://www.greens.org.nz/trade_and_foreign_investment_policy))
- Aligning ‘carbon farming’ with ecological resilience ([Climate Change Policy](https://www.greens.org.nz/climate_change_policy))
